plugins.name: Survey Engine
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Leave it running and come back to a list of what is transmitting near you.
plugins.description:
A waterfall tells you whether something is on a frequency while you are watching it. This answers the other question - what is around you at all - which needs days rather than minutes and therefore needs nobody sitting there. Point it at a band, leave it on a machine that is on anyway, and come back to the frequencies that were actually used, how wide they were, how strong they got, and what fraction of the visits they were present for.

It reads the whole receiver bandwidth at once rather than one channel at a time, so a 2 MHz slice is surveyed per dwell, and it steps across the band on its own. Stepping needs the 'allow tuning' permission on its row - a plugin cannot grant itself the VFO - and without it the survey still works perfectly well on whatever you have tuned, and says so rather than appearing broken.

Findings go to survey.csv beside its configuration, rewritten every dwell so it is always current, and read back at startup so a survey resumes across a restart instead of being erased by one.

ADDED IN 0.2.0, from settings or a survey.cfg file, with the defaults unchanged from 0.1.x: FFT size, window shape, edge crop, receiver gain (needs the 'radio settings' permission) and a ppm correction, which is taken off the frequencies it reports because FoxSDR has no call to retune for ppm; several bands in one run; peak-hold and minimum-hold traces; and a time-on-air percentage per channel with an hour-of-day record, if you ask for sub-dwells. Keys on its panel save a baseline of what is normally there, and later runs raise a status line, a log warning and a spectrum marker for a signal not in it. A limit file can mark a frequency range that rises too far above the noise or above a level, and the panel shows pass or fail. It can also draw a sweep heat map as a picture, where a click tunes to that frequency (needs the 'allow tuning' permission), and write an rtl_power-style CSV, an occupancy CSV and a PNG of the heat map; those three files are off until you ask for them.

LIMITS OF THE NEW FEATURES. A mask breach is shown as a marker and a panel row; it cannot record I/Q, and FoxSDR cannot draw a horizontal limit line. The picture window, click-to-tune and the extra panel columns have not been tried in the full application, and a host may choose to show the new picture decoder instead of the decoder output.

WHAT IT WILL NOT TELL YOU. It does not know who is transmitting; no power spectrum does. The guess column is derived from the occupied bandwidth alone and always carries a question mark - 'NFM?' means 'about 12 kHz wide, which is what narrowband FM looks like', not 'this is narrowband FM', and never 'this is the local taxi firm'. A band name is shown where one is known, from an editable file of ITU allocations that ships with sections for all three regions; naming the actual operator of a channel needs a licence register, which is somebody else's compiled work and not ours to ship. If you have one, paste its rows into that file and it stays on your machine.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.2.1: A band with an absurdly large stop frequency (for example 1e308) no longer refuses the whole survey on some processors (the heat map column count overflowed). 0.2.0: Adds settings for FFT size, window, crop, gain and ppm, several bands in one run, peak and min-hold traces, new-signal alerts against a saved baseline, duty-cycle figures, a limit-mask check and a clickable sweep heat map. The defaults behave like 0.1.x; the picture window, clicks and extra panel columns have not been tried in the full application.

plugins.name: SSTV and KG-STV Image Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Receives slow-scan television (SSTV) pictures and, experimentally, KG-STV pictures and short texts from audio, on HF and 2 m.
plugins.description:
Decodes slow-scan television - amateur pictures sent as audio over SSB - and builds the image on screen line by line as it arrives. The mode is identified automatically from the transmission's own VIS header, so there is nothing to select unless you want to: Martin M1 and M2, Scottie S1, S2 and DX, and PD50, PD90, PD120, PD160, PD180, PD240 and PD290 are all recognised.

KG-STV is one more mode, and it is EXPERIMENTAL: type KG-STV in the Force mode field and the plugin listens for pictures (320 x 240, in 16 x 16 blocks) and short texts sent with the KG-STV amateur program (1200 baud FSK or four-level FSK, with or without a convolutional code), from USB or FM audio. Pictures of both modes go to the same gallery and the same PNG saving (off until you tick it); KG-STV texts keep their own lines in the text output. Each block carries its own check, so a damaged one is refused and the neighbours survive. KG-STV is receive only and EXPERIMENTAL: its packet format and codec are taken from the open-kgstv project, which says full compatibility with the original program is not established; nothing here has seen a signal from the original program, the tests use signals made by an encoder written from the same reading, there is no automatic frequency correction, and text in the Japanese code page shows as question marks.

Tune to 14.230 MHz USB, the main international calling frequency, or use one of the plugin's own presets for the other bands. A picture takes a minute or more to arrive (the PD modes take from 50 to 289 seconds), and you will see it building rather than waiting for the end.

The receiver's clock is never quite the sender's, and that shows as a slanted picture in many decoders. This one measures the difference from the transmission's sync pulses and corrects it, reporting the offset it found in parts per million. It also follows a receiver tuned off by up to about 150 Hz and corrects for it; at 200 Hz off it no longer finds the header.

Robot 36 and Robot 72 are built but OFF until you switch on Robot 36/72 modes in the settings; with the switch off a Robot header is reported and ignored. They decode the sample recordings of both modes to a correct, unslanted picture, but the picture width of 320 is not stated in the source used. Robot 8, 12 and 24 and the black-and-white modes are not built.

The other 1.1.0 additions are also off until you turn them on: a sensitivity level, a forced mode, starting a picture without a VIS header (it needs five matching sync pulses), reading a callsign sent as an FSK ID after a picture, saving finished pictures as uncompressed PNG files, recording the audio of each picture, and a key that decodes a WAV file. There are also RESTART and a 0 to 10 sync-quality reading. The FSK ID format rests on a single secondary source and no recording carried one, so treat it as unverified. The PD modes, header-less starts with PD, and the tuning correction were tried on generated signals only; the Martin, Scottie and Robot modes were checked on real recordings. Written clean-room from published mode specifications, cross-checked against independently published line-rate figures.
plugins.whatsNew: 1.3.1: Finds the next picture after one that was cut off. A picture that began with a header was never ended when the signal stopped, so the decoder stayed in it and read the next header as picture lines: a recording played again, or a second station, gave nothing. After about six seconds with no sync pulse the picture is kept as it is and the decoder listens for a new header. Tried on generated signals. 1.3.0: Starts a picture whose header the old reader could not follow. A faded recording had a leader tone that swung by up to 220 Hz, so the start bit was never found although the VIS bits were clear; the decoder now also reads the header from its spectrum (the start tone, then the eight bits and their parity) and decodes the picture. A header it cannot read clearly, or whose parity or mode is wrong, still starts nothing. Tried on generated signals and on one real recording (a lower-sideband Scottie 1: no picture before, the whole picture now); the other real recordings decode as before. 1.2.2: Hears a picture sent on the other sideband. A transmission received on the wrong sideband arrives with every tone reflected, and the header was read as nothing; the decoder now recognises a reflected header (a steady tone followed by a start tone 700 Hz ABOVE it), turns every tone back, and says so. Tried on generated signals; a real recording of one has its header recognised but its noise stops the picture. 1.2.1: KG-STV in its 4-level mode now follows a signal that is off frequency by up to about 200 Hz (it decoded nothing 30 Hz off). 1.2.0: Adds the KG-STV mode (320 x 240 pictures and short texts, receive only, generated signals only): type KG-STV in Force mode to listen for it. Its pictures use the same gallery and the same PNG saving, which stay off until you tick them. Your SSTV settings are unchanged. 1.1.0: Adds the seven PD modes and Robot 36 and 72 (Robot is off until you switch it on), follows a receiver tuned up to about 150 Hz off, and can save finished pictures as PNG, decode a WAV file and record each picture's audio. Everything new is off by default. The PD modes were tried on generated signals only.

plugins.name: WEFAX Weather Fax Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Receives HF weather charts from the meteorological services.
plugins.description:
Draws the weather charts that national meteorological services still broadcast on shortwave for shipping - surface analyses, wind and wave forecasts, ice charts and satellite pictures - line by line as they arrive. A chart takes about ten minutes.

TUNE 1.9 kHz BELOW THE PUBLISHED FREQUENCY, in USB. That is the rule for every radiofax station in the world and it is the one thing that stops a working receiver from decoding anything at all: schedules list the assigned frequency, and the picture lives 1.9 kHz under it. The plugin's presets have the offset already applied for Hamburg/Pinneberg, Northwood and the US Coast Guard station at Boston.

The station guide opens beside the decoder before a signal is heard. It lists Northwood's and DWD Hamburg's official and USB dial frequencies, and names their station-wide weather products. The products are not assigned to individual frequencies.

Nothing has to be set. The transmission's own start tone says which index of cooperation is in use - 576 for the usual charts, 288 for the coarser ones - and the line rate is measured from the phasing signal that follows it, so 60, 90, 120 and 240 lines per minute are all read. The stop tone ends the chart, and the tone itself is trimmed off the bottom of the picture.

How far the receiver is off tune is measured from the phasing signal and reported in hertz, because a mistuned radiofax produces a picture whose shades are all wrong for no visible reason. It is reported rather than silently corrected.

It also opens an instrument window drawn as a marine facsimile recorder - phase lamps, illuminated IOC and line-rate selectors, a line counter, a centre-zero tuning meter and a paper slot with the chart feeding out of it - so you can tell within seconds whether the ten-minute chart now arriving will be worth having, with a log of the transmission's events beneath it.

The recorder has keys of its own. START NOW prints at once, without waiting for a start tone or phasing - for a chart you tuned in to late, or one whose phasing never locks - at a line rate and IOC you set (120 lines per minute and IOC 576 unless you change them). STOP NOW ends the chart where it is. SLANT -10 and +10 ppm straighten a chart that leans: + for edges that run down to the right, - for down to the left, or type the figure into the Slant box. The correction redraws the whole chart, even one already finished, and is kept for the next one, because it comes from the sound card's clock. SET LEFT EDGE, then a click on the picture, moves the chart's margin to where you clicked, which is what a chart started by hand needs. The settings boxes appear in FoxSDR 0.99.43 and later, the keys sit in the recorder's list on FoxSDR 0.99.77 or later, and the click needs 0.99.81 or later.

The slant is set by eye rather than measured: unlike SSTV and APT, radiofax carries no sync inside the picture, so there is nothing to re-anchor a drifting line clock against. SAVING (1.2.0). Tick Save finished chart (PNG) in the settings and each chart is written, when it ends, as a grey PNG with a new name every time into the folder you set (else a folder under the FoxSDR data folder). It is off by default. The file is the chart as drawn, so the slant and left edge in force at that moment are in it; a chart you re-slant afterwards is not saved again by itself. Saving was proven on generated charts and on four recorded clips run through the decoder, but not inside the FoxSDR window.

Written clean-room from published format specifications and from the meteorological services' own broadcast schedules.
plugins.whatsNew: 1.2.0: Save the finished chart as a PNG. The Save finished chart (PNG) box in the settings is off by default; when ticked every chart is written to a new file, with the slant and left edge you had set already applied.

plugins.name: Morse (CW) Decoder and Skimmer
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Reads Morse (CW) from the one note you tune to and reports the sender's speed, or, in its Skimmer view, finds and decodes every CW signal in the radio's wide I/Q at once and lists each with its speed, strength and any callsign heard.
plugins.description:
Turns received Morse into text. It reads the station you tune to the 700 Hz note - where CW mode puts a carrier on the dial frequency, and where every preset puts its station. It follows that station up to 60 Hz either way, for tuning slop and drift, but it does not search the channel for other signals: a station further off the note is not read until you tune it there. The speed and the spacing are worked out from the signal itself, and learnt again after every pause of about twenty dot lengths - a second at 25 words per minute, two at 12, about five at 5, and longer after wide word spacing, never more than six seconds - so the other station's reply at its own speed, or an operator who slows down after such a pause, is read at the new speed. Anything from about 5 to 45 words per minute is read, and up to about 50 when the key edges are sharp (3 ms or less); faster sending with softer edges prints nothing. The speed it has settled on is reported alongside the text - which is the one number that explains a poor decode. A keyer's weighting and soft key edges are allowed for; a straight key's uneven timing and a bug's long dashes are read too, the bug much less reliably: in testing, a bug with uneven spacing lost 40 to 55% of its characters. For slower sending it narrows its own filter around the note, down to about 40 Hz, which reads a weak signal that a wide filter loses in the noise.

A 3 kHz channel often holds more than one signal. A word is printed only if what produced it was keyed like Morse. In testing, twelve minutes each of RTTY, MFSK, Olivia, an FT8-like signal, MSK and fading or switched carriers on the note mostly printed nothing. The worst printed a few stray letters a minute: RTTY with one tone on the note about four, a wide Olivia signal about a dozen, and a carrier switched on and off at random about the same. 1.0.0 printed hundreds a minute. A stretch of a digital signal can still pass for Morse now and then.

Farnsworth sending, where the characters are sent fast but the gaps between them are stretched, is read as words - tested down to 18-WPM characters at 5 WPM overall, where the first word can still come out split. Decoders that assume even spacing turn it into correctly-spelled words broken into single letters.

The presets tune the CW calling frequencies of each amateur band, and one tunes SAQ Grimeton: the 1924 Alexanderson alternator in Sweden, a World Heritage site, which sends Morse on 17.2 kHz on a few occasions a year. Like the others it tunes in CW mode, on 17.2 kHz itself, so SAQ's carrier arrives as the same 700 Hz note. SAQ has to arrive on that note to be read: the older way of tuning it, 16.4 kHz in USB, puts it at 800 Hz, where this decoder prints nothing. 17.2 kHz is very low frequency (VLF): receiving it needs a radio or sound card that reaches that low, or an up-converter.

An empty band produces an empty screen rather than invented letters, which matters more than it sounds: text on screen from a dead frequency is far harder to disbelieve than nothing at all.

The code table is transcribed from ITU-R Recommendation M.1677-1 and cross-checked against an independent published table.

Since 1.2.0 the plugin's panel shows the speed and the signal-to-noise ratio (in a 2500 Hz bandwidth, kept for 20 seconds after the signal stops) and reads the text for callsigns and messages. A callsign is recognised by its shape, with /P, /M, /QRP and PREFIX/CALL forms, and counted at once after DE, CQ, TEST or QRZ, otherwise at the second sighting. No callsign list is used, so a string of the right shape is not proof of an issued callsign. The message line says whether the text is a CQ, a CQ TEST, a QRZ, an exchange, a closing or an answer, and whether the sender looks to be running or searching and pouncing. Callsigns stay in memory and on the panel only; a setting hides them from the panel. SPEED LOCK holds the dot length at a speed you choose (5 to 60 words per minute), or a slowest and fastest speed limits the range; the default is the automatic behaviour above. Prosigns (BK, CL, AA, and AR, BT and KN) print by name only if you switch that setting on; otherwise the output is what it was, and in tests on generated signals the character error rate is identical to 1.1.0 at every level measured. In the One signal view it still reads one note, so there is one speed and one signal-to-noise figure. The signal-to-noise figure was within 2 dB of the truth on generated signals; on real band noise with fading and interference treat it as a guide. The callsign shape was written from memory of the ITU Radio Regulations and has not been checked against the text, and the new panel was driven through a stand-in host, not seen in a FoxSDR window.

CW SKIMMER (the Skimmer view). Tick "Skimmer (off: One signal)" in the settings, or press the View key on the panel, to switch from reading one note to skimming the band. The default is the One signal view described above, and its settings are unchanged. A skimmer listens to a stretch of a band and decodes every keyed CW signal in it at the same time, where the One signal view reads the one note you tune to. This takes the wide I/Q from the radio (any sample rate from 8 kS/s to 61.44 MS/s) and analyses about 48 kHz either side of the tuned centre, less when the radio's rate is low (about 38 kHz either side at 2.4 MS/s), or a range you type, for example 28000 to 28070 kHz, if it lies inside what the radio delivers. Each signal it finds gets its own Morse decoder that follows the sender's speed, from about 8 to 50 words per minute, and its drift. Up to 48 signals are followed at once (you can raise that to 64), and signals closer than about 150 Hz count as one.

A table in the plugin's window lists each signal: frequency, speed, signal-to-noise ratio (in 500 Hz), callsign, last text and age. Signals below 2 dB are hidden unless you change that. Callsigns are recognised by shape only, the form the ITU Radio Regulations allow, and in context: after DE, CQ, TEST or QRZ, or read twice. One is listed at once only from a strong, clean signal, otherwise when the same string has been read twice on that signal within 90 seconds. There is no callsign list or database, so a string of the right shape is not proof of an issued callsign.

Two things are off until you switch them on. MARKS ON THE WATERFALL puts the callsign (or "CW 22" for a signal with none yet) at each signal's frequency. SPOT SERVER (THIS COMPUTER) opens a TCP port, 127.0.0.1:7300 by default, that talks like a DX cluster node: a logging program connects, sends any login, and receives lines such as "DX de FOXSDR-#:    28043.2 W1AW         CW 24 dB 22 WPM CQ           1756Z". Up to four clients by default; a client that does not log in or stops reading is dropped, and the login text is never kept or echoed. You can change the address and the spotter name in the lines; if you bind it to anything other than 127.0.0.1 the host log warns that other computers can reach it. The settings boxes appear in FoxSDR 0.99.43 and later.

WHAT IT WILL NOT DO / LIMITS: it sends nothing to any outside service; there is no upload to the Reverse Beacon Network or anywhere else. It is receive only. Heard callsigns stay in memory and on screen: they are never written to a file, a log or a setting. The table shows them whenever the plugin runs; the marks, when switched on, show them on the waterfall. A new signal takes 3 to 6 seconds to lock, so very short bursts are not copied.

TESTED ON GENERATED SIGNALS AND A FEW RECORDINGS, NOT PROVEN ON A BAND. On generated bands of 20 and 40 signals with fading, drift and clock error, about 86% of transmitted characters were read (the seconds before each signal locks are counted as lost) and 19 of 20 and 39 of 40 callsigns were listed at 9 dB, with no wrong callsign and no false row; about 6 dB is the floor, where roughly four callsigns in five came through. Noise alone produced no rows. Three ARRL code-practice files, sent by an operator and converted from audio to I/Q, so not off the air, were read at 99% of characters at 13 and 20 WPM and 81% at 5 WPM. Two off-air maritime recordings listed signals but have no reference text, so how much was read is known and how much was right is not; and the 28 MHz captures available held no CW, where it listed no signals and gave no spots. The signal-to-noise figure is not calibrated against a signal generator. It has been loaded only by a stand-in host in tests, not seen in a FoxSDR window, and only the Windows build has been run.

Only one view works at a time; FoxSDR remembers the view you used last.
plugins.whatsNew: 1.3.0: The CW Skimmer is now part of this plugin: tick "Skimmer (off: One signal)" in its settings, or press the View key on its panel, to see every CW signal in the radio's wide I/Q at once, with its speed, signal strength and callsign, optional waterfall marks and an optional spot server on this computer (off until you switch it on). The default view, One signal, and all its settings are unchanged from 1.2.0. 1.2.0: Shows the speed it is reading and the signal-to-noise ratio of the note on its panel, picks callsigns and message types out of the text, and can lock the speed or limit it to a range. Prosigns such as BK and AR can be printed by name; the decoded text is unchanged unless you switch that on.

plugins.name: RTTY Teleprinter Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Decodes amateur and utility radioteletype on HF, 45.45 to 100 baud.
plugins.description:
Decodes RTTY - the radioteletype mode amateurs have used since mechanical teleprinters - and prints the text. The amateur standard of 45.45 baud with a 170 Hz shift is the default, and the settings offer 50, 75 and 100 baud and 425, 450 and 850 Hz shifts for the faster and wider services, 450 Hz being the German weather service's maritime RTTY. The tone pair stays centred as the shift changes, so the 170 Hz default keeps the exact 2125/2295 Hz tones, and a changed setting takes effect on a running decoder at once. The panel shows the mark and space frequencies in use; a stored setting that is no longer valid falls back to the default and says so rather than decoding silently wrong.

Which way round the two tones are sent is not standardised, and receiving through the wrong sideband inverts them again: four combinations, three of which produce fluent nonsense. Rather than ask you to choose, the decoder tries both and settles on whichever one is framing correctly, so a transmission decodes whether it is sent normal or reverse shift - and the panel names the polarity it settled on. The Reverse switch forces swapped mark and space instead, with no detection delay, for a station known to be sending inverted.

Tune on LSB, which is the amateur convention; the presets do that on the RTTY segment of each band, and ask for a channel wide enough to pass the tones. A listed RTTY frequency is the centre of the tone pair, not the dial: in LSB the dial belongs 2.21 kHz above it, in USB 2.21 kHz below, and the panel says so. Three presets tune the German weather service's around-the-clock stations - DDK2 4583.0, DDH7 7646.0 and DDK9 10100.8 kHz - at the right dial. Tuned near one of them, the panel names it, gives the exact dial and says when you are on it, and sets its 50 baud and 450 Hz with one key. The settings boxes appear in FoxSDR 0.99.43 and later, and on FoxSDR 0.99.77 or later the baud, shift and Reverse rows of the plugin's own panel are keys that step the same settings.

By default the character set is the international (ITA2) alphabet, transcribed from ITU-T Recommendation S.1 and cross-checked against an independent published table, with unshift-on-space applied: after a space the shift reverts to letters, so one lost letters-shift character does not turn the rest of the line into figures.

Since 1.3.0 the tone pair no longer has to sit at the fixed 2210 Hz centre. Press FIND TONES and the decoder listens for about three seconds, picks the pair of tones one shift apart that are both strong (a lone carrier cannot win) and locks to it; or type the audio frequency of the middle of the pair (600 to 3400 Hz) into the Tone pair centre setting. The 2.21 kHz dial rule above is for the default centre; the panel works the dial out from whatever centre is set. AFC, off by default, follows a drifting pair by up to 60 Hz either way. Framing can now be 1, 1.5 or 2 stop bits (a character whose stop bit is not held is dropped and counted on the panel), 5-bit ITA2 or 7- and 8-bit ASCII without parity, with a custom shift of 50 to 1000 Hz, figures held through spaces, and the US-TTY figures set as options. The panel shows two level bars for the mark and space tones. A change to the slicer, which no setting turns off, also changed the default decode: on generated signals the character error rate fell at every level measured, and the stray character in front of each message is gone.

WHAT IT WILL NOT DO / LIMITS: clicking the waterfall to tune is not available because the host offers plugins no such click, and the tone-scope picture is not drawn, only the two bars. FIND TONES and the new framings were proved on generated signals and on five audio recordings (four test patterns and one contest recording), on which it turned noise into text; no recording of the German weather service's own stations was available. The panel was driven through a stand-in host, not seen in a FoxSDR window.
plugins.whatsNew: 1.3.0: FIND TONES locates the tone pair for you, so a signal that is not at the old fixed pitch now decodes, and AFC (off by default) can follow drift. It adds 1, 1.5 and 2 stop bits, 7- and 8-bit ASCII and any shift from 50 to 1000 Hz. A slicer fix removes the stray character that used to start a message, and in tests on generated signals the error rate was never worse than 1.2.0's.

plugins.name: 433 MHz Sensors, Remotes and X10
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Reads 433.92 MHz weather sensors (Oregon Scientific v1.0, v2.1 and v3.0, AcuRite 00955, SL-109H), X10 RF remote controls (ON, OFF, DIM, BRIGHT) and key-fob remotes (the Remote Monitor: is the code fixed or changing), from raw I/Q.
plugins.description:
Decodes the little battery-powered temperature and humidity transmitters that come with a home weather station, on 433.92 MHz (and the remotes at 315, 345 and 868.3 MHz), and prints each reading: sensor model, channel, temperature to a tenth of a degree, relative humidity and the low-battery flag.

SUPPORTED PROTOCOLS: Oregon Scientific version 1.0 (new in 1.1.0), 2.1 and 3.0, the AcuRite 00955 and the Oregon Scientific SL-109H (both new in 1.1.0), and, among the sensors, only those. The version 1.0, AcuRite and SL-109H decoders are written from the published protocol description and have been tested on signals built from the same description, not on a real sensor: if you have one and it does not read, switch on 'Show unknown bursts' and send the line it prints. Oregon version 2.1 and 3.0 sensors identified by name are the THGR122NX / THGN123N, THGR810 / THGN801, THGR8101 and BTHR968 (temperature and humidity), and the THN132N / THR238NF and THWR800 (temperature only). A sensor whose identity code is not one of those is still reported - its code, channel, rolling code and battery state - but its measurements are not decoded, because the data layout differs from sensor to sensor and guessing one is how a decoder reports a temperature that was never transmitted. Other 433 MHz sensor families (LaCrosse, Nexus, Fine Offset, Bresser, tyre-pressure sensors and the rest) use different protocols and are not decoded.

THE SENSORS TABLE (new in 1.1.0) lists every sensor heard: protocol, model, id, channel, reading, battery, signal level and signal-to-noise figure, when it was last heard and how many times. The checkbox 'Show unknown bursts' (off unless you switch it on) adds a line, and a row in the table, for every burst of pulses that none of the protocols above recognised - how many pulses, how long, the carrier frequency, the first pulse widths and gaps, and (new in 1.2.0) the pulse coding the analyser makes of it and the first bits it carries - so a sensor this plugin cannot read can be reported without being guessed at. The AcuRite 00955 and SL-109H are accepted only when two repetitions of the message agree.

Every message is checked against the protocol checksum, against Manchester coding rules, and against its digits being decimal, so noise does not turn into weather. Sensors send each reading more than once; repeats within five seconds are folded into one line, while a genuinely new reading is always shown.

This decoder works on raw I/Q rather than demodulated audio: the signal is on-off keying, so what it needs is the envelope of the band. 250 kS/s is plenty and is what the preset asks for - a wider span only piles the rest of a busy band on top of the sensor. The receiver DC offset is tracked and removed before detection, so a zero-IF dongle such as an RTL-SDR - whose offset sits exactly where these sensors do - hears them.

It also fits an INSTRUMENT WINDOW: a weather station's base unit, with a channel panel for each of the three remote sensors showing its temperature in seven-segment digits, its humidity and a low-battery symbol, a channel it has not heard showing dashes exactly as the real console does, and the last hundred readings logged beneath it.

NEW IN 1.2.0 (settings page): a tick box for each of the four protocols (all on); temperature units C, F or K for the sensors table and the readings log (the instrument window stays in Celsius); a signal level and signal-to-noise figure for every reading; an FSK burst analyser (off) that reports the bit rate, deviation, carrier and first bits of an FSK transmission without decoding any device; and a band hopper (off) that steps the receiver through the bands you tick - 433.92 MHz, 868.3, 315, 345 and 915 MHz, 90 seconds each by default - using FoxSDR's tune request. It needs your tune permission, shows a 'not granted' row without it, and stops asking if you tune elsewhere.

X10 RF REMOTE DECODER (tick the box on the settings page): reads the radio frames of X10 remote controls (433.92 MHz Europe, 310 MHz US) and prints the function (ON, OFF, DIM or BRIGHT) once per press. House letters and unit numbers belong to devices in other people's homes, so by default each line shows only a session tag such as device #3. Tested on generated signals only; the security-sensor frames and the 41-bit variants are not decoded.

REMOTE MONITOR (tick the box; it unticks itself at every start): a receive-only test instrument for key fobs, gate remotes and alarm sensors you own or are authorised to test, at 315, 345, 433.92 or 868.3 MHz. It says whether a code is fixed or changing; it never transmits, records or replays a signal, never works out a code, and stores nothing. Device identifiers are hidden by default. Four presets tune its bands. With both boxes off the plugin behaves exactly as 1.2.0.

WHAT IT WILL NOT DO / LIMITS: Fine Offset weather stations and tyre-pressure sensors are not decoded, because no free published frame description was found; the FSK analyser only measures. The OOK decoders exist only for 433 MHz, so hopping to the other bands only feeds the analysers. The FSK analyser and the band hopper have been tried on generated signals and a stand-in host only, never on a real FSK sensor or a real retune. Seven off-air Oregon recordings decode as before. A changed setting takes effect when the panel is next polled or the receiver next starts.

Written clean-room from the published Oregon Scientific RF protocol description; no decoder implementation was consulted.
plugins.whatsNew: 1.3.1: The FSK burst analyser no longer misses narrow bursts: a two-tone FSK burst (a few kBd, about 10 kHz each side) that stands well over the noise in its own few kilohertz but only a few dB over the whole passband was never reported (67 in real recordings); it is now found by its spectrum and reported as a burst, with its bit rate when the bits are readable. Tick 'Analyse FSK bursts' to see them. 1.3.0: The X10 RF Remote Decoder and the Remote Monitor (key fobs, fixed or changing codes) join the sensors as two protocol families, each off until you tick its box; with both off the plugin behaves exactly as 1.2.0. Four presets for the Remote Monitor's bands. 1.2.0: Choose which protocols to decode, show temperatures in C, F or K, and see a signal level and signal-to-noise figure for every reading. Unknown bursts now show their pulse coding and first bits. An FSK burst analyser and a band hopper (433, 868, 315, 345, 915 MHz) are included, both off by default and tried on generated signals only.

plugins.name: Two-Tone Paging Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Reads fire and EMS two-tone pages, and reports the tones even when they match no table.
plugins.description:
Decodes two-tone sequential paging - the "fire tone-out" that dispatch centres have used to alert fire and EMS crews since the 1960s and still use. A first tone of about a second, a second tone of about three, and every pager whose two reeds match that pair opens up.

The decoder measures both tones and then looks them up, which is the other way round from how these things are usually built and is the point of it. A department's tone pair is a local fact, so a page whose tones are in none of the published tables is still reported, with its two frequencies, its two durations and the gap between them - which is everything you need to programme a pager or identify the department. A decoder that stayed silent because it did not recognise the tones would be throwing away the only thing you were listening for.

Where the tones ARE recognised it names the format and reconstructs the code: a Motorola cap code, a GE Type 99 three digit code, a Reach code, or a Plectron pair. The tables are Motorola Quick Call II, GE Type 99, Reach and Plectron, transcribed from the published Midian Electronics tone signaling charts. Tones from different formats sit within 1% of each other in 115 places, so a pair is checked against each format's own code plan rather than against one flat list, and where a pair is a legal code in more than one format all of them are named.

Long group calls and single-tone calls are reported too. Tune the receiver to your dispatch channel in NFM; there are no presets because these channels are allocated locally and a shipped frequency would send almost everyone to a dead one.

It also opens an instrument window drawn as the equipment it replaces - a fire station's two-tone alert monitor, with a red alert lamp that blinks while a page is held, both measured tones indexed on an engraved frequency scale with their durations, the code and the format on glass, and the last hundred pages as a call log beneath.

NEW IN 1.1.0 (settings page; with every field empty the output is exactly the 1.0.1 output): your own tone sets, each a name, two tones in order, a tolerance, minimum durations, an optional group name and an action of alert, show or hide (up to 16). A matching page adds a line naming the set, lights the lamp with the set's name on the glass, and raises a host notice carrying only the set name; a set outranks the published tables. A pre-alert tone can be required before a set counts. A repeat blocker drops the same page heard again within a number of seconds. Recording of the dispatch audio (off) saves 5 to 120 seconds as an 8 kHz mono WAV after an alert.

WHAT IT WILL NOT DO / LIMITS: no tone frequencies are built in; the sets are yours. Motorola Quick Call I and AVCALL 2+2, which send pairs of simultaneous tones, are still not read, because the tone table could not be read from a free copy. Recordings are not sent by email, FTP or HTTP, and no command is run on an alert. The recording is the audio the decoder is given, so it is silent while the host's squelch is closed. The new settings were checked on generated tones and one public two-tone sample recording (origin unverified), not on a live dispatch channel.
plugins.whatsNew: 1.2.0: A new setting, Announce after quiet (0.3 to 3 s, default 1): how long the channel must stay quiet after a page before it is announced. The same time decides whether a tone that follows belongs to a chain (Morse, a modem) and not to a page. Shorter announces sooner and lets more chains through; longer refuses more; the default is the old behaviour. 1.1.1: No more invented calls: Morse, FSK, modem, picture and fax tones, a melody or a chain of tones are no longer announced as a page; a page is two steady tones standing alone, announced about a second after the second tone, and a recording still starts where the page ended. 1.1.0: Define your own tone sets with tolerance, minimum durations, group name and an alert, show or hide action, require a pre-alert tone, reject repeat pages, and optionally record the dispatch audio. With the new fields empty the output is unchanged.

plugins.name: SELCAL Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Reads the four-letter calls HF ground stations send to alert one aircraft, and says when a call is not to specification.
plugins.description:
SELCAL - selective calling - is how an aeronautical radio station on HF gets the attention of one aircraft's crew without making them listen to the whole frequency. The station sends the aircraft's four-letter code as two one-second pulses of two simultaneous tones, and the flight deck chimes. This decodes those calls: one line each, "SELCAL AB-CD", with the four measured tones, both pulse lengths and the gap between them.

It knows all 32 tones of the ICAO table, including the 16 added in November 2022, and names a code that uses them as a 32-tone code. Each pulse is timed to the sample, so the timing the standard sets - pulses of 1.0 plus or minus 0.25 seconds, a gap of 0.2 plus or minus 0.1 - is actually checked.

A call that does not meet the standard is still reported, marked "SELCAL?" with the reason in words: a pulse too short or too long, a gap out of range, a tone that is in no table (with its measured frequency and how far it is from the nearest one), a tone used twice, or a first pulse whose second never came. On a fading HF channel that is often the real call, damaged, and hiding it would hide what you were listening for.

The presets tune ten North Atlantic HF frequencies from the ICAO NAT families that Shanwick, Gander and the other oceanic stations work - listen in USB on the listed frequency, with no offset. A receiver a few hertz off still decodes: every tone is accepted within 1.5 percent and the error is printed.

REGISTRATION LIST AND REPEATS (1.1.0). If you give it a CSV of your own, one CODE,LABEL per line such as AB-CD,G-ABCD, through the FOXSDR_SELCAL_FILE environment variable or at foxsdr/selcal/registry.csv in your cache folder, a clean call line gains '= LABEL'. Codes are matched in the order the pulses were sent. Each clean call also shows how many times that code has been heard (call N); when the same code is called again within 120 seconds the line adds REPEAT N and the time since the last call, and the tuned frequency is shown.

WHAT IT WILL NOT DO / LIMITS: no registration list is shipped, because the registrar's assignments are not published as open data, so without your file it names nothing. The labels live in memory only and are never written out. Calls marked SELCAL? are neither named nor counted. The 120 second repeat window is our choice, not from a standard, and whether real calls repeat inside it was not checked. Tried on generated signals only, and the file is set through an environment variable, not a settings screen.
plugins.whatsNew: 1.1.0: Can name the aircraft behind a code from a list you supply, counts repeat calls of one code within 120 seconds, and shows the frequency the receiver is tuned to. Calls that fail the standard are never named or counted.

plugins.name: FT8, JT65 and WSPR Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Decodes the weak-signal amateur modes FT8, FT4, JT65 (sub-modes A, B, C) and WSPR (experimental, receive only), slot by slot, in WSJT-X's own layout - and, only if you switch it on, reports FT8 to PSK Reporter.
plugins.description:
FT8 is the weak-signal amateur mode WSJT-X introduced in 2017 and now the busiest thing on the HF bands: 15-second transmissions, started on the UTC clock, each carrying one short message - a CQ, a callsign pair with a signal report or a locator, a 73. This decodes every one it can hear in each slot and prints them the way WSJT-X does: the slot's UTC time, the signal-to-noise ratio, the time offset, the audio frequency and the message.

Tune a preset and leave it running. The presets are WSJT-X's own FT8 dial frequencies from 160 m to 2 m, in USB with a 3 kHz channel; the messages appear at the end of each 15-second slot. Like WSJT-X, FT8 needs this computer's clock to be right to within about a second, so keep it synchronised.

FT4 (new in 1.2.0, RECEIVE ONLY). Set the mode field ("Mode: FT8 FT4 JT65 WSPR") to ft4, or press the Mode key on its panel until it says FT4, and it decodes FT4 instead of FT8: the faster sibling mode, 7.5-second slots on the UTC clock with four tones 20.8 Hz apart. Three FT4 presets (40 m, 20 m, 15 m) tune the usual dial frequencies; the lines come out in the same layout with a '+' where FT8's have a '~'. FT4's SNR column is the plain signal to noise ratio in 2500 Hz, which may differ from WSJT-X's printed FT4 figure by a constant. FT4 decodes are not sent to PSK Reporter. The FT4 authors allow independent implementations that disallow robotic or unattended operation under the name; this has no transmit path at all. Set the mode back to ft8 to return to FT8. (The old checkbox "Decode FT4 (receive only)" is gone from the form; its stored value is still read when the mode field is empty.)

Standard QSO messages and free text are decoded. At the default setting it reaches down to about -18 dB. Since 1.3.0 the Decode depth setting (1 Fast, 2 Normal, 3 Deep; 0, the default, leaves the engine as it was) can subtract each decoded signal and decode the slot again, as WSJT-X does, and can add a-priori decoding when your callsign is set and a look-out for calls from a list you supply. On generated signals the level at which half the slots decode moved from about -18.4 dB to between about -19 and -21 dB, depending on the options; on a real 28 MHz recording, depth 3 found 31 to 33 messages where the old engine found 28. There is no comparison against WSJT-X itself. Deep decoding costs up to about 0.6 s of computing per 15-second slot. A deeper decode that falls below the engine's confidence line is marked with a ? and carries no callsign, so it is never reported to PSK Reporter; the others are treated like any other decode. The SNR column follows WSJT-X's own convention so the two can be compared. This is a receiver only: it never transmits.

NEW IN 1.3.0, VIEW AND LOGGING HELPERS, all off or empty by default, so with none of them touched the output is exactly 1.2.0's. SHOW CQ ONLY hides everything that is neither a CQ nor addressed to your callsign. An RX FREQUENCY with a tolerance sends decodes near it to a separate list in the plugin's window. MARK DECODES appends tags such as [CQ], [ME], [NEW CALL] and [DT?] to a line, and the distance and bearing from the locator you type. A DT CORRECTION is added to the printed time offset. A WORKED LOG, read from your own ADIF file, marks calls, grids and countries not in it as new. SEND DECODES AS JSON TO UDP sends one line of JSON per decode to 127.0.0.1 only, in a layout of this plugin's own, not WSJT-X's. No country data is shipped: without your own cty.dat-style file there are no country, zone or new-country marks. Callsigns, grids and messages are never written to a log or stored in a setting; they go only to the Decoder output, the window and, if you switch it on, the loopback UDP port. It does not keep a QSO log, look callers up online or transmit, and it does not decode SuperFox or FT2. The panel (now six columns) was driven through a stand-in host in tests, not seen in a FoxSDR window.

JT65 (new in 1.4.0, a mode of this plugin, RECEIVE ONLY). Set the mode field to jt65, or press the Mode key on its panel until it says JT65. JT65 (by K1JT) was made for moon-bounce on the VHF bands and is also used on HF: each station sends one 47-second transmission, starting a second into every UTC minute, of 64-tone frequency-shift keying with a Reed-Solomon (63,12) error-correcting code, carrying two callsigns and a locator. Signals can be read several dB below the noise: in tests on generated signals it decoded all of them down to 22 dB below the noise in a 2500 Hz channel and most at 23 dB (the author gives about -25 dB for the best programs). Tune a JT65 frequency in USB and leave it running; the decodes appear in the Decoder output. Every minute it decodes the minute just finished and prints one line per signal - UTC minute, signal-to-noise ratio in 2500 Hz, time offset in seconds, the audio frequency of the sync tone, the sub-mode (A, B or C) and the message. Like JT65 itself it needs this computer's clock to be right to within a second. Receive only, and no network: it never transmits, never tunes your receiver and makes no internet connection. Messages of two callsigns and a locator are shown as text, and 'CQ xx' (the directed CQ form the user guide documents). Other message types - plain CQ, signal reports, RRR and 73, add-on prefixes, free text - are decoded and checked by the error-correcting code, but the sources used do not publish their codes, so they are shown as the raw numbers of their fields. The OOO report and the shorthand RO / RRR / 73 tone pairs are not read. A decode needs a codeword that agrees with the received tones and a sync tone of the right strength, so noise does not print lines: over 20 hours of generated noise it printed none. Written from K1JT's QEX paper 'The JT65 Communications Protocol' (2005) and the WSJT-X user guide; no WSJT, WSJT-X or JT65 source code was used. It has been tested on generated signals only: no JT65 recording has been decoded, so treat it as unproven on the air.

WSPR (new in 1.4.0, a mode of this plugin, EXPERIMENTAL, RECEIVE ONLY). Set the mode field to wspr, or press the Mode key on its panel until it says WSPR. WSPR (Weak Signal Propagation Reporter, by K1JT) is a beacon mode: each station sends one 110.6-second transmission, starting a second into every second UTC minute, carrying its callsign, a 4-character grid locator and its power in dBm. The signals are only about 6 Hz wide and can be read well below the noise: the author gives about -28 dB in a 2500 Hz bandwidth as the limit. Tune a preset (its ten dial frequencies, offered while the mode is WSPR, from 160 m to 6 m, from the QST article 'WSPRing Around the World') in USB and leave it running. Every two minutes it decodes the slot just finished and prints one line per station - UTC time, signal-to-noise ratio in 2500 Hz, time offset, frequency, drift in Hz per minute and the message - and keeps the latest in the plugin's window with the callsign, locator and power in separate columns. Like WSPR itself it needs this computer's clock to be right to within a second, so keep it synchronised. Its two options, how many spots to keep and whether other message types are reported, are keys on the panel in WSPR mode (keys wspr.spots_keep and wspr.log_other). Receive only, and no network: it never transmits, never tunes your receiver and makes no internet connection - nothing is uploaded to wsprnet.org. Only the standard message type (callsign, 4-character locator, power) is decoded. Messages with a compound callsign or a hashed callsign and 6-character locator are counted ('Other types, not decoded') and never printed. A decode is printed only if the callsign has the standard form, the power is one WSPR allows and the decoded message agrees with what was received, so noise does not print spots. Written from K1JT's WSPR 2.0 User's Guide, his QST article and textbook sequential-decoding methods; no WSJT, WSJT-X or WSPR source code was used. It has been tested on generated signals in white noise only; no off-air WSPR recording has been run through it, so treat it as unproven on the air.

Each mode keeps its own slot length and decode list (FT8 15 s, FT4 7.5 s, JT65 one minute, WSPR two minutes). FoxSDR remembers the mode you used last. JT65 and WSPR were tested on generated signals only.

PSK REPORTER (new in 1.1.0, OFF unless you switch it on). When you type your callsign and locator into its settings and switch 'Report to PSK Reporter' on, it sends your callsign, your locator, the decoder's own name and version, and each station it decodes - callsign, frequency, signal report, mode and the time - to pskreporter.info, which shows them PUBLICLY on its map as heard by your callsign. (It has no intermodulation-distortion measurement of its own, so that optional field always goes as zero.) Nothing is sent while the switch is off. This plugin can read FoxSDR's receiver position - GPS, 'Set RX here', or a typed location - as a 6-character Maidenhead square, and uses it to prefill the Locator box ONCE, the first time one is set; after that the box is yours, including if you clear it. Reports go no more than once every five minutes - a little sooner only when many new stations fill one report at once - and each station at most once an hour unless it moves to another band or dial frequency. A report is only ever sent from the RECEIVER, with a real radio open and running in USB on a steady dial - never from the patch page, a sound-card source, or an I/Q recording being played back, and not while a second FT8 decoder is open elsewhere - because each of those would be a public claim about a station that was never actually live at that frequency at that time. Lookups are IPv4 only. Its 'FT8, JT65 and WSPR' window shows what it is doing; the CQ filter, marks and Rx focus act on FT8 and FT4 only, and PSK Reporter on FT8 only.

The settings boxes appear in FoxSDR 0.99.43 and later. On an older FoxSDR this version still loads and decodes FT8 exactly as 1.0.0 did (only FT8 runs there, because the mode is a setting) - there is just nowhere to type a callsign, so it never reports, and its window says which FoxSDR it needs.

Built on ft8_lib by Karlis Goba (YL3JG), MIT licence, and KISS FFT by Mark Borgerding, BSD 3-clause licence: Copyright (c) 2003-2010 Mark Borgerding, all rights reserved; provided by the copyright holders and contributors "as is" and without any express or implied warranties. The full licence texts are in the FoxSDR plugins repository under third_party/ft8_lib.
plugins.whatsNew: 1.4.0: JT65 and WSPR are now modes of this plugin (they were separate plugins before any release): choose FT8, FT4, JT65 or WSPR in its settings, or with the Mode key on its panel; FoxSDR remembers the mode. Each keeps its own slot length and decode list; the CQ filter, marks and Rx focus act on FT8 and FT4 only, and PSK Reporter on FT8 only. WSPR's two options are keys on the panel in WSPR mode. The FT4 checkbox is replaced by the mode field. 1.3.0: Optional deeper decoding: Decode depth 2 or 3 subtracts each decoded signal and decodes the slot again, which found more stations in tests on recordings and generated signals. New view options mark and filter CQ calls, your own call and new calls, and keep a list for one Rx frequency; with none of them touched the lines are exactly as in 1.2.0.

plugins.name: DTMF Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Reads touch-tone (DTMF) keys 0-9, *, # and A-D from the audio, with time stamps, and says how far off frequency each key was.
plugins.description:
DTMF is the two-tone keypad signalling of telephones, and of radio: repeater controllers, remote-control links, radio-to-phone patches and many club and emergency-service systems still use it. Each key is the sum of one tone from a low group (697, 770, 852, 941 Hz) and one from a high group (1209, 1336, 1477, 1633 Hz). This reads the audio, finds each key and prints one line for it: when it started, counted in seconds of audio since the decoder was started, and which key it was. When the keys stop for two and a half seconds it prints the string of keys it just saw.

It applies the checks ITU-T Recommendation Q.24 describes for a receiver: exactly one tone from each group, the two tones' level difference (twist) within limits, each tone's frequency within its tolerance, and a tone that lasts long enough - 40 ms keys at full dialling speed are read, a 20 ms burst is not. A key held down is counted once. Tick 'Show error, twist, duration' in its settings to see the measured frequency error of both tones, the twist and the duration on every line.

Speech and noise do not produce keys in the tests it ships with: no false key in an hour of noise, none in about six minutes of recorded speech, about a dozen per hour in a synthetic speech-like signal that is harsher than real speech. It has no preset frequencies: DTMF is a signalling method, not a frequency, so tune whatever carries it, in FM or SSB, with the audio passband open to at least 1.7 kHz.
plugins.whatsNew: 1.0.0: New. Reads DTMF keys from demodulated audio with the Q.24 frequency, twist and duration checks.

plugins.name: ILS Meter
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Measures an ILS localiser or glide path: the depth of the 90 and 150 Hz tones, their difference, and the 1020 Hz Morse ident. Not for navigation.
plugins.description:
An instrument landing system's localiser and glide path are AM carriers modulated with a 90 Hz and a 150 Hz tone. Which of them is stronger, and by how much, is what a cockpit needle shows. This reads the demodulated AM audio and prints, once a second, the depth of each tone in percent of the carrier, their difference (the DDM) with its sign, and what that sign means: on a localiser 90 Hz is stronger to the left of the course, so 'fly RIGHT'; on a glide path 90 Hz is stronger above the path, so 'fly DOWN'. A localiser's Morse identification, keyed on a 1020 Hz tone and always starting with the letter I, is decoded and printed each time it is heard.

THIS IS A MEASURING DISPLAY. IT IS NOT FOR NAVIGATION: a software-defined receiver, its demodulator and its audio path are not certified for it. Tune the localiser (108.10 to 111.95 MHz) or glide-path carrier in AM and set Mode to LOC or GS. The depth can be measured only if the demodulator leaves the carrier in the audio; if it removes it, the plugin says so and shows only which tone is larger and the ratio in dB. It has been tested on generated signals only: no ILS recording was available.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.1.0: New. Tone depths, DDM with its sign and the 1020 Hz ident of a localiser, from AM audio.

plugins.name: Packet Error Rate Tester
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Counts bit errors and bad packets against a PN9 or PN15 test pattern sent as FSK data, at a symbol rate you choose.
plugins.description:
A radio link is tested by sending a known pseudo-random pattern and counting what comes back wrong. This reads the demodulated audio of a two-level FSK or GFSK link at a symbol rate you set, finds the symbol timing, locks to a PN9 or PN15 pattern (either polarity: it tells you if the data are inverted), and prints once a second the bits compared, the bit errors, the bit error rate, and how many packets of the length you choose had at least one error, with a 95 % interval on the packet error rate. If sync is lost it says so and searches again.

It needs something that sends the pattern: a transmitter under test, or an I/Q file such as the one tools/make_per_iq.cpp writes (FoxSDR's built-in signal generator makes tones and noise, not data). Tune the channel in narrow FM so the audio is the discriminator output, with the squelch open. Tested on generated signals: injected error counts are reproduced exactly, and on noise the receiver is within 2.0 dB of an ideal one.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.1.0: New. PN9 and PN15 bit and packet error counting for two-level FSK audio.

plugins.name: M17 Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Shows who is calling on M17 digital radio - callsigns, text, position and packet messages - from the FM audio. No voice.
plugins.description:
M17 is an open digital mode for amateur radio: 4-level FSK at 4800 symbols a second in a 9 kHz channel, with voice, short packets and data. This reads the signalling and the data, not the speech. For every transmission it prints the link setup - who is calling (the source callsign), who they are calling (a callsign, a reflector or ALL) and the type: voice, data or packet, the channel access number and whether it is encrypted - then any text and GNSS position the sender put in the link information, and when a stream ends how many frames it held, how many were missed and an estimate of the bit error rate. A packet-mode message, such as an SMS text, is shown once its checksum passes; one that fails is reported as wrong and not shown.

A transmission picked up part-way through is joined from the link information repeated in every frame. Frames that fail their own checks are refused rather than shown wrongly: tick 'Show refused frames' to see them.

NO VOICE. M17 voice is carried by the Codec 2 vocoder, which is not part of this plugin; voice transmissions are announced and their signalling shown, and the speech is not decoded. Encrypted transmissions are labelled and their contents left alone.

Tune a channel in narrow FM with de-emphasis off (the two presets do that); it needs the discriminator audio, flat, at least 3 kHz wide. The two presets are the frequencies the M17 Project's news page quoted for IARU Region 1 (144.875 MHz and 433.475 MHz): check your own band plan before relying on them.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.1.1: A stream now ends on the end marker only when two windows in a row match it, and a new transmission whose link setup was missed is started afresh when the frame counter goes backwards, instead of being merged with the one before. Generated signals only; no voice.

plugins.name: FreeDV Receive
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Plays FreeDV digital voice (1600, 700C, 700D, 700E, 2020) from sideband audio and shows the text and sync the transmitter sends, through a Codec 2 library that you add yourself; none is shipped. Receive only.
plugins.description:
FreeDV is the open digital-voice mode amateurs use on HF. This plugin takes demodulated sideband audio (8 kHz), plays the speech through the receiver's speakers, prints the text the transmitter sends (usually a callsign) as a line of Decoder output, and reports sync and signal-to-noise.

THE PLUGIN CONTAINS NO FREEDV CODE, NO MODEM AND NO CODEC. They live in the Codec 2 library, which is under the LGPL and which YOU add: put codec2.dll next to the plugin or give its path in the settings. Without it the plugin says so and does nothing. Receive only: no transmit function is even looked up. The decoded text is held in memory only and is never written to a file, a setting or the log.

WHAT IS AND IS NOT PROVEN. The names of the eleven library calls it uses were checked against the export table of an unmodified Codec 2 1.2.0 library (read as bytes, nothing executed). Their argument types and the number the library uses for each mode were written from understanding and are NOT confirmed, because the only document that gives them is the library's source header, which was not read; a setting lets you give another mode number. The whole chain was tested against stand-in libraries written for the test: no FreeDV signal and no real Codec 2 library has been run through it.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.1.0: first release. FreeDV 1600, 700C, 700D, 700E and 2020 through a Codec 2 library you add; tried against stand-in libraries only.

plugins.name: Time Signals
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Reads the time and date from the long-wave time stations DCF77, MSF, WWVB and JJY, with the parity result and the flags each one carries.
plugins.description:
Four national time stations send the time as a pulse every second: the carrier is lowered (DCF77 at 77.5 kHz, MSF and WWVB at 60 kHz) or raised (JJY at 40 and 60 kHz) for a tenth to eight tenths of a second, and the length of the pulse is a bit. A minute of bits is the time, the date and a few flags. This listens for all four at once. It finds the second from the pulses, the minute from each code's own marker, and prints the minute and the hour once their parity bits are in, then the whole frame at the next minute marker: local time with its zone, the same in UTC, and what the station carries besides - DCF77's change-of-time and leap-second warnings, MSF's DUT1 and summer-time warning, WWVB's DUT1, leap-year and leap-second bits, JJY's leap-second and service bits - with how many seconds it has been locked.

A frame whose parity fails, whose time or date is impossible (a 30th of February, a weekday that is not that date's) or whose fixed bits are wrong is named and refused, never printed as the time. WWVB's legacy code has no parity bits, so there the other checks are all there are. It needs the carrier's on-off keying to reach it as audio, so the presets are USB with the dial 1 kHz below the carrier (the AM mode of this application removes the carrier's DC level and would lose the keying; set the AGC to Off or Slow). A frame takes a minute; in the tests it decoded every frame down to 6 dB carrier-to-noise in a 4 kHz audio band. A 45-second recording of DCF77 made through a public receiver gave the hour with its parity; a full minute has not been recorded, and no frame has been decoded off the air.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.1.0: New. DCF77, MSF, WWVB and JJY time codes from the demodulated carrier, with parity and flags.

plugins.name: CCIR Selcall
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Reads five-figure selective calls sent as a series of tones (the CCIR tone set of ITU-R M.257), with the repeat check and any coast-station or channel group.
plugins.description:
A selective call of this kind is five figures sent as five audio tones in a row, each 100 milliseconds long, one tone per figure from 1124 to 1981 Hz; a figure that repeats the one before it is sent as 2110 Hz in its place. The call is sent twice, and this reads both: it prints the call, and says 'confirmed' when the second send, 900 milliseconds later, is the same. A group of four figures sent after a call is read as additional information: a coast station's identity, or, if it starts with two zeros, the VHF channel to reply on. The tone table and the timings are those of ITU-R Recommendation M.257 (the maritime sequential single-frequency system, now withdrawn).

It takes the demodulated audio and applies the Recommendation's timing: a tone must last about 100 milliseconds and the next must follow within a few. A run of tones that does not fit - four, six, a repeat tone first, a tone held for seconds - is ignored, never printed as a call. In the tests it makes no false call in an hour of noise, an hour of speech-like audio or six minutes of recorded speech. Since 0.2.0 the Tone set setting (1 to 8, 1 is CCIR) also reads the EEA, EIA, ZVEI-1, ZVEI-2, ZVEI-3, DZVEI and PZVEI sets, with some letters left out where the sources disagree. The sent-twice check and the additional-information groups are CCIR only, and the 'all ships' call is not read. No call has been decoded off the air.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.2.0: Adds the EEA, EIA, ZVEI-1, ZVEI-2, ZVEI-3, DZVEI and PZVEI tone sets, chosen with a Tone set setting (1 to 8, 1 is CCIR). Some letters are left out where sources disagree, and it has been tried on generated signals only.

plugins.name: Feld-Hell
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Shows Feld-Hell (Hellschreiber) as the picture it is: a scrolling strip you read with your eyes, with every sample drawn twice.
plugins.description:
Hellschreiber sends text as a picture. Each character is a grid of dots, sent a column at a time by switching a tone on and off, 17.5 columns a second; nothing is coded, so noise makes a character harder to read but cannot turn it into a different one. This finds the tone (between 700 and 2000 Hz, or the frequency you give it) and draws what the tone does, as a grey-scale strip scrolling to the left, 21 samples for every column. Each sample is drawn twice, one column's height apart, which is how the mode has always been received: it makes the letters readable whatever the receiver's timing is against the sender's, so you read the text on whichever copy sits square.

It does not turn the picture into letters. The mode was never meant to be read by machine, and the standard font is not in the specification it was written from. Nothing is drawn until a steady carrier has been found, which takes about five seconds; noise and speech do not start it in the tests. The traditional on-off mode only: the multi-tone Hell modes (C/MT, S/MT), PSK-Hell and FM-Hell are not here. No Hell signal has been received off the air.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.1.0: New. Feld-Hell picture strip from the audio, carrier found automatically.

plugins.name: DGPS Corrections Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Reads the differential GPS correction messages that marine radiobeacons send on 283.5 to 325 kHz, from the MSK audio, and shows what each frame says. Receive only.
plugins.description:
Marine DGPS radiobeacons send correction data for GPS receivers on the long-wave band between 283.5 and 325 kHz, as continuous minimum-shift keying at 25, 50, 100 or 200 bit/s. This decoder reads that stream from demodulated audio, finds the frame headers, checks the parity of every 30-bit word and prints each frame it can trust: pseudorange and range-rate corrections (message types 1 and 9), reference-station coordinates (3), the constellation health table (5), the beacon's own messages (6, 7) and its text messages (16). Choose the bit rate and the carrier tone in its settings.

Written from Recommendation ITU-R M.823-1 and the parity rules in IS-GPS-200. RECEIVE ONLY, and no network. It has been tested on generated signals only: no recording of a real beacon was available, so treat it as unproven on the air. The carrier must be within about 5 Hz of the setting at 100 bit/s, and GLONASS message types 31 to 36 are not decoded. The radiobeacon band is below the tuning range of most receivers: it needs a receiver or converter that reaches 283.5 kHz.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.1.1: A preamble pattern inside a real frame's own words (a Z-count of 3264 to 3295, a data word) no longer starts a second, false frame and no longer makes the next real frame disappear. 0.1.0: New. DGPS correction frames from MSK audio, message types 1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 9 and 16, with parity checking. Generated signals only.

plugins.name: RF Measurements
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Two measurements with your receiver: the noise figure of an amplifier or of the receiver itself by the Y-factor method, and the 21 cm hydrogen line with a fitted line velocity. Off until you switch it on.
plugins.description:
Noise figure: connect a noise source with a known ENR (you type it, there is no default), store a HOT and a COLD reading in a band you choose, and optionally a second calibration step with the source straight into the receiver, which removes the receiver's own noise. It shows Y, the noise factor and figure, the gain and a one-sigma uncertainty from the radiometer equation. The gain is only the ratio of the two steps: the radio's I/Q scale is arbitrary, so absolute level does not cancel.

Hydrogen line: a long integration with a stored reference (off the source, or the receiver tuned away), channel averaging, a baseline fit that leaves the line out and a Gaussian fit that gives centre frequency, width and amplitude with their errors, and the velocity on the radio definition (positive receding) from the rest frequency 1420.405751768 MHz. The result can be written to a CSV file at a path you set. Correction to the local standard of rest and absolute temperature are NOT done.

No network. Proven on generated I/Q only: it has not been tried on a real aerial, a real noise source or the accuracy of the radios themselves (ADC linearity, AGC, image rejection), so treat the numbers as unproven.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.1.3: The panel says where the NF: take HOT and NF: take COLD keys are (on the plugin's page under Fitted modules). 0.1.2: Fixes the Y shown beside the receiver noise figure (it printed 10.000 whatever the readings). 0.1.1: Adds the equivalent noise bandwidth of the analysis window to the panel, and a quasi-peak detector model with the CISPR band constants (not certified, no panel mode). Generated I/Q only.

plugins.name: MPT 1327 Monitor
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Reads the control channel of an MPT 1327 trunked radio system: system code, calls set up, acknowledgements and announcements. Signalling only, no voice. Receive only.
plugins.description:
MPT 1327 is the British signalling standard for trunked private land mobile radio. Its control channel sends 1200 bit/s tone-shift data. This decoder reads that data from FM discriminator audio, checks each 64-bit codeword with its error-checking code (one bit error is repaired) and prints what the system says: its system code, Aloha broadcasts, acknowledgements, ahoy calls, channel allocations for speech or data calls, and announcements.

Signalling only: it does not follow a call onto its traffic channel and decodes no voice or data. One setting, Hide radio IDs (off by default), replaces each unit's number with [hidden]; nothing is written to disk. Receive only.

Written from the 1997 issue of the standard. It has never met a real MPT 1327 signal: it was tested on generated audio only, and the pair of tones it listens for comes from a data sheet and a manual rather than the standard, so treat it as unproven on the air. Requests from radio units, short data and standard data messages are not read.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.1.0: New. MPT 1327 control-channel signalling from FM audio. Generated signals only.

plugins.name: NOAA HRPT Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Reads the 1.7 GHz HRPT picture signal of NOAA weather satellites from raw I/Q and draws the five AVHRR channel pictures. Receive only.
plugins.description:
HRPT is the high-resolution picture signal that NOAA polar weather satellites send at about 1.7 GHz, 665,400 bit/s. This plugin finds the carrier, recovers the bits, finds the frame synchronisation and draws the five AVHRR channels side by side as they arrive, with a line of text per frame. It needs complex samples at 2.4 million samples a second or more (3.0 preferred) from a receiver that tunes that high.

No calibration, no temperature or telemetry decoding, and no Metop, FengYun or Electro-L. Written from the NOAA KLM Users Guide. It has been tested on generated frames only: no real HRPT signal has been decoded, so treat it as unproven on the air. Whether any NOAA satellite still transmits HRPT has not been checked.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.1.0: New. NOAA HRPT frame synchronisation and five-channel AVHRR pictures from raw I/Q. Generated frames only.

plugins.name: Short-Range Frames (EnOcean, Zigbee / 802.15.4, nRF24, Z-Wave)
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Shows the frames of four short-range radios from raw I/Q - EnOcean (868.3 MHz), Zigbee / IEEE 802.15.4 (2.4 GHz), nRF24L01 (2.4 GHz) and Z-Wave (868 MHz, ITU-T G.9959) - by their headers and framing only, never the payload.
plugins.description:
Four short-range radios in one plugin - EnOcean, Zigbee / IEEE 802.15.4, nRF24L01 and Z-Wave - chosen with the setting "Protocol" (label "Protocol EnOcean/Zigbee/nRF/ZW", key frames.mode; type enocean, zigbee, nrf24 or zwave). Left blank it follows the tuned band, and where bands overlap the narrowest band wins: 868.7 to 869.9 MHz is Z-Wave, the rest of 860 to 880 MHz is EnOcean, 2.4 GHz is 802.15.4 (up to 2.5 GHz nRF24); EnOcean and Z-Wave share the 868 MHz band and nRF24 shares 2.4 GHz with 802.15.4, so choose explicitly when you are not on a protocol's own preset. The plugin opens on the protocol you used last and you can change it while it runs. Each protocol keeps its own presets and settings. Receive only: nothing is transmitted, written to disk or sent anywhere.

ENOCEAN MONITOR: EnOcean ERP1 telegrams at 868.3 MHz (the energy-harvesting switches and sensors): it finds the preamble, undoes the line code, checks the telegram check and prints the telegram type byte and its name (RPS, 1BS, 4BS, VLD), the data bytes as raw values, the sender and the status. Device addresses are hidden by default. Typing an equipment profile such as A5-02-05 adds that profile's name; what a value means is not interpreted.

IEEE 802.15.4 (ZIGBEE, THREAD): the 2.4 GHz channels 11 to 26: frame type, sequence number, PAN and shortened addresses, length and whether the check passed; never the payload. Needs a whole multiple of 4 MS/s (8 suggested).

NRF24L01 FRAMING: Enhanced ShockBurst packets of the nRF24L01 / nRF24L01+ (wireless keyboards, mice and sensors) at 2.4 GHz: channel, air rate, address width, payload length and whether the check passed; never the payload; addresses hidden by default. Needs a whole number of MS/s that is a multiple of 4 or 6 (8 suggested).

Z-WAVE MONITOR: Z-Wave (ITU-T G.9959), the low-power radio of home-automation switches, sensors and locks, on the European 868 MHz carriers (EU R1 9.6 kbit/s, R2 40 kbit/s and R3 100 kbit/s): preamble and start of frame, the frame's own check sequence, then one line per frame with the data rate, the header type (singlecast, multicast, acknowledgement or beam), the sequence number, whether an acknowledgement was asked for, the payload LENGTH and whether the check passed. Network and device numbers are hidden by default (shown as "network 1" and "device 1", held in memory only; the setting "Z-Wave: hide network/device IDs" turns that off). The payload is never read, nothing is decrypted and no key is held. Tune the preset "Z-Wave EU 869.1 MHz (R1 R2 R3)" with 2 MS/s or more. Tested on generated signals and on one recording of the owner's own band; the 9.6 kbit/s rate on generated signals only.

LIMITS: tested on generated signals only (Z-Wave also on one recording); no payload of any protocol is ever read.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.5.0: On FoxSDR 0.99.109 and later the Protocol setting is a drop-down list (Automatic by tuned band, EnOcean, Zigbee, nRF24, Z-Wave) instead of a text box; the setting is unchanged and an older FoxSDR still shows the text box. 0.4.1: nRF24 no longer lists phantom links when one device repeats the same frame hundreds of times (a one-byte check passing by chance on a wrong reading of the same frame was heard twice and became a link). 0.4.0: EnOcean Monitor, IEEE 802.15.4 (Zigbee), nRF24L01 Framing and Z-Wave Monitor are now one plugin with a Protocol setting (enocean, zigbee, nrf24 or zwave; blank follows the tuned band) and one frame table; each keeps its own presets and settings. Tested on generated signals only.
plugins.legalNotice: The EnOcean telegram-type names, function-group names and equipment-profile titles (213 titles) come from two MIT-licensed projects: enocean-js/eep-spec (Copyright (c) 2017 node-enocean) and kipe/enocean (Copyright (c) 2014-2016 Kimmo Huoman), MIT licence. Only identifier and title pairs were taken; no code. The full notice, with both licence texts, is enocean/THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md in the plugin source.

plugins.name: DVB-S and DVB-T Receiver
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Locks onto a digital TV transmission (DVB-S or DVB-S2 satellite, or DVB-T terrestrial, including hierarchical DVB-T HP or LP) from raw I/Q and lists the services in it. Tables only: no video and no sound.
plugins.description:
Demodulates DVB-S (QPSK) and DVB-T (2K and 8K carriers; QPSK, 16-QAM and 64-QAM, hierarchical or not) from raw I/Q, corrects the errors and recovers the transport stream. It reads the programme tables and shows the service names, the stream types and whether a service is scrambled, with a plot of the constellation. It never decodes video or audio.

You set the system, symbol rate or bandwidth and code rate in its dvb.cfg file. Optionally it can pass the clear transport stream to a UDP port on this computer; that is off by default and goes to 127.0.0.1 unless you change it. Nothing else leaves the program.

Receive only. Proven on generated signals only: it has not met a real DVB signal. Since 0.2.0 DVB-T needs roughly 0.3 to 0.8 of one processor core at 9.14 MS/s in the modes measured (2 to 6.4 before), using a second thread for the error correction and fast code that needs a processor with AVX2. Without AVX2 the 64-QAM modes will not keep up and the plugin drops input, which the panel counts.
