If your radio runs faster than 9.14 MS/s (10 or 20 MS/s is typical) the worst mode measured needs about 1.2 cores on one thread, so a busy or slow computer can still fall behind. DVB-S at code rate 1/2 now locks down to about 2.5 dB Es/N0 (it needed about 5.5 dB), also on generated signals only. Since 0.3.0 DVB-S2 normal frames are decoded too (set system dvbs2 in dvb.cfg; it is never part of auto); short frames, multiple input streams and DVB-S2X are counted, not decoded, and DVB-T2 is not supported. Some digital television systems are covered by patent pools; whether any applies to you is for you to check. Since 0.4.0 hierarchical DVB-T (alpha 1, 2 and 4) is decoded too: the high-priority stream by default, the low-priority stream with "hierarchy lp" in dvb.cfg, on generated signals only.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.4.0: Decodes DVB-T hierarchical transmission (alpha 1, 2 and 4): the high-priority stream by default, the low-priority stream with "hierarchy lp" in dvb.cfg. Proven on generated signals only; no real hierarchical DVB-T signal has been tried. 0.3.0: Adds DVB-S2 normal frames (all 28 MODCODs, pilots on or off), chosen with "system dvbs2" in dvb.cfg. Short frames, multiple input streams and DVB-S2X are counted but not decoded. Proven on generated signals only; no real DVB-S2 signal has been tried.

plugins.name: Analogue TV
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Draws the black-and-white picture of an analogue television transmission (PAL B/G or NTSC M) from raw I/Q. Picture only: no colour and no sound output. Receive only.
plugins.description:
Finds the vision carrier, recovers the luminance, finds the line and field timing and draws frames as 720 by 576 (PAL B/G) or 720 by 480 (NTSC M) grey pictures. The sound carrier is demodulated inside the plugin but is not passed to the audio output, and colour is not built.

Tested on generated test cards only: no real analogue transmission could be received here, and the line window, first active line and field order are this plugin's own choices, so treat it as unproven. Receive only, and no network.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.1.0: New. PAL B/G and NTSC M luminance pictures from raw I/Q. Generated signals only.

plugins.name: Loran-C Receiver
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Finds the pulse groups of a Loran-C chain in the 100 kHz band and reports the group repetition interval and the time delays between stations. Receive only.
plugins.description:
Loran-C is the 100 kHz pulsed navigation system. This plugin looks for the eight-pulse groups (with the ninth pulse on the master), reads the phase codes, works out the chain's group repetition interval and reports the delays of the secondary stations after the master. It needs the radio centred within the 100 kHz band at 100 kS/s or more.

Tested on generated signals only. The phase codes come from a 1992 receiver program and were cross-checked, not from the Coast Guard specification, which was not obtained. Treat it as unproven; receive only, no network.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.1.0: New. Loran-C pulse-group detection with chain and station delays. Generated signals only.

plugins.name: UAT 978 MHz
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Reads the aircraft messages and ground uplink frames on the 978 MHz UAT channel from raw I/Q: message types, rebroadcast counts, the ground station's position and uplink headers. It shows no aircraft identities or positions. Receive only.
plugins.description:
UAT is the 978 MHz data link used by some general-aviation aircraft in the United States. This plugin finds the bursts, corrects them with the Reed-Solomon code and reports ADS-B messages (basic and long) and ground uplink frames. It needs I/Q at 2.083 million samples a second or more around 978 MHz. From 0.2.0 it also reads the payload layers: the ADS-B message types, the address qualifiers (including TIS-B and ADS-R rebroadcasts and the uplink site that sent them), the position of the uplink ground station, and the uplink frames' headers and the product headers inside them, shown as counts and short text lines. It never prints an aircraft address, call sign or position, and it does not decode the weather and radar products carried in the uplink.

Tested on generated bursts only. Receive only, no network.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.2.0: Now reads what is inside the bursts: ADS-B message types, TIS-B and ADS-R rebroadcast counts, the uplink ground station's position and the uplink frame and product headers. No aircraft address, call sign or position is shown, and the weather products inside the uplink are not decoded. Generated signals only.

plugins.name: VOR Navigation Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Reads the radial you are on from an aviation VOR beacon, and its Morse ident.
plugins.description:
A VHF omnidirectional range is a ground beacon that tells every aircraft in range which bearing from the station it is on, and it does that by transmitting two 30 Hz signals whose phase difference IS the bearing. This reads them and prints the answer once a second: the radial you are sitting on, clockwise from magnetic north at the station, and the reciprocal course that would take you to it - both of them, because confusing the two is the classic way to read a VOR backwards.

It reads the station's callsign as well. Every VOR sends two or three letters in Morse at about seven words a minute, three times in each half minute, and without them a bearing is a number from nowhere in particular.

It also opens an instrument window - the cockpit course indicator the reading belongs on, with the compass card turned to your radial, the ident and its Morse on the glass beneath, an OBS knob that selects a course and swings the deviation bar and the TO/FROM flag from the bearing being received, and a NAV warning flag across the face whenever there is no valid signal.

SET THE CHANNEL WIDE. Tune anywhere from 108.000 to 117.950 MHz in AM, and make the channel AT LEAST ABOUT 22 kHz wide. That is the one thing you have to get right and the one thing that fails silently: the bearing reference rides on a 9,960 Hz subcarrier that a normal 6 or 10 kHz AM filter removes entirely, and what is left still sounds exactly like a VOR. Rather than sit there producing nothing, the decoder says so in as many words when the subcarrier is missing.

There are no preset frequencies, deliberately. Every other decoder here ships them because a mode lives on the same frequency the world over; VOR channels are assigned station by station, so any list would be wrong for almost everyone who installed it. Find your local beacon on a chart, or turn on the Airports and Navaids plugin, which knows where they are.

Nothing is invented from an empty channel: the decoder wants both 30 Hz signals present, at the strengths the standard specifies, before it will report a bearing at all. Written clean-room from ICAO Annex 10, Volume I, section 3.3, with the Morse alphabet reused from this project's own CW decoder. Conventional and Doppler VOR both read correctly - the standard requires them to look the same from the receiver's side - and the bearing is magnetic, as the station transmits it. A true-north radial is added only when it can be: from a declination you set, or, once the ident has matched, from the magnetic variation the navaid list gives that station.

NEW IN 1.1.0. If the Airports and Navaids plugin's navaid list is cached on this machine, the decoded ident is compared with the VOR stations listed within 5 kHz of the tuned frequency, and the plugin says whether it matches or is NOT on the list (it says nothing if there is no list). Each line also shows the strengths of the 30 Hz reference and variable tones, and from the third reading a circular average for that station over the last readings (up to 12 within 60 seconds). An optional scan (FOXSDR_VOR_SCAN=113.6,114.5, off by default) asks FoxSDR to retune across the channels you list, which needs the receiver-control permission, and reports each station's average.

WHAT IT WILL NOT DO / LIMITS: the true radial needs a declination (FOXSDR_VOR_DECLINATION_DEG, east positive) or a matched ident; none is claimed otherwise. The 30 Hz strengths are relative qualities, not absolute levels. These switches are environment variables only; there is no settings screen for them. Tried on generated signals and test files only: no real VOR recording was available, and the scan on a real FoxSDR, or a station whose tuned frequency differs from the list by more than 5 kHz, was not checked.
plugins.whatsNew: 1.1.0: Checks the Morse ident against the navaid list of the Airports and Navaids plugin, adds a true-north radial from a declination you give or the station's listed variation, a running average per station, and an optional scan across channels you list. Generated signals only.

plugins.name: ACARS Aircraft Datalink Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Decodes the short data messages airliners send on the AM airband.
plugins.description:
Airliners exchange short text messages with their airline and with air traffic control over ordinary VHF AM - position reports, departure clearances, weather requests, engine data, and the occasional message typed by a human. This decodes them and prints one line per message: which aircraft sent it, by registration, the message label, the flight number, and the text.

It brings its own instrument window as well, drawn as the thermal message printer fitted to an airliner's flight deck: the latest message's header on a strip of paper emerging from the slot, a counter of how many have been printed, and the roll itself listed underneath.

Tune it with one of the presets - 131.550 MHz over North America, 131.725 MHz over Europe - and LEAVE THE SQUELCH OPEN. A transmission is a burst lasting a fraction of a second, and a squelch that has to open first will have missed the start of it.

Every message carries a 16-bit check sequence and every character carries a parity bit, and nothing is printed unless the check sequence agrees. A block whose check sequence passes but which has a bad parity bit is still printed, and the line says how many parity errors it had. A burst that arrives damaged produces no line rather than a line with the wrong aeroplane in it. An optional setting, off by default, retries a block that has exactly one bad character with each of that character's bits flipped and marks the result 'crc fixed'; it can let through about 8 in 65,536 blocks damaged some other way.

Written from the published description of the air-ground protocol: 2400 bit/s minimum shift keying on AM, characters of seven ASCII bits and an odd parity bit, and the block check sequence verified against ten real ACARS blocks published in the CRC RevEng catalogue.

WIDE CAPTURE, JOINING AND FILTERS. Given the receiver's raw baseband (2.4 MS/s preferred, anything from 40 kS/s), it decodes up to eight channels at once, each as its own receiver: by default the six standard ACARS channels that fall inside the capture, or a list of channels you type. A message sent in several blocks is joined into one line (marked INCOMPLETE if the last block does not arrive within 20 seconds), and a block sent again is dropped. Every line ends with the signal level and the parity and check state. You can show only chosen labels, registrations or flights, hide uplink or empty messages, and a message heard on two adjacent channels is shown once.

OUTPUTS, ALL OFF BY DEFAULT. One JSON record per message can go to a rotating log file you name and to a UDP address (numeric IPv4, 127.0.0.1 unless you type another). Until you set them nothing is written, no folder is created and no socket is opened. The records carry registrations and message text, so they are for you, on your machine. A file of airline codes and names that you supply adds the airline to the flight; none is shipped. Messages wrapped in the ARINC 622 form are checked and summarised after the line as 'app': CPDLC (pilot-controller) messages are spelled out, ADS-C reports are spelled out (the aircraft's own broadcast position appears in the text line), AFN is named, MIAM and OHMA messages are decoded and OHMA payloads that are protected are reported, never decrypted, and a wrapper whose check value fails is reported rather than decoded.

WHAT IT WILL NOT DO / LIMITS: the signal level is relative to full scale of the capture, not calibrated, and the level of the audio decoder is not comparable with the level of the wide-capture decoder. It was tried on generated signals and on two real recordings (a short audio recording and a 3.5 second I/Q one) plus a 70 second band file assembled from them. No ARINC 622 message was found in the real recording checked for it, so the CPDLC, ADS-C, MIAM and OHMA decoding is proven only on published examples and on generated messages and has never read a real one (a later 300 s recording held none either). It does not feed airframes.io or any community site or write the PlanePlotter format. Which of this plugin's two decoders FoxSDR feeds when both are declared was not checked; a message seen by both is shown once.
plugins.whatsNew: 1.1.2: ARINC 622 payloads are read further: ADS-C reports are spelled out (position, altitude, speed, flight-plan groups), MIAM messages and OHMA operations messages are decoded, and OHMA payloads that are protected are reported and never decrypted. Proven on generated messages and one published ADS-C example only; no real one has been read.

plugins.name: Map Imagery (OpenStreetMap)
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Draws street-level OpenStreetMap tiles under the aircraft, ship and station maps, not on the satellites map. Works on install.
plugins.description:
Replaces the built-in coastline with real street-level map imagery, so aircraft, ships and stations are plotted over roads and place names instead of an outline. The map switches to the projection the tiles are drawn in while this is active, and back again when it is removed. The satellites map is the exception: it keeps the built-in coastline, because the tiles are drawn in a projection that would tear a satellite's ground track apart, and it says so on that page while this plugin is running.

INSTALLING IT IS THE WHOLE OF THE SETUP. It works on first run with nothing to configure, drawing OpenStreetMap tiles. Earlier versions shipped with no server and drew nothing until you wrote a config file; that is no longer the case.

If you would rather serve your own tiles - for more detail, for volume, or to be independent of somebody else's server - put a one-line openmaptiles.conf next to the plugin giving your server's address, and it uses that instead. Any server that publishes ordinary map tiles will do.

WHAT IT TELLS A SERVER. Every tile it asks tile.openstreetmap.org for tells that server, along with your internet address, roughly where the map is looking. It asks only for the tiles a map is showing, and only while one that draws tiles is on screen. With your own server in openmaptiles.conf, OpenStreetMap is not contacted.

Map data is (c) OpenStreetMap contributors, and that credit is displayed under the map whenever the tiles are on screen - the application will not draw a basemap it cannot credit.

Tiles are cached on disk, so an area you have looked at works again without a network, nothing is fetched twice, and only what you are actually looking at is ever requested. The cache is now kept under 2048 MB by default (oldest tiles removed first; the limit and an optional maximum age in days can be changed, and 0 means no limit).

MORE SOURCES, WRITTEN BY YOU. A file named openmaptiles.sources can hold several named sources, and a Map source field in the settings picks one while the program runs. Each source can use {s} subdomains, @2x tiles and an API key read from the FOXSDR_TILE_KEY environment variable or typed in the Map key field - the key is never shown or put in a file name. There are grey and dimming filters, and an overlay (for example a weather layer) with its own opacity. A source or overlay without an attribution line is refused, and every source's credit is shown under the map. Only OpenStreetMap is on by default; since 1.3.0 a presets line in openmaptiles.conf adds named sources (OpenTopoMap, NASA GIBS, CARTO styles) with their credits, and CARTO needs your own API key. For any other provider it is up to you to follow that provider's terms. An offline folder of tiles can be used instead of, or before, the network. The maxzoom setting, which older versions read and ignored, now limits what is asked for.

LIMITS. MBTiles files cannot be read (convert them to a folder of tiles first). The Map source field is a text box, not a list. Looking up the newest weather frame from a provider is not done; you type the time. The new features were tested against stand-in servers and tile folders, and have not been tried in the full application. The satellites map never draws these tiles.
plugins.whatsNew: 1.3.1: Text only; the module behaves as 1.3.0. The catalogue no longer implies tiles on the satellites map (it keeps the coastline) and now says what a tile request tells the OpenStreetMap server. 1.3.0: Adds optional named tile sources (OpenTopoMap, NASA GIBS, CARTO styles and OpenStreetMap) chosen with the "presets" line in openmaptiles.conf, off until you add it, a field for your own API key where a source needs one, and a per-source cache age. Their address and credit text have not been tried against the live services.

plugins.name: Example RMS Reporter
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Reference plugin: reports the RMS level of the demodulated audio.
plugins.description: A minimal, fully working decoder plugin built from examples/example_plugin in the application source. It consumes demodulated audio and periodically emits a line of text reporting the block's RMS level. It exists to prove the plugin ABI and the catalogue install path end to end, and to serve as the template for real decoders. The version number tracks what the plugin does, not which ABI it was built against - the ABI is recorded separately and appears in the filename, so the same version can be published for more than one.
plugins.whatsNew: 2.0.0: Reports the RMS level of the demodulated audio; the reference plugin for the plugin ABI and the catalogue install path.

plugins.name: Decoder Workbench
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Decodes a whole band at once from one radio - every ACARS, weather, paging or APRS channel, merged into one window.
plugins.description:
Four sets of channels sit close enough together that one radio is already sampling all of them: the six ACARS frequencies, the seven NOAA weather channels, the four US paging channels and the two APRS ones. Until now you could only decode one at a time, because those decoders work on demodulated audio and a receiver demodulates one channel at a time - which is what the presets on those plugins are for.

This plugin takes the raw stream instead, splits every channel out of it, and runs a separate decoder on each. Every message lands in the same window with the frequency it arrived on at the start of the line, so you watch a whole band rather than picking a channel and hoping.

WHAT IT DECODES FOLLOWS WHERE YOU TUNE IT. Point the radio at the weather band and you get all seven NOAA channels; at 931 MHz, four paging channels; at the ACARS band, six aircraft channels; at 144 MHz, both APRS frequencies. There is a preset for each. Its panel lists every channel of whichever band you are on - whether your radio can currently reach it, the signal on it, and how many messages it has carried - so a half-covered band cannot look like a fully covered one.

YOUR OWN CHANNELS (0.3.0). Two settings, both empty by default, add a fifth band of your own: Own list: decoder (ACARS, POCSAG, weather or APRS) and Own list: MHz (up to 12 channels, each a frequency, optionally with a label such as RAMP=129.125, no two within 5 kHz of each other). When your list and a built-in band reach the same number of channels at the current tuning, yours is used. A list that does not parse is named in the decoder output and ignored whole, so a half-read list never puts a receiver on a frequency you did not write. The settings are read once when the plugin starts, so change them and restart the receiver or reopen the plugin; the presets stay the four built-in bands. In a test with generated ACARS frames at 129.125 and 129.375 MHz and the radio centred at 129.25 MHz, the built-in band decoded none of the two frames and the custom list decoded both; no off-air recording at those frequencies was tried.

Needs a receiver whose rate divides down to something the decoder accepts: 2.4, 1.2 and 0.24 MS/s all work, and the weather channels fit in 0.24 MS/s with room to spare. A rate that cannot (2.048 MS/s, for instance) is refused with a line saying so rather than decoding silently wrong. The demodulators are the same ones the ACARS, POCSAG, weather and APRS plugins use, unchanged; this plugin is the part that lets you run several of each at once.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.3.0: You can now give it your own list of up to 12 channels, with labels, and the decoder to run on them, so a band the built-in tables do not cover can be decoded too. Empty by default, read when the plugin starts. Tried on generated frames only.

plugins.name: ADS-B Aircraft Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Plots aircraft at 1090 MHz with flight trails, callsign, altitude and speed.
plugins.description:
Decodes Mode S / ADS-B transmissions from aircraft at 1090 MHz and reports callsign, position, altitude, ground speed, track and vertical rate. Every frame is validated against the 24-bit Mode S CRC. A frame carrying a single damaged bit is repaired - the CRC identifies which bit, so a weak aircraft at the edge of range is heard rather than lost - and anything the CRC cannot account for is discarded rather than shown as phantom aircraft. A position is recovered from an even/odd CPR frame pair, or, as described below, from a single frame.

Once an aircraft has a position less than five minutes old, each position frame it sends updates that position: one frame is enough, with no pair to wait for. A new aircraft below about 32,000 ft and within 100 nautical miles of the receiver is placed from a single frame, against the receiver position set in FoxSDR, and the next frame pair confirms that position or corrects it. With FoxSDR 0.99.75 or newer, the aircraft the decoder hears but cannot place yet are listed in the target list as "heard without a position"; older versions do not list them.

This decoder works on raw I/Q rather than demodulated audio, so it needs a receiver capable of 1090 MHz at 2 MS/s or more; 2.4 MS/s or higher is recommended, because at exactly 2 MS/s one sub-sample timing alignment in eight is unrecoverable in principle. A 1090 MHz antenna makes far more difference than any setting. The receiver's own DC offset is tracked and removed before detection, so a zero-IF dongle such as an RTL-SDR - whose offset would otherwise bury every aircraft not on top of the antenna - hears what it should.

Airborne and surface positions, callsign, velocity, vertical rate, geometric height, squawk and emergency status are decoded, and each aircraft draws a flight trail on the map. Aircraft that stop transmitting are released rather than accumulating for the session. Written clean-room from the published Mode S specification.

Mode A/C replies can be listed as well, from the same 1090 MHz stream: tick "List Mode A/C replies" in the plugin's settings (off by default). Each reply is shown with BOTH readings - the four-digit identity (squawk) and the Gillham pressure altitude - because a reply does not say which one it is: that is decided by the interrogation on 1030 MHz, which this receiver does not hear. Where the pulses cannot be a legal altitude the line says so. Replies are read only when they stand alone on the pulse grid and are 12 to 16 dB or more over the noise; garbled or weak ones are skipped, not guessed.

MORE DECODED IN 1.11.0. Besides position and identity it reads what an aircraft says about its own accuracy and equipment (ADS-B version, NACp, SIL, NICbaro, GVA), alert and SPI flags, TCAS (ACAS) replies including resolution advisories, geometric altitude and its difference from barometric altitude, and counts of messages per aircraft by type. It works out outside air temperature from other registers an aircraft answers with, and wind too if you give it a magnetic variation. Altitude can be shown against a QNH you enter, below the transition altitude. Extra Comm-B registers (1,0 1,7 3,0 4,4 4,5) can be identified, off by default, because some random fields look like them (0.011 percent in a test on random data). Error repair depth, a minimum frame count before listing, a speed limit, a range limit, and dropping unassigned addresses or DF18 frames are words in the 'Accept and decoder options' setting; the defaults leave the decoder as it was.

NEW IN 1.12.0. Aircraft in a military address block are marked military with no flag file, and the airline and route are looked up from the callsign in tables built into the plugin (Virtual Radar Server standing data, CC0, about 3.8 MB added to the plugin). The magnetic variation at your receiver is worked out from the World Magnetic Model 2025 for the derived wind. The readsb layout of the aircraft list is served at /data/aircraft.json and /readsb/aircraft.json and written beside the JSON file. The military flag is per address block, and the route data is what Virtual Radar users filed, so it is not complete.

LOCAL OUTPUTS AND TOOLS, ALL OFF OR INERT BY DEFAULT. The plugin keeps aircraft for 15 minutes after their last message (settable, 1 to 120), carries the last position along the last course for at most 3 minutes and marks it rough, and shows the country from the ICAO address. You can supply a flag file (military, interesting, PIA, LADD; none is shipped), filter the map by altitude, range, callsign and more, and write the aircraft list as JSON to a file or a local port, as a Virtual Radar style list, as SBS lines, raw AVR, Beast frames, ASTERIX CAT021 datagrams and Prometheus metrics, and read other receivers' SBS, Beast or JSON feeds from this PC. Every output binds 127.0.0.1 and every input connects to 127.0.0.1; nothing is sent to an outside service.

WHAT IT WILL NOT DO / LIMITS: the target state message's selected altitude, selected heading and autopilot modes are not decoded (no free layout was found), nor are its TCAS flags. The country table comes from an older edition of the ICAO allocation. The outputs were tried against stand-in listeners only, not against real SBS, Beast, ASTERIX or Virtual Radar consumers, and the readsb aircraft.json layout follows the published key list only: it leaves out the climb rates and the keys the decoder does not hold. Rough (carried-forward) positions reach the map only on a FoxSDR that holds estimated tracks. Wind and the extra Comm-B registers were not seen in the recordings, so they are checked on worked examples only.
plugins.whatsNew: 1.12.0: Works out magnetic variation from the World Magnetic Model 2025 for the derived wind, marks military aircraft from address blocks, and gives airline and route from the callsign using built-in public-domain (CC0) tables, with no network needed. It also writes the aircraft list in the readsb aircraft.json layout at /data/aircraft.json and /readsb/aircraft.json, as a second JSON file beside the first, and adds a Trt field to the Virtual Radar list.

screenshots.caption: The receiver at 1090 MHz beside the map: eight aircraft with trails, callsign, altitude and speed.
The map alone, as the plugin's own window shows it.

plugins.name: Wireless M-Bus Meter Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Reads the 868 MHz bursts European heat, water, gas and electricity meters transmit, and decrypts your own with your own keys.
plugins.description:
Decodes Wireless M-Bus (EN 13757-4, OMS) telegrams - the short bursts European utility meters send at 868 MHz so a walk-by or drive-by receiver can read them. Modes S (868.30 MHz), T and C (868.95 MHz) are all heard at once from one wide slice of band. For each telegram it reports the meter's manufacturer letters, number, version and kind (water, gas, heat, electricity, heat cost allocator and so on), the signal level, and the data records it carries: the register, instantaneous values, dates and status.

EXPERIMENTAL. Six off-air captures in the project's sample set decode 8 telegrams and refuse 3 by their CRC; apart from that it was proved only on documents and a transmitter written by the same author. It was written clean-room from published documents only. It decodes and decrypts every complete example telegram in OMS Specification Volume 2 Annex N exactly, and passes a self-test against a transmitter written by the same author, but the physical-layer details that only the paid EN 13757-4 states (the 3-out-of-6 table's mapping, the Manchester and NRZ conventions, frame format B) are listed in the README as unverified, and an encoder and a decoder written by one author can agree with each other and both be wrong.

ENCRYPTED METERS. Most meters encrypt their readings (AES-128, OMS security modes 5 and 7). Without the meter's key the telegram is still named and counted but no reading is shown. The plugin has one text setting, AES keys, in which you may list `meter number=32 hex digits` pairs for meters YOU own or are authorised to read; a wrong key is reported as wrong, never shown as data. The plugin does not guess, search for or ask for keys.

Every block of every telegram is checked against the 16-bit CRC and anything that fails is discarded or reported as refused, never shown as a reading. It opens an INSTRUMENT WINDOW drawn as a utility meter: the newest reading on a register, and beneath it a roster of every meter heard, with signal level, mode, whether a key was used and how long ago each last transmitted.

The presets tune 868.95 MHz (T and C), 868.30 MHz (S) and 868.625 MHz, which holds all three at 2.4 MS/s. Any rate from 250 kS/s to 61.44 MS/s works; 2.4 MS/s is suggested.

NEW IN 0.2.0 (settings page, all off or neutral unless noted): a switch that hides meter addresses (they become m1, m2 and so on on screen and in outputs); a repeat window that drops an identical telegram heard again; a silence alarm that flags a meter not heard for a number of minutes; a Rate column giving the change per hour of a meter's register between two readings; an analyse mode that prints the structure of each telegram without any address; OMS standard field names and a driver name (gas, water and so on) in the JSON output; and JSON lines over UDP and one CSV log file per meter, the files named and filled by a session pseudonym, never by meter address.

WHAT IT WILL NOT DO / LIMITS: by default nothing leaves your machine: no network, no files written, and the keys stay in FoxSDR's own settings. Switching on the JSON output (to an address you choose, 127.0.0.1 by default) or the per-meter log changes that. Not built: the 169 MHz N-mode, maker-specific meter drivers (only OMS-standard records are named) and a command run per telegram. A changed setting takes effect when the panel is next polled or the receiver next starts. The UDP and CSV outputs were run on Windows only.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.2.0: Adds a switch to hide meter addresses, a repeat window, a silence alarm, a Rate column, an analyse mode, OMS standard field names, and optional JSON output over UDP and a per-meter CSV log. All are off or neutral by default; decoding is unchanged.
plugins.legalNotice: Wireless M-Bus telegrams carry a meter's number and, once decrypted, its consumption: personal data about whoever lives there. Receive and decode only your own meters, or meters you are authorised to read, and enter AES keys only for those. Using or disclosing the content of messages not addressed to you can be an offence in your country (in the UK, Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006 s.48). This plugin never transmits and sends nothing off your machine.

plugins.name: DAB / DAB+ Radio
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Plays one station of a DAB or DAB+ multiplex from Band III, with its text and slideshow; DAB+ sound needs ffmpeg, or FFmpeg's libraries, installed on your computer.
plugins.description:
READ THIS FIRST. DAB+ sound needs a decoder on your computer. DAB+ stations are coded with HE-AAC, a patented codec, and this plugin contains no AAC decoder: it runs ffmpeg, which you install yourself (winget install Gyan.FFmpeg, or the download page at ffmpeg.org), as a separate program, handing it each station's audio and taking its sound back. Since 0.7.0 it can instead load FFmpeg's shared libraries (avcodec and avutil, a build you installed) from the folder you name in the setting 'FFmpeg libraries (folder)' and decode inside this process; with the setting empty, or if the libraries do not load, it uses the ffmpeg program as before. The library route has been tried against stand-in libraries only. FoxSDR does not ship ffmpeg and does not install it. The plugin finds ffmpeg on your PATH or in the places winget, Chocolatey and a hand install use, or at the path you give in the settings (with a BROWSE FILES key on FoxSDR 0.99.74 and later). Without it a DAB+ station is silent in FoxSDR, the panel says "DAB+ sound needs ffmpeg" and what to do about it, and the receiver's own audio carries on. DAB stations (MPEG-1 Layer II) need nothing: they are decoded inside the plugin. The program ffmpeg is yours, under its own licence, and the plugin only starts it and exchanges bytes with it.

Decodes Eureka 147 DAB and DAB+ in Band III - the digital radio multiplexes carried across the UK and Europe. It synchronizes to the 96 ms transmission frame, reads the Fast Information Channel, lists the multiplex's name and every service on it, and plays one station through the receiver's own audio output: MPEG-1 Layer II for DAB, HE-AAC v2 (through ffmpeg) for DAB+. While it plays it shows the station's scrolling text - and, where the broadcaster tags it, which part is the title and which the artist - and the pictures of its slideshow.

YOU PICK THE STATION IN THE PLUGIN'S OWN WINDOW. The panel numbers every audio service (#0, #1, ...). Type a number into Service number, or part of a name into Station name ('planet' finds 'Planet Rock'; a name wins over a number), or press the NEXT STATION and PREVIOUS STATION keys to step through the list. Each multiplex remembers the station you last chose on it, so tuning back to a block resumes where you were. A dab.cfg file beside the plugin's data still works for choosing a station, and is the only way on a FoxSDR older than 0.99.43, which draws no boxes.

IT NEEDS EXACTLY 2.048 MS/s and says so. At that rate every duration in the standard is a whole number of samples, so the 2048-point transform, the guard interval and the null symbol all line up with no resampler in the way; at 2.4 MS/s not one of them does. Both the RTL-SDR family and the USRP B200 offer the rate, and the preset asks for it along with the block.

Sixteen presets: the three UK national ensembles by name - 12B for BBC National DAB, 11D for Digital One, 11A for SDL National - and thirteen more Band III blocks in wide use across Europe. The complete 5A to 13F raster is built in, so tuning by hand to a block that is not in the list still names it. The panel shows whether the receiver is synchronized, the signal-to-noise ratio, the carrier offset and, while it is searching, how deep the null symbol it can see is - the number that tells 'there is no DAB transmitter on this block' from 'there is one and it cannot be decoded'. When a DAB+ station is playing it also shows what the decoder program is doing: whether it was found, its process, and how many units of audio it has been sent.

WHAT HAS BEEN HEARD, AND WHAT HAS NOT. Most of it is tested against a DAB transmitter written for the test from the standards: the built plugin end to end in transmission mode I, and the demodulator in all four modes. Off the air, in West Yorkshire on 2026-10-12 with a USRP B200 at 2.048 MS/s, it locked to BBC National DAB (block 12B) and to Digital One (11D) and played a station from each through FoxSDR. On 12B every Fast Information Block passed its check, 744 super frames decoded with no Reed-Solomon failure, the audio ran for 85 seconds with nothing dropped, and NEXT STATION and PREVIOUS STATION changed station; the station's scrolling text came through as well. SDL National (11A) was marginal: about half its information blocks passed and the audio broke up, whatever the gain. On 2026-10-12 version 0.5.0 played a DAB+ station of Digital One (11D) through FoxSDR with ffmpeg found on the PATH - 662 super frames with no Reed-Solomon failure and 78 seconds of audio with nothing dropped - and with no ffmpeg anywhere the panel said what was needed and a DAB station of the same ensemble still played. NOT seen on a real signal: the slideshow pictures and the DL Plus title and artist tags - which is why this is still experimental. Those runs measured the audio's level and continuity; how it sounds was not recorded. Services are read in transmission mode I, the only one in service in Europe; the other three are demodulated and named, nothing more. It will not decode where the signal is weak or the aerial is not meant for Band III (174 to 240 MHz).

NEW IN 0.6.0. Transmitter ID: it reads the transmitter codes (TII) in the null symbol and lists the transmitters it hears; with a CSV table of your own (eid, main, sub, name, lat, lon, kW) those it can place appear on the map. No transmitter database is shipped. Band scan: the keys SCAN BAND III, SCAN CONTINUOUSLY and STOP SCAN step the receiver through the 38 Band III blocks and list each ensemble found; this needs you to give the plugin the TUNE grant, and it has never been run on a real radio. Also decode: up to three more services are decoded beside the playing one. More information: ensemble country, time and local offset, alarm and other announcements, other frequencies, programme types, and the channel (impulse response, delay spread, bit error rate of the information channel). Packet-mode data: a slideshow carried in a packet component is read (generated signals only).

RECORDINGS AND THE EDI STREAM ARE OFF BY DEFAULT. You can switch on a recording of each decoded service's own frames, a CSV log of titles (both can be limited to a daily UTC window), an ensemble recording in ETI format, and an EDI stream over TCP that listens on 127.0.0.1 only (this computer) at a port you choose; port 0 is off and nothing connects out. The ETI file and the EDI stream have not been read by any other program. Journaline, TPEG, the programme guide (EPG), secondary audio components and EDI over UDP are not supported.

Needs FoxSDR 0.99.43 or later for the boxes; the keys appear on the plugin's plate in FoxSDR's Fitted modules (NEXT STATION, PREVIOUS STATION and the three scan keys).

Written clean-room from ETSI EN 300 401, TS 102 563, TS 101 756 and the related ETSI specifications, and from ISO/IEC 14496-3's LOAS/LATM syntax for the framing it hands ffmpeg; no GPL DAB receiver, and no source of ffmpeg or any other AAC decoder, was used as source material (the library route was written from FFmpeg's public API documentation, with no FFmpeg source or header in this tree). Layer II audio is decoded by kjmp2 by Martin J. Fiedler, included unmodified under the zlib licence with its notice intact. Slideshow pictures are decoded with stb_image by Sean Barrett, public domain or MIT. The plugin contains no AAC code: the Fraunhofer FDK AAC library that 0.4.0 carried is no longer compiled into it.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.7.1: the settings file (dab.cfg) is now noticed when it is edited twice within the same second (the change time was compared in whole seconds). 0.7.0: DAB+ sound can now be decoded inside the plugin through FFmpeg's shared libraries (avcodec and avutil) that you installed, by naming their folder in a new setting; the ffmpeg program route is unchanged and is used when the setting is empty. Tried against stand-in libraries only, never against a real FFmpeg.

plugins.name: Aircraft Info (registry lookup)
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Looks up who each aircraft on the map is - registration, type, operator - from foxsdr.com's aircraft database.
plugins.description:
ADS-B gives each aircraft's 24-bit address and sometimes a callsign; who the aircraft IS lives in registry databases. With this plugin installed, the map tooltip and the flight list show the registration, airframe type and operator for every aircraft the ADS-B decoder is tracking.

Since 1.1.0 it asks foxsdr.com's own aircraft database first - built from the OpenSky Network's aircraft database (Schäfer et al., "Bringing Up OpenSky", IPSN 2014; opensky-network.org) - and only asks api.adsbdb.com, a free volunteer-run service, for an aircraft foxsdr.com does not know or when foxsdr.com cannot be reached.

Every answer is cached on this machine (%LOCALAPPDATA%\foxsdr\aircraft), so each airframe is looked up once ever, not once per session, and lookups are spaced out so neither service is hammered. Once an airframe is cached, it is identified offline.

Requires FoxSDR 0.45.0 or later and an internet connection for airframes that are not cached, unless you supply an offline database.

OFFLINE DATABASE (1.2.0). You can point it at a CSV file of your own with the FOXSDR_AIRCRAFT_DB environment variable, or put bulk.csv in the cache folder named above. Columns are found by their header names (address, registration, type, operator, engines, wake and a few alternatives), and an aircraft found in the file is answered from it with no request to anyone. Wake class letters L, M, H and J are shown as Light, Medium, Heavy and Super and added with the engine text to the type, for example 'A319-111 (Medium wake, 2 jet)'. Setting FOXSDR_AIRCRAFT_OFFLINE (or placing an empty file named offline-only in the cache folder) makes no request at all, and an aircraft not found is shown as unknown for the session.

WHAT IT WILL NOT DO / LIMITS: since 1.3.0 a built-in table of 17,139 aircraft (Virtual Radar Server standing data, CC0) is asked after your file and before any web service; it holds only what Virtual Radar users submitted and is not a world database, and no other database file is shipped. The column names your own file needs are our own, not taken from any particular public export, so a file from elsewhere may need its header renamed. The switches are environment variables or a marker file; there is no settings screen for them. It does not look up flight routes, operator logos or aircraft pictures, and it does not decode the three-symbol type description such as L2J. Tried against a stand-in server and test files only.
plugins.whatsNew: 1.3.0: Carries a built-in table of 17,139 aircraft (Virtual Radar Server standing data, CC0) that is asked after your own file and before any web service, so those aircraft are identified offline with no request. The table is only what Virtual Radar users submitted, not a world database.
plugins.legalNotice: This plugin sends the ICAO address of every aircraft your receiver hears to foxsdr.com, and - for aircraft foxsdr.com does not know, or when it cannot be reached - to api.adsbdb.com, a third-party service, to look up its registry details. The set of aircraft you can hear is a coarse indication of where your receiver is located. foxsdr.com keeps no record of which addresses were asked about or by whom, only running totals (see foxsdr.com/privacy.html). The application itself never makes these requests; installing this plugin is what enables them. Do not install it if you do not want those lookups to leave your machine.

plugins.name: AIS Ship Tracking Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Decodes AIS ship positions and voyage data on the marine band.
plugins.description:
Decodes AIS - the Automatic Identification System that ships broadcast for collision avoidance - and reports vessel identity, position, speed, course and heading, together with ship name, callsign, type, destination and draught where the vessel sends them. Output includes a standard !AIVDM sentence for every frame that passes the checksum, so it can be fed to charting software.

Both AIS channels (161.975 and 162.025 MHz) are decoded at the same time from a single receiver: tune to 162.000 MHz and both are covered. This decoder works on raw I/Q rather than demodulated audio and needs 192 kS/s.

Vessels are plotted on the map, labelled with the ship's name once a Class A (or extended Class B) vessel has sent it, and by MMSI otherwise.

Class A and Class B position reports and static voyage data are parsed into fields, and so are base-station time (types 4 and 11), SAR aircraft (9), safety text (12 and 14), aids to navigation (21), Class B static data (24) and long-range reports (27), together with the published weather, aids-to-navigation monitoring, area-notice and inland-waterway application messages, and the rate of turn, accuracy, UTC second, ETA, dimensions and similar fields that older versions dropped. Other message types are still reported with their type and sender. Each line also carries the signal level, the frequency offset in ppm and the channel, the country is named from the MMSI and the ship type is given in words. The decoder reports changes - a new name, destination, ETA or safety text, a vessel going silent or returning - and can keep a table of ships that you filter by type, name, MMSI, country or range and sort by a setting.

Optional extras, all off or empty until you set them: a closest-approach (CPA/TCPA) alarm, a geofence ring and an anchor-drag alarm, using your own receiver position and own-ship MMSI typed into the settings (the plugin never writes your settings); a places file that you supply, for counting visits (none is shipped); and a UDP input that listens on 127.0.0.1 only, on a port you choose (10110 by default), for !AIVDM sentences from another program on the same machine. The plugin sends nothing over the network.

WHAT IT WILL NOT DO / LIMITS. Only message types 1 and 5 have been checked against a real recording (12 lines before and after); every other new message type was tested on generated signals built from the published tables, which proves the decoder agrees with the transmitter, not with a ship. The country table was read from the ITU page by a page reader and checked on a sample of rows only. Several regional application messages, and message types 7, 10, 13, 15, 16, 20, 22, 23, 25 and 26, are still reported as not parsed. Click-to-sort table headings and drawing places on the map are not built, and the settings screens, ship table and fence have been tried only against a stand-in host, not in the full application.

Written clean-room from the published ITU-R M.1371 specification.
plugins.whatsNew: 1.1.1: At a sample rate below 192 kS/s (so that neither AIS channel is in the band) it now says what it needs and what it got, instead of only that the channels are out of the passband. Decoding is unchanged; only message types 1 and 5 have been checked against a real recording.

plugins.name: APRS / AX.25 Packet Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Decodes APRS and AX.25 packet radio from 144.800 MHz NFM audio; can also read APRS-IS if you switch it on.
plugins.description:
Decodes Bell 202 AFSK packet radio - the 1200 bps mode used by APRS worldwide - from demodulated narrowband FM audio, and emits one line of text per frame. Frames are validated against the AX.25 frame check sequence, so corrupted packets are discarded rather than shown as garbled text. Position reports are parsed into latitude and longitude, in both the uncompressed and base-91 compressed forms, along with timestamps, status reports and addressed messages. Any frame type it does not parse is still shown verbatim rather than dropped. Since 1.2.0 Mic-E positions (with speed, course, altitude and message code), weather reports, PHG, DFS and RNG station data, objects and items, telemetry with its definitions, message acknowledgements and bulletins are parsed into fields, and the map symbol is named. Not parsed, and shown verbatim: raw NMEA sentences, third-party packets, Ultimeter weather, the obsolete Mic-E telemetry bytes and the path meaning of the Mic-E destination SSID. Stations are plotted on the map: one that moves draws a trail of the last five minutes, and an altitude sent in the comment (/A=) is reported with its position. Written clean-room from the AX.25 v2.2 and APRS 1.0.1 specifications.

NEW IN 1.2.0, THREE DEMODULATORS AND OPTIONAL REPAIR. Three demodulators with slightly different settings now run on the same audio (Parallel demodulators, 1 to 6), and a frame that two of them decode is shown once. On a real recording (a TNC test disc, 1549 s) the old single demodulator decoded 961 frames and three together 977, and every frame the old one decoded is still decoded; the cost is roughly 1% of one processor core. REPAIR ONE FLIPPED BIT is off by default: a frame whose check fails but is fixed by changing one bit, and then has the shape of a valid UI frame, is shown ending "[repaired 1 bit]". A repair can be wrong, and by code reading, not by a test, repaired frames are never gated to APRS-IS. DIGIPEATER PATHS ON THE MAP is also off; it hands FoxSDR each station's repeater path as a line, and drawing it is up to FoxSDR. Tested on that recording and on frames generated by the same author as the decoder. The specification was read through a page summary, not the original PDF, so field widths match its worked examples but were not compared against the PDF. Windows only.

NEW IN 1.1.0, APRS-IS. Two switches, both off by default, with no host, callsign, passcode or filter filled in. SHOW APRS-IS TRAFFIC logs in to the server you name with your filter and adds the stations it sends to the station table and the map. GATE RF PACKETS TO APRS-IS (an iGate) sends the packets this plugin decodes off the air to that server, following the APRS-IS gating rules (it drops what must not be gated, and never sends a packet twice within a window you set); it needs your own callsign and passcode, and the plugin never makes up a passcode. Nothing connects until you switch one on. The passcode box is drawn masked on FoxSDR 0.99.105 or later; older versions skip that field. Tested against a stand-in server on this computer only, not against the real APRS-IS.
plugins.whatsNew: 1.2.0: Mic-E positions, weather, objects, items, telemetry, bulletins and message acknowledgements are read into fields, and map symbols are named. Three demodulators now run at once, which decoded about 1.7% more good frames on a real recording; one-bit repair and digipeater paths for the map are available, both off.

plugins.name: Inmarsat-C EGC and Inmarsat Aero (P channel)
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Inmarsat-C EGC / SafetyNET maritime broadcasts and, as a mode, the Inmarsat Aero P channel (600 and 1200 bit/s, ACARS aircraft messages; aircraft identifiers and text hidden unless you turn that off). Tried on generated signals only, never on a real transmission.
plugins.description:
READ THIS FIRST. This decoder is EXPERIMENTAL and has never successfully decoded a real satellite transmission. It is published at a version below 1.0 to make that status explicit.

Roughly ten constants of the Inmarsat-C air interface could not be confirmed against any published source and were reconstructed from first principles: the frame synchronisation word, the scrambler, the interleaver geometry, the packet header layout and the message header format among them. The plugin passes an extensive self-test, but that test uses a transmitter built from the same reconstructed constants, so the two agree with each other and would agree even if the constants are wrong. **If any of them is wrong, this plugin will decode nothing off air, and that is the most likely outcome.**

It is published so that anyone who can receive the band can help correct it. If you have a working Inmarsat-C setup, a raw I/Q capture of an NCS channel is what this needs.

What is sound is the layer beneath: the demodulator measures within 1-2 dB of theory, acquires the carrier over a plus or minus 200 Hz offset, and tracks a 50 ppm clock error. Tune to the NCS channel centre; it does not search the band. Needs raw I/Q, 24 kS/s preferred (Inmarsat Aero needs 9.6 kS/s or more). ADDED IN 0.2.0, all off or empty until you set them: hiding a message that repeats an earlier one (the repeat window is six hours, this plugin's own choice), showing only messages that contain a word you type, a lowest priority setting, and a message log file at a path you choose (it holds broadcast safety messages only). EGC messages that name a circle or rectangle are drawn on the map as closed areas for three hours, again the plugin's own choice, with a marker at a circle's centre. Packets of types other than EGC and idle are not decoded - no free source for their layout was found - and are only counted by type code and length.

INMARSAT AERO (new in 0.3.0, a mode of this plugin). The Aero P channel (the continuous packet channel an aircraft earth station listens to) at 600 or 1200 bit/s is read when you set "Aero P bit rate (0/600/1200)" to 600 or 1200; 0, the default, is Inmarsat-C only, and while Aero is on the Inmarsat-C chain pauses. Tune the P-channel carrier within about 1.5 kHz of the VFO with 9.6 kS/s of I/Q or more. It finds the carrier, detects MSK without a phase reference, finds the unique word (either polarity), undoes the interleaver, scrambler and rate-1/2 convolutional code, checks each signal unit's CRC, names the unit types, assembles ISU and SSU messages and prints ACARS fields (aircraft registration, label, text) with the odd-parity check; lines start with AERO. The R and T burst channels, 8400 and 10500 bit/s, the C (voice) channel and channel-assignment frequencies are not decoded. Written from a published open-source receiver's reading of the air interface; tried on generated signals only, never on a real Aero signal, so the polynomial order, scrambler start state and frame-info bits are unconfirmed on air. Aircraft addresses and ACARS text are hidden by default: the setting Hide Aero aircraft IDs and text is on until you turn it off, and while it is on the Aero lines show the ground station, mode and label but no aircraft address, registration, message text or signalling-unit bytes. Only the P channel at 600 and 1200 bit/s is built: the R and T channels, 8400 and 10500 bit/s and voice are not, so most of what an aircraft sends is not decoded.

WHAT IT WILL NOT DO / LIMITS. Everything above sits on the reconstructed frame layer described at the top, so if that is wrong none of it will show anything off air. The area shapes use the plugin's own field layout, which is also unconfirmed. The settings form and the map areas have been tried only against a stand-in host.

Written clean-room from the published air-interface description.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.4.0: new setting Hide Aero aircraft IDs and text, on by default: the Aero lines no longer show an aircraft address, registration, message text or signalling-unit bytes unless you turn it off; the notice names both services it decodes. 0.3.0: Inmarsat Aero P channel (600 and 1200 bit/s) as a mode (setting Aero P bit rate); generated signals only. 0.2.0: Adds optional repeat suppression, a text filter, a lowest-priority setting, a message log file and EGC areas drawn on the map, plus a count of packets of other types. It has still never decoded a real transmission, and these features rest on the same unconfirmed frame layer.
plugins.legalNotice:
This plugin decodes two services. Inmarsat-C carries SafetyNET maritime safety broadcasts, which are intended for general reception, but the same system also carries private ship-to-shore and shore-to-ship correspondence. Inmarsat Aero (a mode you switch on) carries messages between aircraft and the companies that operate them, which are not broadcasts for the public. In the United Kingdom it is an offence under section 48 of the Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006 to intercept a message you are not authorised to receive, or to disclose its contents, and comparable restrictions apply elsewhere. You are responsible for ensuring your use of this plugin is lawful where you are.

Separately, and just as importantly: this plugin is EXPERIMENTAL. Its decoding of the Inmarsat-C air interface rests on constants that have never been checked against a real transmission, and it will most likely decode nothing at all. Do not rely on it for any purpose, and in particular do not rely on it to receive safety or distress information.

plugins.name: HFDL Aircraft Datalink Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: HFDL, the HF half of airliners' ACARS: squitters, log-ons, messages and positions, from USB audio.
plugins.description:
READ THIS FIRST. This decoder is EXPERIMENTAL. Since 0.2.4 it reads real HFDL traffic at 300 bit/s (BPSK, rate 1/4): on one real 127 second recording it finds 18 bursts and in them 4 squitters, 17 MPDUs and 27 LPDUs, each unit closed by a CRC-16 that matches, and from them 13 ACARS messages, 5 aircraft positions and 12 log-on exchanges; noise gives nothing. A reference decoder run separately on the same file finds 58 units in about 25 bursts, so this plugin gets most of the bursts. Not read: the altitude, time and frequency lists inside position and frequency messages, and every format other than 300 bit/s (600, 1200 and 1800 bit/s are unchanged guesses that no recording has tested).

HFDL is the HF half of airliners' ACARS: 1800 symbol/s PSK on a 1440 Hz audio carrier in a USB channel, thirteen slots to a 32-second frame. The outline of that physical layer - the symbol rate, the carrier, the pulse, the constellations and data rates, the frame, the 249 ms pre-key tone - is published, and this follows it. What lies below the outline is in ARINC 635 and ICAO Doc 9741, which are paid documents and were not read. The code (rate 1/2, constraint length 7, repeated for 300 bit/s), the scrambler, the interleaver, the CRC and the format words 0 and 4 were measured from the recording and proved by decoding it; the six other format words, the constellation labelling for QPSK and 8PSK, the PDU layouts and the position encoding of the old reconstruction are not used any more. The plugin's self-test has 175 checks; the ones on the real recording are the only ones that do not rest on its own transmitter, and they run only where that recording is present.

What it does regardless: it finds each burst by its published pre-key tone, measures the carrier to a fraction of a hertz, and says so - 'pre-key tone seen at 1440.2 Hz, preamble not recognised' - so a user with a real signal learns that the plugin heard it and where its carrier sat. It is published so that anyone who can record a real HFDL channel can help correct it.

It prints ground-station squitters (which station, which frame), MPDU headers (which direction, which station), log-ons (the aircraft's address), ACARS messages (registration, label, flight, text) and aircraft positions with the flight, one line each, names anything it cannot read by type and length rather than dropping it, refuses any burst with no CRC-checked unit, brings an instrument window drawn as the cockpit message printer, and draws aircraft positions on the map. Positions carry no altitude: that field was not matched.

Tune one of the twelve presets (ground stations from the HFDL system table) in USB with no offset, in a 3 kHz channel; the audio decoder needs USB audio at 12 kHz, or the plugin can take raw baseband (8 kS/s to 61.44 MS/s) and pick out up to eight channels itself: those you list, and every preset or learned frequency that falls inside the capture. It has no equaliser, so a real HF channel's multipath will cost it. Written from the published documents and measured from a real recording; no GPL HFDL decoder's source was read.

ADDED IN 0.2.x, ON AN UNVERIFIED FOOTING (none of these frame types was in the recording). It reads further frame types (log-on denied, log-off, log-on resume, numbered data and acknowledgements, frequency data, the system table, and ground speed and track after a position), keeps a table of stations and frequencies learned from squitters and an aircraft cache (in memory unless you name files for them), and prints noise and signal statistics for every 32-second frame span. It can pass what it decodes on as JSON lines to a file, to a UDP address (numeric IPv4) or to a TCP port on 127.0.0.1; all three are off until you switch them on. An ACARS block that passes its checks is also searched for CPDLC messages, as the ACARS plugin does.

LIMITS OF THE ADDITIONS: the layouts for these new frame types are reconstructed in the same way as the earlier ones, so none of it has been seen decoding a real signal; the tests use a transmitter built from the same reconstruction. How FoxSDR chooses between this plugin's audio and wideband inputs was not checked, and if it feeds both a burst may be shown twice. No station names or aircraft data are shipped beyond the 16 stations in its table. It does not output SBS, ZeroMQ or Kafka.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.2.4: Reads real HFDL traffic at 300 bit/s: MPDU headers, log-ons, ACARS messages and aircraft positions, checked field by field against a reference decoder on one real recording (13 ACARS messages, 5 positions, 12 log-on lines, 48 CRC-checked units; before: nothing). Also finds more bursts: a weak or faded pre-key tone is no longer thrown away.
plugins.legalNotice:
HFDL carries messages between airliners and their airlines and air traffic control - operational and weather messages, engine and fuel data, crew and passenger-related traffic - and aircraft position reports. They are not addressed to you. In the United Kingdom it is an offence under section 48 of the Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006 to intercept a message you are not authorised to receive, or to disclose its contents, and comparable restrictions apply in many other jurisdictions; some permit reception but forbid disclosure or use. This plugin is distributed separately from the application, and is not included in it, so that installing it is your informed decision. You are responsible for ensuring that your use of it is lawful where you are.

Separately: this plugin is EXPERIMENTAL. It reads 300 bit/s HFDL traffic checked against one recording; other rates and several message types have never been checked against a real transmission. Do not rely on it for any purpose, and in particular do not rely on it for aviation-safety information.

plugins.name: POCSAG Pager Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Decodes POCSAG (CCIR Radiopaging Code No. 1) pager messages from NFM audio.
plugins.description:
Decodes POCSAG paging messages from NFM audio. Text is the default for every function code. Its persistent settings page displays the latest eight text or numeric messages, newest first, plus the most recent tone-only page on released ABI 3 hosts. Tone pages never replace text. Long pages wrap across rows; history is in memory. Show frame details adds the zero-based address frame, received polarity, per-page corrected/discarded codeword counts and up to 360 raw hexadecimal codewords before correction. The raw words include the address, payload and any failed word closing the page, normalized for polarity; sync, idle and the next address are excluded. Truncation is marked explicitly. Message text stays first, with baud, RIC, function and type. Toggling details exposes retained history without interrupting decoding or requiring the shared Decoder window. Numeric messages selects numbers instead. Use function codes takes priority, mapping function 3 to text and functions 0-2 to numeric. Searches 512, 1200 and 2400 bit/s and both polarities automatically.

Six preset buttons select UK 153.350 MHz, DAPNET 439.9875 MHz (ham), or four US 900 MHz channels. Older hosts leave de-emphasis unchanged and may retune to the first preset on opening. Released FoxSDR 0.99.74 and later keep your tuned frequency, select NFM with a 20 kHz channel and de-emphasis Off, and open shared decoded output beside the settings page. Written from the published specification. Windows decoding was verified on the tested B200 signal at 153.350 MHz; no coverage guarantee.

NEW IN 1.1.0 (all on the settings page; the defaults give the 1.0.5 output): a watch list of capcodes, capcode ranges and text fragments, each with a label and a row colour, and reject entries that drop a page; hit counts on the panel; a host notice that carries only the label. Duplicate blocking within a number of seconds (off). Error correction of 0, 1 (default) or 2 bits. Pruning of unlikely pages (off). National character sets de, gb, fr, it, es, se and no (blank means ASCII), output as UTF-8. A page cut off by loss of signal is delivered marked partial instead of vanishing. A daily log file, off by default; history otherwise stays in memory.

WHAT IT WILL NOT DO / LIMITS: Skyper messages are not decoded, because no free description of their encoding was found. There is no alert sound and no command run on a hit. Two-bit correction raises the rate of wrong repairs on noise (on a noisy sample recording it turned several uncorrectable words into pages, and nothing shows which output was right), so pair it with pruning. The national tables were read from a comparison chart only, and Danish and Portuguese are missing. When you switch the log on, addresses and text go to a local file in the folder you choose, and nowhere else. Checked on generated pages and the project's sample recordings; the Linux build of the new file-writing thread has not been run.

plugins.name: FLEX Pager Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Decodes Motorola FLEX pager messages at 1600, 3200 and 6400 bps from NFM audio.
plugins.description:
Decodes the Motorola FLEX paging protocol from demodulated narrowband FM audio and emits one line of text per page: CAPCODE, message type and message.

Speeds: all four speed and modulation combinations FLEX defines are decoded - 1600 bps 2-level FSK, 3200 bps 2-level, 3200 bps 4-level and 6400 bps 4-level - with all four phases (a to d) at the faster speeds. A frame's synchronisation is always sent at 1600 bps whatever speed follows it, and it names that speed; the decoder then switches its clock to it. On an audio rate below 16 kHz the fast speeds cannot be read, and the decoder names the unusable speed once rather than appearing to do nothing.

Alphanumeric, numeric and tone-only pages are decoded, for both short (21-bit) and long (two-word) addresses, and the CAPCODE is computed the way the standard's own appendix defines it. Receive polarity is detected automatically. The BCH(31,21) error correcting code is implemented to its full capability: one- and two-bit errors in a word are corrected and anything worse is discarded, with the damage marked in the affected message rather than hidden. Written clean-room from the published specification and pinned to that specification's own worked examples.

Also shown: the short instruction vector (temporary address assignment and system event flags), group calls (a page sent to a temporary address is shown as group=n members=k, with members=? if the instruction that formed the group was not heard), operator messaging addresses (shown as opmsg=n, not as a CAPCODE) and the time and date frames, as one line when the clock information changes. Three settings are all off by default: one JSON object per page instead of text lines, a CAPCODE filter (show only the listed codes and ranges, or hide them; group calls and operator messages are never filtered) and a repeat blocker that drops an identical page heard again within a number of seconds you choose. The plugin does not write settings or print to a console; the filter list is the text you typed, kept by FoxSDR like any other typed setting, and repeat memory and group members are kept only as hashes in memory.

WHAT IT WILL NOT DO / LIMITS: 6400 bps 4-level is confirmed on two real recordings (39 and 37 pages of plain text) and 1600 bps 2-level on a third; 3200 bps 2-level and 4-level have been tried on generated signals only, because no real recording of them was available, and the generator was written by the same author from the standard's tables. The group call, instruction and time and date displays have not been seen in a real recording either. Secure messages and HEX/binary messages are still only named, not read. Roaming identifier words and the channel set-up instruction fields are not shown. There is no alert sound and no command run on a match. The pager instrument window shares one set of pages, so two FLEX decoders running at once would mix their pages.

It also contributes an instrument window: the host draws the decoder as a 1990s alphanumeric pager, with the latest page on a four-line liquid-crystal display, the capcode and unread count on its counters, and the last fifty-two pages in the message memory beneath it.
