plugins.name: EAS / SAME Alert Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Reads US Emergency Alert System and NOAA Weather Radio alert headers.
plugins.description:
Decodes the digital headers that carry every United States Emergency Alert System message and every NOAA Weather Radio alert - Specific Area Message Encoding, the bursts of tones before the announcement - and prints each one in words: what the event is, who issued it, which counties it covers, how long it is valid for, and which station sent it.

The header is transmitted three times so that a receiver can vote on it, and this decoder does. Two copies that agree are reported immediately; three are merged character by character, so an alert survives noise that damages each copy in a different place. A single copy is still reported, and says that it was alone and unconfirmed. The raw header string is printed under every alert, so the reading can be checked against what was actually sent. The two-tone attention signal is reported separately, with the duration it ran for.

The presets tune the seven NOAA Weather Radio channels between 162.400 and 162.550 MHz, which carry these headers in normal service - a Required Weekly Test goes out on every transmitter, every week, which makes them the way to check the decoder is working. EAS headers on broadcast stations decode the same way; they simply have no fixed frequency to offer as a preset.

There is deliberately no county-name table built in: over three thousand US counties, a list that changes, and naming the wrong one during a tornado warning would be worse than printing the number for you to look up. By default the state is named and the county is numbered; if you name a county file of your own in the settings (the Census Bureau's national_county.txt layout, or a plain code,name list), the names from your file are shown beside the numbers.

Written clean-room from 47 CFR 11.31, the FCC section that defines the EAS protocol, with the state numbers from the Census Bureau and the channel list from the National Weather Service. NEW IN 1.1.0 (settings page; the defaults give the 1.0.0 output): areas to watch (state, county or six-digit location code) and events to watch, each event with an action - alert (the block is marked and the host gets a notice naming the event), show or hide - and a switch to drop alerts outside the filter; extra event codes you name yourself; a Canadian location display (CLC nnnnnn); one JSON object per line instead of text; a daily log (off); and a recording (off) of the spoken message, saved as a 12 kHz mono WAV from the alert report to the end-of-message code, capped between 10 and 180 seconds.

WHAT IT WILL NOT DO / LIMITS: no command is run per alert. The Mexican SASMEX event code is not built in (add it yourself as an extra event code), and there is no Canadian province table - Canadian codes are displayed as numbers, with names only from your file. The recording is the audio the decoder itself is given, so it is silent while the host's squelch is closed. No off-air EAS signal has been decoded. The one public sample tried (origin unverified, possibly synthetic) has a seven-character station field, which the strict parser calls a malformed header, so it is reported as malformed.
plugins.whatsNew: 1.1.0: Filter alerts by area and event with an alert, show or hide action, name counties from your own file, add extra event codes, and get JSON output. A daily log and a recording of the spoken message are available and off by default.
plugins.legalNotice:
THIS IS NOT AN ALERTING DEVICE. It decodes what it hears on the frequency it is tuned to. It has no county database and cannot tell you whether an alert applies where you are, it sounds no alarm, and a receiver tuned elsewhere, squelched shut, or simply not running is enough to miss an alert completely. Do not rely on it for safety information: use a certified NOAA Weather Radio receiver for warnings that matter.

Receiving these broadcasts is lawful - they are public safety transmissions intended for general reception. Transmitting them is not. 47 CFR 11.45: "No person may transmit or cause to transmit the EAS codes or Attention Signal, or a recording or simulation thereof, in any circumstance other than in an actual National, State or Local Area emergency or authorized test of the EAS." This plugin only receives. Do not put its output, or a recording of what it decoded, on the air.

plugins.name: 406 MHz Distress Beacon Decoder (EPIRB / ELT / PLB)
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Decodes COSPAS-SARSAT 406 MHz distress beacons - the 15 Hex ID, country, beacon type and encoded position. Second-generation beacons are proven on two real test-beacon recordings; first-generation ones on generated bursts only.
plugins.description:
Decodes the bursts that maritime EPIRBs, aviation ELTs and personal locator beacons transmit on 406 MHz when they are activated. Each burst gives the beacon's 15 hexadecimal character identity - the number a rescue co-ordination centre looks up in the national beacon register - together with the country of registration, which coding protocol the beacon uses, what kind of beacon it is, and, for the location protocols, the position it has encoded from its own navigation receiver.

THIS IS FOR MONITORING, AND HEARING ONE IS A REAL EMERGENCY. A 406 MHz beacon is not a hobby transmission: every burst decoded here, unless it is marked as a test, is a distress alert from somebody who has activated a beacon. If you hear one, report it to your national rescue co-ordination centre. Do not treat it as a curiosity, do not assume somebody else has heard it, and do not wait to see whether it repeats. Equally, never transmit on this band to test a receiver - the band exists for one purpose, and a false alert puts real people to work.

A first-generation beacon transmits for about half a second once every fifty seconds, so patience and an antenna matter far more than any setting. The decoder works on raw I/Q rather than demodulated audio and copes with any sample rate from 8 kS/s upward for first-generation beacons (second-generation beacons need 150 kS/s or more), decimating internally to a 40 kHz working band - wide enough that one preset covers all four assigned channels at once. The receiver's own DC offset is measured and removed before anything else, so a zero-IF dongle such as an RTL-SDR, whose local-oscillator leakage would otherwise sit on top of the beacon, hears what it should.

The 160 ms unmodulated carrier at the head of every burst is used to measure the beacon's exact frequency and phase before a single bit is judged, so bursts well off the tuned centre, and beacons whose bit clock is at the edge of tolerance, still decode. Both error-correcting codes in the message are checked: up to three damaged bits in the identity field and two in the position field are repaired and the repair is declared, and any burst the codes cannot account for is discarded rather than shown as a beacon that does not exist. Beacons radiating in self-test mode, and messages using the test protocols, are labelled as tests.

ADDED IN 1.1.0. The burst line now carries the identity the beacon's protocol holds - an MMSI or call sign for a maritime beacon, an aircraft address, an operator designator and serial number, or a certificate number - together with the equipment type, the 121.5 MHz homing device flag, whether the position came from the beacon's own navigation receiver, the activation type and the emergency code. Second-generation (250-bit, spread-spectrum) beacons are decoded as well: up to six damaged bits are repaired, and a burst the code cannot account for gives no output. A second burst of the same beacon within ten minutes is marked as a repeat sighting, with a separate REPEAT SIGHTING line for a live (non-test) beacon, and a beacon that reports a position is put on the map with a track if it moves. Identities are kept in memory and shown in the text feed; the plugin writes them to no file. The printed 15 Hex ID no longer changes as a beacon's position changes, as the specification requires. Each second-generation decoder holds about 17 MB of memory.

It also fits an INSTRUMENT WINDOW: a distress-beacon alarm panel with a red DISTRESS lamp, the 15 Hex ID on a seven-segment readout, engraved plates for country, protocol and position, a centre-zero meter for the beacon's carrier error and a log of every burst heard.

Written clean-room from the published COSPAS-SARSAT specifications C/S T.001 (beacon specification and message coding) and C/S T.012 (channel assignment plan), with country names from the ITU Maritime Identification Digit table. No first-generation beacon has been decoded off air - deliberately radiating one to test a decoder would put a rescue co-ordination centre to work - so for those the proof is the specification's own worked examples, which the self-test reproduces bit for bit; a first-generation recording from a public signal wiki gave no decode before or after this version. Second-generation decoding has been checked on two published real recordings of test beacons (a self-test beacon and a test-protocol beacon), which decode with no bit errors to the identities published with them. The second-generation rules were read from C/S T.018 Issue 1 Revision 4 of 2019; a field changed in a later revision would not show up in those recordings, and the in-flight (ELT(DT)) rotating field has not been checked against any recording.
plugins.whatsNew: 1.1.0: Shows who a beacon belongs to when its protocol carries it (MMSI, call sign, aircraft address, serial number, operator), decodes second-generation 250-bit beacons, flags repeat sightings of a live beacon and puts beacons that report a position on the map. Second-generation decoding is proven on two real test-beacon recordings; first-generation decoding on generated bursts only.

screenshots.caption: The 406 MHz beacon receiver window (shown idle): hex id, country and position as the beacon sends them.

plugins.legalNotice:
THIS IS NOT AN ALERTING DEVICE AND IS NOT PART OF THE COSPAS-SARSAT SYSTEM. Real alerting is done by the satellites and the rescue co-ordination centres; this plugin only prints what your receiver happened to hear. A receiver tuned elsewhere, switched off, or without a usable antenna will miss a beacon completely, and nothing here sounds an alarm.

If it does decode a beacon that is not marked as a test, treat that as an emergency and report it to your national rescue co-ordination centre with the frequency, the time and the 15 Hex ID.

Receiving is lawful. TRANSMITTING ON 406.0-406.1 MHz IS NOT: the band is reserved internationally for distress beacons, a false alert diverts search and rescue resources from real casualties, and it is an offence in most jurisdictions. Do not put a beacon on the air, or a recording of one, to test this.

plugins.name: NAVTEX & DSC (marine)
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Decodes NAVTEX maritime safety warnings (518, 490 and 4209.5 kHz) and GMDSS Digital Selective Calling on VHF channel 70 and the HF distress and safety frequencies, and plots DSC positions.
plugins.description:
Decodes the two text services a ship's radio keeps watch on. NAVTEX is the navigational and meteorological warning broadcast from coast stations on 518 kHz (international, English), 490 kHz and 4209.5 kHz (national): SITOR collective B-mode, 100 Bd, every character sent twice and checked for four marks and three spaces, framed ZCZC B1B2B3B4 ... NNNN. Each message is printed whole under a header naming the transmitter letter, the subject and the message number and counting the characters the second copy repaired and the ones neither copy could supply, which are printed as an asterisk. Digital Selective Calling is the GMDSS's calling system: distress alerts, all-ships urgency and safety calls, and individual calls and their acknowledgements, 1200 Bd on VHF channel 70 and 100 Bd on 2187.5, 4207.5, 6312, 8414.5, 12577 and 16804.5 kHz. A call prints as one line - format, category, the sender's MMSI, the nature of distress, the position and the UTC time where the call carries them - and a call whose error-check character does not match is refused and named, never printed as if it were good. A call that carries a position (a distress alert, a distress relay or acknowledgement, a position acknowledgement) also puts that vessel on the map.

TUNE UPPER SIDEBAND, 1.7 kHz BELOW THE PUBLISHED FREQUENCY. NAVTEX and HF DSC frequencies are published as the centre of the two tones, which a single-sideband transmitter sends 1.7 kHz above its carrier: for 518 kHz tune 516.3 kHz USB. The presets already do this. Tuning the published frequency decodes nothing; tuning lower sideband puts the tones the wrong way round and the plugin says so once in five minutes. VHF channel 70 is 156.525 MHz in narrowband FM, with no offset.

WHAT IT DOES NOT DO. It is an audio decoder and does not know the frequency, so a NAVTEX header shows the transmitter letter and not the NAVAREA. It reads the 7-unit signals the right way up only: selectively addressed NAVTEX transmissions are sent inverted so that only the station called prints them, and are not decoded. A NAVTEX message whose preamble is damaged is not printed; every repeat of a message is printed; and a DSC call with an unreadable character is refused, not guessed. It decodes no DSC telephone-number or automatic-connection messages.

It fits a TELEPRINTER instrument window with the printed lines on its paper, and offers ten presets.

OPTIONS ADDED IN 1.1.0 - ALL OFF OR EMPTY BY DEFAULT, so the output is as before until you set them. Station (B1) and subject (B2) filters for NAVTEX, with a line naming why a message was not printed; the urgent subjects A, B, D and L are never hidden by the subject filter, and a message numbered 00 prints through both filters. Repeat suppression, which prints a message once for 72 hours. An alarm, which puts an ALERT line before the message and raises the instrument's ALERT flag for 60 seconds for those NAVTEX subjects and for a DSC distress alert, relay or acknowledgement; it is a visual notice only and plays no sound. Country, kind of station and ship type shown after a DSC MMSI from the ITU MID table, with names from a file of your own (no station-name list is shipped). The next 24 hours of NAVTEX broadcast slots offered to the host as schedule hints.

LIMITS OF THE OPTIONS. The country table was typed in from the ITU page and has not been checked row by row against the ITU spreadsheet. A DSC call whose check character fails is refused and raises no alert, even if it looks like distress. The settings form, the schedule hints and the ALERT flag have been tried only against a stand-in host; whether FoxSDR lists the hints or records anything from them is up to the host.

Written clean-room from ITU-R M.625, M.476, M.540, M.493 and M.541 and the IMO NAVTEX Manual (MSC.1/Circ.1403); no NAVTEX or DSC decoder was read. The 32 7-unit signals and all 128 DSC characters are checked in the plugin's own test against the Recommendations' tables, and the NAVTEX messages it transmits are the IMO manual's own worked examples. NAVTEX has been tried on generated signals only (the manual's own worked messages). DSC has also been run on five real recordings of VHF channel 70 calls - two individual calls, a distress relay, a distress acknowledgement and an all-ships call - which decoded to the sender identities listed with the recordings. No Recommendation publishes a numerically complete DSC call, so the DSC calls in the built-in test are built from the message tables: they prove the decoder agrees with the transmitter, not with a ship. Nothing was transmitted to test it - a DSC distress alert is not something to radiate.
plugins.whatsNew: 1.1.0: Adds optional NAVTEX station and subject filters, repeat suppression and an ALERT line for urgent NAVTEX and DSC distress calls, plus country names for DSC MMSIs. All of it is off until you switch it on. DSC has now also decoded five real VHF channel 70 recordings; NAVTEX is still generated-signal only.
plugins.legalNotice:
THIS IS NOT A GMDSS WATCH RECEIVER AND IS NOT PART OF THE GMDSS. Nothing in this plugin sounds an alarm. A receiver that is tuned elsewhere, switched off, or without a usable antenna misses a call completely, and a line on a screen is no substitute for the radio watch the SOLAS Convention requires a ship to keep.

A DISTRESS ALERT DECODED HERE IS REAL. If it decodes a DSC distress alert, relay or acknowledgement, or a NAVTEX message with subject letter D, contact the coastguard or your national rescue co-ordination centre with the frequency, the time, the MMSI and the position. Do not assume somebody else has heard it, and do not wait to see whether it repeats. Never transmit a distress alert or any DSC call to test a receiver: a false alert puts real people to work.

Receiving is lawful. TRANSMITTING ON THE DSC DISTRESS AND SAFETY FREQUENCIES, OR ON 518, 490 OR 4209.5 kHz, IS NOT: those channels are reserved internationally for distress and safety traffic, and transmitting on them without authority is an offence in most jurisdictions.

Most DSC calls are addressed to a particular ship or coast station: individual and group calls, their acknowledgements and position replies. Distress, urgency, safety and all-ships calls and NAVTEX broadcasts are meant for everybody; the addressed ones are not. In the United Kingdom it is an offence under section 48 of the Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006 to intercept a message you are not authorised to receive, or to disclose its contents, and comparable restrictions apply in many other jurisdictions. This plugin is distributed separately from the application, and is not included in it, so that installing it is your informed decision. You are responsible for ensuring that your use of it is lawful where you are.

plugins.name: Satellites
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Tracks satellites on the map, predicts passes, and Doppler-corrects a downlink.
plugins.description:
Satellite tracking built into the receiver: the ISS, amateur birds and weather satellites drawn live on the map with their predicted ground track, a pass table for your own station - when each one rises, how high it gets, where to look - and Doppler correction that keeps the radio on a moving downlink through a pass.

Orbits come from CelesTrak element sets, fetched automatically and cached for offline use. Configuration is one commented text file the plugin writes on first run (the panel names its location): your latitude and longitude, which satellites to track by name or NORAD number, and optionally one satellite's downlink frequency to Doppler-correct. Retuning the radio additionally needs the 'allow tuning' permission on this plugin's row - a plugin cannot grant itself the VFO.

The orbital model is SGP4, written clean-room from the published Spacetrack/AIAA model papers and verified against the published verification tables to their own printing precision - about seven micrometres.

The GOES weather satellites are tracked too (1.1.0). They are geostationary, which SGP4 does not propagate, so from 1.1.0 they were placed from their own mean elements (GOES 18 and GOES 19 landed within a tenth of a degree of the slots NOAA publishes for them), and since 1.3.0 they are placed with the SDP4 deep-space model, the mean-element placement being kept only as a fallback. A geostationary bird is drawn as a fixed point and gets a live look-angle row - always in view, with where to point - rather than a pass list, because it never rises or sets. GOES 16, 18 and 19 are in the default configuration.

DDE (1.2.0, Windows only): a line dde SERVICE TOPIC in satellite.cfg makes the plugin serve the satellite with the Doppler line (else the first one tracked) to another Windows program over DDE, once a second: name, NORAD number, azimuth, elevation, range, range rate, downlink and corrected frequency, above or below the horizon. Off unless the line is present; you choose the service and topic names. Tested on this computer only against a test client, not against any other program.

SINCE 1.3.0. The SDP4 deep-space model places orbits of 225 minutes or more, so GPS and Molniya satellites get a pass table like any other (a bird fixed in the sky keeps its look-angle row); it was checked against 128 published state vectors of 20 element sets. Options in satellite.cfg, none of them on until you add the line: a look-ahead of 1 to 10 days; up to four extra observer places, each with its own pass table; a pass alarm, one notice in the host log a set number of minutes before a rise; an iCalendar file passes.ics of the passes (no position of yours is written into it); a polar sky-plot PNG per satellite; a simulated clock, during which Doppler tuning is refused; and your own transmitter list, JSON or CSV. The transmitter list gives pick-and-go downlinks as plate keys and pressable rows, and uplink Doppler as numbers and text only: the plugin never transmits. Passes are marked visible when the satellite is in sunlight and the Sun is below the twilight limit, and the Doppler satellite gets a sunlit-or-in-shadow row.

WHAT IT WILL NOT DO / LIMITS. No transmitter data is shipped and nothing is fetched for it: you supply the file. There is no sky-plot window, only the PNG file and compass points in the pass row, because the host has no widget for it. The new code was tested with a stand-in host and the plugin interface, not in FoxSDR's own window. Since 1.4.0 the transmitter file can be a SatNOGS DB answer you save from db.satnogs.org (CC BY-SA 4.0, credited in the panel); its field names were checked against a real 50-row answer, but the full list of about 5,400 rows was not tried in the plugin.

FoxSDR 0.64.0 draws the predicted ground track dashed, as a prediction should be; on older versions the line simply draws solid.
plugins.whatsNew: 1.4.0: Reads a SatNOGS DB transmitter list that you save yourself from db.satnogs.org, checked against a real answer of 50 rows, and credits SatNOGS DB (CC BY-SA 4.0) in the panel when the file is one. No transmitter data is shipped with the plugin.

plugins.name: NOAA Weather Pictures (APT)
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Receives the weather pictures the NOAA satellites broadcast as they pass overhead.
plugins.description:
The NOAA weather satellites transmit a picture of whatever they are flying over, continuously, in plain FM on 137 MHz - and anything that can hear them can have it. This decoder turns that transmission into the picture, building it line by line as the satellite crosses the sky, two lines a second for the ten or so minutes a pass lasts.

Both of the satellite's channels arrive side by side, exactly as sent: usually a visible-light image beside an infrared one, so the same clouds appear twice and the pair is worth more than either alone. Nothing has to be set up. Pick the satellite from this plugin's presets - NOAA 15, 18 and 19 each have their own frequency - and the picture starts when the pass does.

Install the Satellites plugin alongside this one and the two work together: that one tells you when NOAA 19 next comes over your house and where to point an antenna, this one draws what it sends while it is up.

A word about what you need. APT is a wide signal by amateur standards and the presets ask for a 40 kHz channel accordingly; a narrower one clips the picture's own sidebands and washes it out. The transmitter is 800 km up and moving, so a simple antenna and a clear view of the sky matter more than an expensive receiver.

SINCE 1.1.0. At the end of a pass the decoder finds the 16-step calibration wedges in the telemetry strip, works out the receiver's gain and offset from them, names the channels that were sent (3A and 3B are told apart from the other channels by the wedges) and reports the patch temperature. A pass needs about a minute of lines for this; a shorter one says so. A northbound pass arrives upside down: the plugin works out the direction from orbit mechanics, using the element file in its settings (by default the Satellites plugin's tles.txt, which it only reads), and turns the picture over when the pass is northbound. It does nothing, and says so, when the element set is more than 20 days old, the frequency is not a NOAA one or the satellite is near the top or bottom of its orbit; the Turn northbound passes setting can force it on or off, which is what to use for a replayed recording. Save finished picture (PNG) is unchecked by default; when ticked each pass is written as a new PNG file (never overwriting) into the folder you set, else a folder under the FoxSDR data folder.

WHAT IT WILL NOT DO / LIMITS. Since 1.2.0 the NOAA 15, 18 and 19 infrared constants from the NOAA KLM User's Guide are built in, so a temperature in kelvin comes out of the box (you can still supply constants in a text file named in the settings); its absolute accuracy has not been checked against a reference, only found plausible on one real pass. It makes no false-colour picture and puts nothing on the map. The wedge reading and channel identification were checked on two recorded passes (NOAA 18 and NOAA 19, both southbound); the northbound turn has been tried only on generated passes and against an orbit model, never on a real northbound pass. None of this has been run inside the FoxSDR window.

Written clean-room from the published NOAA KLM User's Guide format description. The sync detector's thresholds were set by measuring the decoder's own response to noise rather than guessed, and it requires the satellite's sync train to repeat on the line cadence before it will draw anything - so a noisy band produces no picture rather than a convincing picture of nothing.
plugins.whatsNew: 1.2.0: Carries the infrared constants of NOAA 15, 18 and 19 from the NOAA KLM User's Guide, so a temperature can be worked out without a constants file of your own. On one real NOAA 18 pass the result was plausible; it has not been checked against a reference temperature.

plugins.name: Meteor-M LRPT Weather Pictures
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Meteor-M weather-satellite pictures on 137 MHz.
plugins.description:
EXPERIMENTAL, and proven on one recording only. Version 0.2.0 drew, and 0.3.0 still draws, a picture from the one raw I/Q recording of a Meteor-M N2-2 pass that was available (frame lock, 3687 frames corrected, a recognisable coastline and cloud). The way an image packet becomes pixels was worked out from that recording, because the operator's description could not be obtained: it comes from ONE satellite on ONE pass, so other satellites, other passes or other channel choices may not draw correctly. The radio layers were written from published CCSDS documents and tested against the numbers printed in them. A packet it cannot read is refused, out loud, rather than drawn wrongly.

What it does. It reads raw I/Q at any sample rate from 144 kS/s to 61.44 MS/s and needs nothing set up: it searches 20 kHz either side of the tuned frequency for the carrier, so Doppler and a dial that is not exact are dealt with, works out which way round the constellation is (an inverted spectrum included), and follows you if you retune mid-pass. It decodes both QPSK and offset QPSK (OQPSK) at once and tells you which it locked to: the 2014 satellite is reported to send QPSK, the current ones OQPSK, but that rests on two secondary sources and no operator document, so both are tried. Presets for 137.100 and 137.900 MHz. The picture is three grey channels side by side, building line by line, and the log reports the carrier, the lock, the error rates and the packet types heard. At a sample rate too low for the signal it says so, in words, and does nothing else.

What 0.3.0 adds, configured in lrpt.cfg. A symbol-rate search (symbol-rate auto, the default): if a carrier is heard but nothing locks for about 8 seconds it tries the other of 72 000 and 80 000 symbols a second. The plain 80 000 mode has been tried on generated signals only. The on-board time of each picture row is read and logged (read off the one recording; the epoch of the day counter is not established, so the date is taken from your computer's clock). Saving a finished pass, off by default (save-images yes): one grey PNG per channel, an RGB false-colour composite, an infrared picture and a statistics text file, never overwriting. The composite's channel mapping is an assumption, not from a document. A real pass saved this way gave a recognisable false-colour picture of cloud, land and sea.

What it does not do: decode the operator's picture format from a document (it was worked out from one recording); prove the 80 000 symbols a second INTERLEAVED mode (built in 0.4.0 from the interleaver parameters of the meteor_decode program, with no official description and no recording, so only generated signals have decoded); give factory-calibrated temperatures (you can supply a two-point calibration, which colours the infrared picture and is labelled as yours); or put the picture on the map. It pairs with the Satellites plugin, which says when a satellite is overhead.

Written clean-room from CCSDS 131.0-B, 732.0-B and 133.0-B and ITU-T T.81, apart from the 0.4.0 interleaved mode, whose parameters come from the MIT-licensed meteor_decode. Its test builds its own transmitter and decodes the picture at eight sample rates up to 61.44 MS/s with a carrier offset, clock error, DC offset and noise, as QPSK and as offset QPSK; down to 2.5 dB (QPSK) or 3.0 dB (offset QPSK) energy-per-symbol to noise it recovers the whole picture, and in pure noise it never locks.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.4.0: Decodes the interleaved 80 000 symbols a second mode, using the interleaver parameters read from the meteor_decode program; setting interleaved-80k to no gives the old plain mode. It has been tried on generated signals only, and which sign convention the satellite uses is not known, so all four are tried.

plugins.name: GOES Weather Satellites (HRIT / LRIT)
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Decodes the direct broadcast from the GOES weather satellites over the Americas.
plugins.description:
The GOES satellites sit still over the Americas and broadcast, continuously and in the clear, what they are looking at: full-disk imagery from the Advanced Baseline Imager, the EMWIN text products that carry warnings and forecasts, and the administrative messages that go with them. This decoder takes that signal from raw I/Q all the way to the files it carries.

There are two links and it handles both. GOES 16, 18 and 19 send HRIT at 1694.1 MHz; the older GOES 13, 14 and 15 sent LRIT at 1691 MHz. Pick the preset for the one you are pointed at and the decoder chooses its own symbol rate, filter and framing to match. A panel shows the whole chain at once - whether the carrier and frame sync have locked, the signal-to-noise ratio, the bit error rate before error correction, how many frames arrived and how many the Reed-Solomon layer had to repair, which virtual channels the satellite is using, and what files are being built.

A word about what you need, because this one is not a wire aerial. GOES is geostationary - about 36 000 km away, in a fixed spot in the sky - so it takes a dish of roughly a metre and a low-noise amplifier for the 1.7 GHz band. The reward is that it never sets: point it once and it works all day.

GOES-R imagery is Rice compressed and this version decompresses it: a full-disk ABI image is drawn on screen, named by its band, as the older LRIT pictures already were. EMWIN text products arrive as text (they come zipped, and that is handled too). A product whose compression the decoder does not know is still written to disk as a standard .lrit file any xRIT tool will open, and the panel says so rather than showing an empty picture. One honest caveat: the decompressor is proven against the standard's reference streams and NOAA's published sample files, and no Rice-compressed product straight off a satellite has been through it; a real dish pass is the test that counts.

SINCE 0.3.0. A coarse frequency pull-in measures how far the carrier is from where you tuned and moves the receiver onto it, so an LNB whose oscillator is not locked no longer stops the lock (pull-in no in goes.cfg turns it off). On a recording of a real GOES-17 HRIT signal whose carrier sat 292 kHz off centre, the decoder found 4 frames and refused all 4 before, and after it locked and produced 613 frames and 5 files (EMWIN text and two other products); that recording holds no picture, so no GOES image has been drawn from real air. The Viterbi stage is about 8.5 times faster with identical output. With save-images yes in goes.cfg (off by default) every finished picture is written as a grey PNG, never overwriting a file, named from a template you can change and optionally cut into named crop regions.

Written from the published specifications - the CCSDS synchronization and channel coding, space data link and space packet standards, the CGMS LRIT/HRIT Global Specification and NOAA's own LRIT documents - with the clause each block came from recorded beside it. The test suite carries a complete GOES transmitter and checks the randomiser, the Reed-Solomon dual basis and the convolutional encoder against numbers printed in those standards rather than against the decoder's own opinion.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.3.0: Locks on to a carrier that is hundreds of kilohertz off tune (coarse pull-in, on by default), decodes the error-correction layer about 8 times faster, and can save finished pictures as PNGs, whole or cropped, with a file-name template (off by default). Picture saving has only been tried on generated streams, not on a real GOES image.
plugins.legalNotice: This decoder was written from public specifications and is MIT licensed. goestools by Pieter Noordhuis (BSD 2-Clause, Copyright (c) 2017 Pieter Noordhuis) was read as a reference for the handful of transmitter behaviours the published documents do not state; no code was copied from it. libaec (BSD 2-Clause, Mathis Rosenhauer and the Deutsches Klimarechenzentrum) was consulted for the meaning of the seven flag bits in the Rice header record, which no standard defines; no code was copied from it either. See src/goes/NOTICE in the plugin repository for the full attribution.

plugins.name: Nearby Signal Catch
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Notices a transmitter far stronger than everything else - usually one close by - and brings the receiver to it.
plugins.description:
Works like the Close Call feature on Uniden scanners (Close Call is a trademark of Uniden; this plugin is not made or endorsed by Uniden). It watches the whole band your radio is sampling and catches a transmission that stands far above everything else in it - which usually means a handheld or a mobile close by - then marks it on the spectrum, raises a notice on its plate and logs it: the time, the frequency, the peak level and how long it was up.

IT MEASURES STRENGTH, NOT DISTANCE. A strong signal usually means a nearby transmitter, but a distant one with a big aerial on a hill can be just as strong, and the same signal reads differently at a different gain setting. A hit needs both a level (default -40 dBFS) and a margin over the band's noise floor (default 30 dB), held for 200 ms, so a spike or a burst of interference is not reported.

Modes, on its plate: Off; Alert only (the default - it never moves the receiver); Tune (moves the VFO onto a hit, holds while it lasts and goes back to where you were two seconds after it ends, unless you retuned meanwhile); Sweep (between hits, steps the receiver across a chosen set of bands - handheld bands, 2 m and 70 cm, PMR446, airband, marine VHF, or wider VHF and UHF ranges; turning the dial yourself stops the sweep until you choose Sweep again, and a slice your radio cannot tune is skipped and said rather than retried). Tune and Sweep need GRANT RECEIVER CONTROL on its plate and work exactly as Alert only without it. Stopping the plugin or revoking control during a hold leaves the receiver on the hit - it is no longer allowed to move it back - and it says where. Keys set the level, the margin and the bands, and ignore a frequency that is always strong (a local transmitter mast); all of it is remembered.

On the patch page it is an I/Q part: its hits reach a Text out. A patch radio is never tuned. There is no alert sound - a plugin's only way to make sound would silence the transmission it has just caught. Needs FoxSDR 0.99.31 or later for marks, tuning and remembered settings; older versions show the hits as text only.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.1.0: first release.
plugins.legalNotice: This plugin finds strong transmissions and, if you allow it, moves your receiver onto them so that you hear them. It decodes nothing itself, but what you then listen to may be other people's radio traffic. In the United Kingdom it is an offence under section 48 of the Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006, without lawful authority, to use radio apparatus with intent to obtain information about the contents, sender or addressee of a message of which you are not an intended recipient, or to disclose such information; comparable restrictions apply in many other jurisdictions. What you may listen to depends on the service and on where you are. You are responsible for ensuring your use of this plugin is lawful.

plugins.name: DMR and D-STAR Monitor (voice off by default)
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Signalling from DMR, D-STAR, System Fusion and dPMR: talkgroups, radio IDs, callsigns, colour code and flags, with optional voice (off by default, no decryption); not confirmed off air (generated signals only).
plugins.description:
Decodes the DMR (ETSI TS 102 361) burst structure from demodulated audio and reports what a burst's signalling carries: colour code, whether a call is a group or private call, the talkgroup or destination radio, the source radio ID, the emergency flag, and whether the burst is flagged encrypted. A voice burst is recognised and counted; its payload is not examined unless you switch voice on (see VOICE below).

DMR AND D-STAR. 0.2.0 adds the D-STAR radio header (GMSK, 4800 bit/s): it prints the callsigns and flags a transmission starts with - who is transmitting (MY), who is called (UR), the two repeaters, voice or data, direct or via a repeater, emergency - and never the voice that follows. The header is descrambled, de- interleaved and error-corrected as the JARL D-STAR standard describes; two small parts that the standard shows only in figures (the encoder taps and the scrambler start) are tried in four plausible readings and the header's own check decides, and the line says if it was not the first. NO REAL D-STAR SIGNAL HAS BEEN DECODED: it has been run on generated frames only. P25 Phase 1 frames are followed for their voice only (see VOICE below); NXDN is not implemented.

MORE SYSTEMS, SIGNALLING. DMR also shows the channel-access data (CACH and short link control), the Tier III system identity and channel grants, embedded signalling, talker aliases, GPS position reports and the privacy-indicator flag. D-STAR also shows its slow data. System Fusion (C4FM, 9600 bit/s) and dPMR (6.25 kHz) signalling are read as well. Three settings, all off or empty to start with: Hide radio IDs replaces a radio ID, alias or callsign with [hidden] (and with it any name you have given that radio), Show positions lets a position report show its coordinates, and Alias list file names a text file of your own that gives names to radio IDs and talkgroups (none is shipped; only the path is kept as a setting and the names live in memory). Nothing about a transmission is written to disk. Nothing here has been checked against a real off-air signal: every system was tested on generated signals, and the System Fusion layout comes from a third-party copy of the manufacturer's document.

ROSTER, CALL LENGTHS AND DATA HEADERS (0.7.0). Each call is timed from the bits received and its end line gives the length; for a base-station stream the timeslot of a burst is shown. A DMR roster panel lists the last 12 calls and the last 8 data channel grants (shown only: nothing is retuned), with counts of bursts, colour codes, slots, data headers and data blocks, sync and error figures, the host's own channel-power reading, and the manufacturer feature-set numbers it has seen. Those numbers are counted, not read: Capacity Plus, Connect Plus and Hytera systems are not recognised by name. Data headers (unconfirmed, confirmed, short data, UDT) show the type, destination, source and how many blocks follow; data blocks are counted and never read, so no message text, status code or position in data is shown. An encrypted call is counted by its flag only; the algorithm and key are not read. Hide radio IDs applies to every cell of the roster, which is kept in memory only.

P25 CALLS AND TALKER ALIASES (0.9.1). With P25 voice decoding on, each call's link control word is read and corrected (a Reed-Solomon code, checked against real P25 voice recordings) and one line says a call began; the talkgroup and unit numbers show only if you also switch on Show P25 talkgroup/unit numbers and Hide radio IDs is off, otherwise the line says [hidden]. Only the plain group-voice word is read; the meaning of its bytes is unchecked against the standard's text. No P25 talker alias: the vendor alias words are not documented anywhere this project may read. The DMR roster panel now lists the last eight DMR talker aliases heard (hidden with Hide radio IDs).

VOICE (0.8.0), OFF BY DEFAULT. Five switches in the settings, all off: D-STAR voice decoding, P25 voice decoding (Phase 1), ProVoice voice decoding (0.9.0: the EDACS format, 9600 bit/s two-level FSK, found by its 32-bit sync in either polarity; a ProVoice call carries no flag this program can read, so an encrypted one cannot be told from a clear one and would play as noise; the radio-ID field is never shown), Fusion wide voice (an experiment: the layout inside the voice frame is an assumption that the plugin checks while running, and it mutes the audio and says so when the frames do not look right) and Half-rate voice. Turning one on shows a notice that you are responsible for what the law where you live allows you to listen to. Audio is 8 kHz mono. Encrypted P25 calls and DMR calls flagged private are muted, never decrypted. DMR, NXDN, narrow-band Fusion and P25 Phase 2 use a half-rate vocoder whose patent is still in force, so the program has no half-rate decoder: with the Half-rate switch on, DMR voice is played only if you add an mbelib library (mbelib.dll, in the plugin folder or the folder named in the settings), and with none it says so and plays nothing. NXDN and narrow-band Fusion voice are not wired in. Nothing was listened to: all of this was tried on generated frames, and no real D-STAR, P25, Fusion or DMR voice has been decoded. Whether the D-STAR decoder is covered by a patent was not assessed.

EXPERIMENTAL, AND NOT VERIFIED AGAINST A REAL SIGNAL. Every check runs against a synthetic transmitter built from the same reading of the standard, plus several checks anchored to properties the standard states independently of that transmitter (the Golay (20,8) code's three-error correction, the BPTC interleaver being a genuine permutation, the six SYNC patterns' complement relationship) - stronger than pure self-agreement, but no DMR burst captured off air has been decoded. Version 0.1.1 says EXPERIMENTAL for that reason.

Needs demodulated NFM audio on a DMR channel (12.5 kHz, 4800 symbols/s 4-level FSK). The one preset lands on 446.000 MHz NFM as a starting point only: DMR channels are locally coordinated, so there is no frequency this plugin could publish that would be right for more than a handful of installs - find your own repeater's frequency and tune there.

Written clean-room from ETSI TS 102 361-1 and -2, both freely published. The voice decoders use tables from mbelib and dsd (ISC licence) and p25.rs (MIT); the GPL and AGPL parts of those projects were not read.

Generated signals only: the one ProVoice recording tried had no usable signal in it. 0.8.1: One spike in the demodulated audio (a start-up transient, a click) no longer stops every later symbol from being read. 0.8.0: Can play the voice of D-STAR, P25 Phase 1 and wide System Fusion, and of DMR half-rate voice through a library you add yourself. plugins.name: VDL Mode 2
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Decodes the VHF airband digital data link: ACARS messages and ground station announcements, from raw I/Q.
plugins.description:
EXPERIMENTAL: IT HAS BEEN TRIED ON ONE REAL RECORDING ONLY (a 47 second capture of one channel, from which it decoded 33 frames, including ACARS messages). It was written from ICAO Annex 10 and the ETSI VDL Mode 2 standards; the first real recording showed four of its readings wrong, which are corrected in this version. Other readings remain unconfirmed and a weak or different signal may decode nothing. Do not rely on it for anything.

VDL Mode 2 is the digital data link airliners use in the VHF airband: 8-phase differential PSK at 10 500 symbols/s in 25 kHz channels, 136.975 MHz worldwide and a handful of regional channels between 136.1 and 136.975 MHz. This decodes it from raw I/Q at any receiver rate from 32 kS/s to 61.44 MS/s: the channel the receiver is tuned to and every channel of 136.700 to 136.975 MHz that falls inside the band, up to twelve at once, each as its own receiver. A rate of 1.024 MS/s or more centred on 136.8375 MHz covers all twelve.

It prints one line per frame: the frequency, who sent it and to whom (an aircraft's 24-bit ICAO address, a ground station's), and for an ACARS message the registration, label, block, message sequence number, flight and text. The ground stations' XID frames - including the announcement each sends about every two minutes - are decoded and named, with the parameters they carry: the station's own position, nearby airports, the frequencies to try. A message the error-correcting code mended is marked with how many octets it mended. A burst it cannot mend is refused and named, never shown in part; every frame is checked by its 16-bit frame check sequence. Every frame it recognises but does not decode is named with its length rather than dropped.

It brings an instrument window drawn as the flight-deck message printer, and a track source: the positions an XID frame states, each to a tenth of a degree, about 11 km, never guessed from a message's text.

Under the frames it now reads the network layer: X.25 packets (every packet type, addresses, facilities, clear causes), reassembled into whole data units, and the CLNP and COTP layers inside them, with the CLNP header checksum checked. An ACARS message in a frame is also looked at for an ARINC 622 wrapper; a CPDLC message in it is spelled out on a 'VDL2  app cpdlc' line, ADS-C reports, MIAM and OHMA messages are decoded, AFN is named, and a wrapper whose check value fails is reported rather than decoded. On the one real recording the X.25 layer reads correctly, but CLNP and COTP decoding has been proven on generated signals only, and the CPDLC decoding on one published example and generated messages (the recording holds no CPDLC message).

OUTPUTS AND LISTS, ALL OFF BY DEFAULT: JSON lines over UDP (numeric IPv4, 127.0.0.1 unless you type another) and to a file with hourly or daily rotation, statsd counters over UDP, a message filter, and ground-station and aircraft name lists read from CSV files you supply (none is shipped). The JSON carries aircraft addresses and the message text, so it is for you, on your machine. These were tried against stand-in listeners only, not a real statsd server or tracking program.

WHAT IT DOES NOT DO: it does not decode ATN-native controller-pilot data link (CPDLC), ADS-C or any other message of the ATN above the transport layer (those carried inside ACARS are decoded) - the ATN ones are handed on whole, named and their length given, because their formats are in paid ICAO documents. The 8 information frames of the real recording look like ATN-compressed packets and are described to the X.25 level only. IDRP is not decoded. It uses hard decisions only, so its sensitivity is that of the standard's basic receiver. It will not decode a carrier more than about 3.5 kHz off frequency, so a receiver that is not calibrated to about 20 ppm may miss everything. It plays no audio. It reassembles X.25 data units, CLNP segments and COTP messages, but an ACARS message sent in several blocks is shown block by block.

Written clean-room from ICAO Annex 10 Volume III Chapter 6 and ETSI EN 301 841-1 and -2; no VDL Mode 2 decoder was read. Every constant is cited to its document and clause where it is defined.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.3.1: The optional ZeroMQ output is no longer offered (its four settings are gone and nothing listens on a ZeroMQ port); the JSON, UDP, file and statsd outputs are unchanged. 0.3.0: Adds an optional ZeroMQ output (a PUB socket that listens on 127.0.0.1, off by default) beside the JSON, UDP, file and statsd outputs, and spells out ADS-C, MIAM and OHMA messages carried in ACARS frames. Both tried on generated signals, stand-in subscribers and published examples only.
plugins.legalNotice:
This plugin decodes third-party aircraft data link messages: the text airliners and their ground stations send each other, which can include operational, commercial and sometimes personal information. In the United Kingdom it is an offence under section 48 of the Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006 to intercept a message you are not authorised to receive, or to disclose its contents. Comparable restrictions apply in many other jurisdictions, and some permit reception but prohibit disclosure or use.

This plugin is distributed separately from the application, and is not included in it, so that installing it is your informed decision. You are responsible for ensuring that your use of it is lawful where you are.

It is also EXPERIMENTAL and has been tried on one real recording only. It is not a safety tool and must never be relied on for anything to do with the operation of an aircraft.

plugins.name: Demod Analyzer
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Works out what a digitally modulated signal is (BPSK, QPSK, 8PSK or 16-QAM) and measures it, live or from a recording; never tried against a real off-air signal.
plugins.description:
Reads a digitally modulated I/Q signal - the live receiver's VFO channel, or a recording it reads itself - and works out what it is: BPSK, QPSK, 8PSK or 16-QAM, with a confidence, chosen by which constellation the burst actually fits best rather than by the smallest error alone (which QPSK can win inside 8PSK or 16-QAM by cheating). Everything needed to get there is found automatically: the occupied band and the burst inside it, the symbol rate from the signal's own cyclostationary line, the carrier frequency, the raised-cosine roll-off, symbol timing and carrier phase, then EVM, MER, an SNR measured against the recording's own silence where there is one, timing and phase jitter, and I/Q gain and phase imbalance. Every recovered symbol becomes Gray-mapped bits - printable on the plate (PRINT BITS) or written whole, with every measurement, by EXPORT to a text file and a per-symbol CSV.

LIVE OR A FILE. Live, it reads the receiver's VFO channel exactly as set - whatever it is tuned and opened to - and re-analyses roughly twice a second. From a file, the path is typed into *I/Q file* in the plugin's settings, because the host gives plugins no file-open dialog: cs8 (HackRF `hackrf_transfer -r`), cu8 (RTL-SDR `rtl_sdr`), cs16, cf32 (GNU Radio `.cfile`), or WAV at 8/16/24/32-bit PCM or float. Everything else - forcing a modulation or symbol rate, a sync word to resolve the phase ambiguity, the matched filter, roll-off, sampling offset - is a setting with an automatic default that can be typed over.

ONE DASHBOARD PICTURE. The host gives a decoder exactly one image, so the constellation (density map with the ideal points and decision boundaries), the eye, the spectrum (carrier and occupied band marked), symbol power over the burst, and I/Q after the matched filter all share that one picture rather than a window each. The same numbers are also a panel table, and a line reaches Decoder output whenever the verdict changes.

MEASURE, BIT VIEW AND EXPORT SIGNAL (0.3.0). Three more keys work on the same capture as CLASSIFY ALL and take the strongest signal in it; they add no settings. MEASURE prints the occupied and -3, -6, -20 and -26 dB bandwidths, every burst with its time, length, power and frequency, the repeat period and any hopping, AM depth and FM deviation, a chirp slope, the two tones, shift and baud rate of an FSK signal, the pulse and gap widths of an OOK one, and the sideband lines with harmonics marked. BIT VIEW reads the recovered bits in ten line codes (NRZ, inverted, NRZI, Manchester, differential Manchester), with and without PN9 whitening, ranks them by the sync word you set and by a preamble, compares the frames between sync words, and tries twelve catalogue CRCs and three simple sums over the frames. EXPORT SIGNAL, only when you press it, writes the measured burst as float32 I/Q with a SigMF description and a time table of amplitude, frequency and phase to the export folder. Not built: a library of known signals, automatic field inference, a user-described decoder for unknown devices, a cursor or zoom on the picture, and sending a recording back out through a transmitter.

EXPERIMENTAL - THE PSK/QAM ANALYSER HAS NEVER SEEN A REAL OFF-AIR SIGNAL. The 0.3.0 measurements are checked on generated signals and on one real recording, an Oregon Scientific weather-sensor burst, where MEASURE found both packets at the right times; BIT VIEW did not read that recording's Manchester bits cleanly, so no decoded bits from it are claimed. Every figure in the plugin's own notes is checked by `test_demodan` against a synthetic transmitter the test itself builds from the published constellation and Gray mappings, at several signal-to-noise ratios, on both Windows and Linux - never against a capture from a real modulator. The clearest way this can go wrong: a file read with the wrong sign convention - cs8 read as cu8, or the reverse - folds the constellation into something that still looks like a genuine, if noisy, 16-QAM (confidence 0.5-0.7, EVM around 25%); the EVM figure is the tell, not the verdict alone.

Asks for no permission beyond the ordinary decoder capabilities - it only ever reads the channel already open, and never asks to move the VFO. Needs FoxSDR 0.99.43+ for the settings form, plate keys and spectrum marks; an older host still gets the live picture and measurements with every setting at its default.

Written from the published estimators alone - Oerder & Meyr 1988 for symbol timing, Gardner 1986 for the tracking loop, Pauluzzi & Beaulieu 2000 for the M2M4 SNR estimate, Swami & Sadler 2000 for the classification cumulants - no other analyser's source was read.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.3.1: Reads the extra header of SDR Console-style (auxi), Spectrum Lab (inf1) and SDRuno WAV recordings, for SDRuno the first 72 bytes only. The layout SDR Console itself writes was not checked, and nothing is written back to a file.

plugins.name: Propagation Tools
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Band conditions and solar indices, the NCDXF beacon schedule with tune presets, a meteor-shower calendar, and a world map with the grey line and a heat map of the bands likely to be open - by the built-in VOACAP.
plugins.description:
HF propagation in one picture and one table. The picture has five pages (NEXT PAGE key): a world map with the day and night sides, the grey line, the Sun, your locator, the 18 beacons of the NCDXF/IARU International Beacon Project and a heat map showing, for every 5-degree cell, the highest band of 80/40/30/20/17/15/12/10 m that looks usable from your locator, with a strip of solar flux, A and K indices, the last day of Kp, N0NBH's day and night band words, the beacons on air and the meteor shower of the day; the beacon schedule with bearing and distance from you and the seconds until each beacon next transmits; the meteor calendar with the radiant's altitude and azimuth from your locator; the solar numbers with a week of Kp and NOAA's three-day forecast; and a 24-hour by 8-band table for the path to a target locator. Five presets tune the receiver to the beacon frequencies (14.100, 18.110, 21.150, 24.930 and 28.200 MHz) in CW.

WHAT MADE THE FIGURES. Every picture and panel names its engine. VOACAP, the prediction program of the US Voice of America and NTIA's Institute for Telecommunication Sciences (ITS), is the engine of choice, and it is BUILT IN: ITS's own Fortran program, translated to C and carried inside this plugin with ITS's data, nothing to install and no program started. It shows VOACAP's reliabilities, MUF and signal figures for your power, antenna and noise - monthly MEDIAN predictions, not today's conditions - and the map shows the most reliable band in each 5-degree cell. On ITS's own test circuits it agrees with ITS's program to the printed digit in most cells (a few long circuits differ; the plugin's README gives the counts), but it has never been compared with the air. If the built-in engine cannot run, or you ask for an antenna file only an installed VOACAP understands, the plugin can run a copy YOU have installed (ITS HFWIN32, free from its.ntia.gov) as a separate program. Without either the figures are EMPIRICAL: a rule of thumb (secant law and a hand-made F2 climatology, written out in the plugin's README) that is an INDICATION, not a prediction, never checked against measurements, and says so on every picture.

NETWORK. The plugin makes four requests (and up to two more if you switch on the optional feeds described below), only while one of its windows is open, never faster than each source asks, and backs off after a failure: https://www.hamqsl.com/solarxml.php (N0NBH, at most once an hour), and from services.swpc.noaa.gov (NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center) the Kp history (every 30 minutes), the 10.7 cm flux and the 3-day forecast (every 3 hours). Each server learns your IP address and a user agent, 'FoxSDR-PropagationTools/0.1.0', and nothing else - except that the optional PSK Reporter feed below sends your 4-character grid square. Your full locator and your receiver's position are never sent anywhere. The last answer of each is kept on this machine (%LOCALAPPDATA%\foxsdr\propagation\cache; Linux: $XDG_DATA_HOME/foxsdr/propagation/cache) and shown with its age when you are offline. There is a setting to switch all fetching off. The plugin never contacts voacap.com.

TWO OPTIONAL FEEDS (0.2.0), both off until you turn them on in the settings, and both also need the network setting on. DRAP fetches NOAA's D-Region Absorption Prediction table every 15 minutes and adds a panel block: the highest frequency absorbed by 1 dB at your locator and worldwide, with the product's own time. An overlay setting tints the map red where that frequency is 5 MHz or more. PSK Reporter spots asks pskreporter.info every 10 minutes for the reports heard by receivers in your 4-character grid square in the last 30 minutes (FT8, FT4, WSPR and other modes arrive this way) and shows, for each HF band, how many paths, how many sender squares, the longest and the median distance, with a dot on the map at each sender square. This is a measured opening beside the model's predicted one. The spot reader keeps only the two locators, frequency, mode, SNR and time of each report: callsigns are never read into a variable, stored, shown or logged. The live answers of both services have never been fetched; the parsers were written from their published descriptions and tested against a stand-in server.

The built-in engine writes ITS's data (84 files, under 1 MB) into %LOCALAPPDATA%\foxsdr\propagation\itshfbc (Linux: the same folder under $XDG_DATA_HOME/foxsdr) the first time it is used, and scratch files there that it deletes after each run; nothing else is written and nothing is sent. If you point the plugin at an installed VOACAP it writes an input file into that install's run folder, starts voacapw.exe (a 32-bit ITS program; on Linux voacapl) as a separate process, reads its output and deletes both files. It checks the file's header before starting it and refuses anything that is not a program for your system.

VOACAP: Institute for Telecommunication Sciences, NTIA, U.S. Department of Commerce, translated to C by the FoxSDR project with netlib's f2c and libf2c (AT&T, Lucent, Bellcore); their notices are in the plugin's README and the NTIA terms are in the legal notice. Solar data by N0NBH (hamqsl.com); Kp, flux and forecast from NOAA SWPC (public domain); coastline from Natural Earth (public domain); beacon schedule from ncdxf.org; meteor showers from the IMO's 2027 calendar. Needs FoxSDR 0.99.43 or later; the path field for an installed VOACAP needs 0.99.74 or later (the built-in engine needs nothing).

With the defaults it behaves as 0.1.1; neither feed has been tried against the live service.

plugins.name: Radiosondes
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Follows weather-balloon sondes on 400-406 MHz (Vaisala RS41 and, since 0.3.0, DFM, M10, M20, Meisei and iMet-4): serial, position, height and climb rate.
plugins.description:
Decodes the Vaisala RS41 radiosonde, the weather balloon's transmitter, on 400-406 MHz. Given raw I/Q from a Radio (2.4 MS/s suggested; any rate from about 20 kS/s works), it searches the capture for carriers itself, because a sonde's frequency is set at the launch site and nobody tells you, and follows them as they drift. For each sonde it reports the serial number, position, height, climb rate and wind, and draws its trail on the map as a balloon silhouette. Up to four sondes are followed at once, anywhere in the capture. Three presets cover the band: 400-402, 402-404 and 404-406 MHz. On the patch page, wire it to a Radio to search the whole capture, or to a Channel for the one sonde in it, and its map output into a Map.

EXPERIMENTAL - PUBLISHED WITHOUT EVER HAVING SEEN A REAL FLIGHT. The frame format was written from a published protocol description (bazjo/RS41_Decoding's, plus Vaisala's own datasheet; no decoder's source was read) and is checked by the plugin's own test against frames the test builds itself. Two choices the description leaves open have not been confirmed on frames from a real flight: which CRC-16 variant covers each block, and how the 48 parity bytes and the data are split between the two Reed-Solomon codewords. The test's frames share those choices, so it cannot catch a wrong one. If either is wrong the plugin will report no sondes at all, so it may decode nothing until someone checks it against a real RS41. A real off-air RS41 recording (75 kS/s, 32 seconds) has since been tried: it gave no frames at all, 28 Reed-Solomon failures after a sync, the same result before and after 0.2.0 and with the cause not investigated, so the decoder has still never decoded a real flight.

WHAT 0.2.0 ADDS, all on generated signals only. An RS41 carrying the ozone interface sends a line of text with its readings; the plugin shows pump temperature, cell current, battery, pump current and external voltage as raw readings (the ozone partial pressure is not computed). A Radiosondes table lists each balloon's serial, altitude, highest altitude, climb rate, wind, ozone cell current and frame count. A CSV log with one file per flight is written only if the environment variable FOXSDR_SONDE_LOG is set, and a UDP feed of each frame (the plugin's own JSON layout, or gpsd-style position datagrams) only if FOXSDR_SONDE_UDP is set to a port or an IPv4 address and port; with neither set nothing is written or sent. Serial numbers are cleaned of anything but letters, digits, '-' and '_' before they reach a file name or a datagram. In 0.2.0 Graw DFM sondes were found in the same search and their frames counted without a position; since 0.3.0 their position, speed, climb and temperature are read.

WHAT 0.3.0 ADDS, all on generated signals only apart from the DFM scaling (checked against telemetry printed in a thesis). Meteomodem M10 and M20, Meisei iMS-100 and RS-11G (position, speed, climb and, once its calibration fragments are in, temperature and humidity) and InterMet iMet-4 sondes are found in the same search and reported in the same table, trail and files; a real Meteomodem M10 recording was tried and its frames are of a type (0xAF) this version cannot read, so those makes are checked on generated signals only, and no recording of the others was available; and their offsets and calibration constants come from another program's reading.

What it does not do: no calibrated temperature, humidity or pressure for the RS41 (its calibration maths has no usable published description; the temperatures shown for other makes are not calibrated values), no ozone partial pressure, no landing prediction, no graphs (the per-balloon data is kept but the host has nothing to draw it with), no Lockheed LMS6 or other make of sonde not named above, no Horus or OziMux feed layouts, and no e-mail alerts or uploads to tracking sites. Whether a real ozone sonde puts its text where the plugin looks for it is not known.

It was asked for through the app's feature-request box on 2026-10-02, for weather-balloon tracking.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.3.4: Says plainly when a strong DC component with a wide skirt (an RTL-SDR's) may be hiding a sonde tuned within a few kilohertz of the centre of the capture, and what to do (tune it 10 kHz or more off the centre); a skirt as strong as the sonde in its own band cannot be decoded through. 0.3.3: Hears a sonde that sits within 6 kHz of the centre of a wide capture, which it used to skip (three real recordings gave nothing before and give frames now). 0.3.2: Corrects the error-correction of a regular RS41 frame. The code was laid out wrongly for the short regular frame (right for the long one), so no real regular frame ever corrected, although all its data checked out; they now do (every whole frame of a real recording), and the calibration data they carry is used again. 0.3.1: Takes an RS41 frame whose error-correction bytes are damaged when all its data blocks check out (a lossy recording gave nothing before), and says when it hears a Meteomodem sonde of a type it cannot read instead of staying silent. 0.3.0: Reads more makes of sonde: Graw DFM (position, speed, climb and temperature), Meteomodem M10 and M20, Meisei iMS-100 and RS-11G, and InterMet iMet-4. All tried on generated signals only, apart from the DFM scaling, which was checked against telemetry printed in a thesis; a real Meteomodem M10 recording was tried and its frames are of a type this version cannot read, so these makes are checked on generated signals only.

plugins.name: Packet TNC (KISS)
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: A software TNC: packet radio for Winlink Express, APRS clients and other packet programs, over KISS on a local TCP port.
plugins.description:
A software TNC (the modem a packet program talks to). It decodes 1200 baud AFSK packet radio - AX.25, the mode behind APRS and Winlink over packet - from the receiver's NFM audio, and turns frames back into audio, and exposes both to any program that speaks KISS over TCP: Winlink Express on the same PC (Packet TNC Type KISS, serial port TCP, 127.0.0.1, port 8100), an APRS client, a packet BBS terminal.

Since 0.2.0 it also receives FX.25 and IL2P frames (packet with built-in error correction) and, on up to three extra channels that you choose, 300 baud HF packet, 2400, 4800 and 9600 baud FSK (9600 is the G3RUH design) and HAPN 4800, all from the same audio. A frame heard on an extra channel is printed as RX chN and goes to KISS programs only if you switch that on. The rest is off by default: one-bit repair and pass-all (frames with a bad check, marked in the text and never sent to a KISS or AGW program), a passive monitor of connected-mode links that never sends anything, and an AGW-protocol socket for programs that use it. Transmitting is unchanged: 1200 baud AFSK on the first channel only. The new modes, FX.25 and IL2P are receive only, and AGW transmit requests are ignored unless you switch AGW may transmit on, when they join the same queue and need the same grant and arming. The settings form holds 16 fields, so a few options (the FX.25 and IL2P switches, the AGW port) are set only in the config file. The 2400 and 4800 baud modes are the 9600 design scaled, since no standard for them was found, and the 300 baud tone pair is a setting because the sources disagree.

NETWORK: it opens ONE LISTENING TCP port, 127.0.0.1:8100 by default, for programs on this PC to connect to (up to four); if you switch the AGW socket on (off by default) it opens a second, 127.0.0.1:8000, in the same way. It makes no outbound connection, fetches nothing, reports nothing and writes no file. Setting a bind address other than 127.0.0.1 puts the port on your network, where anything that can reach it can queue a frame for transmission; the plugin warns when you do, and FoxSDR still decides whether anything is keyed.

IT TRANSMITS, BUT NEVER ON ITS OWN AUTHORITY. The plugin supplies audio and says when it wants the transmitter. FoxSDR keys it only if you have granted this plugin transmit (off by default, offered on its plate after it first asks), you have armed the transmitter on the TRANSMIT page (a timed window, every session), and the page is live. It never chooses frequency, power or mode: set the TRANSMIT page to DATA (flat). A frame that cannot go out is dropped after 30 seconds with the reason shown - not granted, not armed, channel busy, or the host did not key - on its panel, in the Decoder output and in the host log.

It listens before it talks: p-persistent CSMA as the KISS document describes it, with TXDELAY, P, SlotTime, TXTAIL and FullDuplex taken from the program's own KISS commands. The channel counts as busy while the squelch is open, the signal is above a threshold you set, or a packet was heard within the slot time. A keying never exceeds 40 seconds, inside the host's 60 second cap. ACKMODE frames are accepted and acknowledged; NORMAL is the mode that was tested.

Its window shows the server and its clients, frames received and sent, whether the channel is clear or busy and why, the KISS parameters, the host's grant and arming state, and the last frames; every frame is also printed in the Decoder output. Two presets (144.800 MHz Europe, 144.390 MHz North America, the APRS channels) put the receiver in flat NFM; a Winlink gateway is on its own frequency, which you tune.

Needs a FoxSDR that offers transmit audio to plugins (host API level 2). On an older FoxSDR it still receives and serves KISS but cannot transmit, and says so. Receiving and the KISS server work on FoxSDR 0.99.43 or later; transmitting needs FoxSDR 0.99.74 or later (the TRANSMIT page's grant and ARM keys). NEVER TRIED ON THE AIR: it has been tested against a simulated host, a scripted KISS client and a stand-in AGW client, and its 1200 baud receiver on one off-air recording of a TNC test disc, where it decodes the same 397 good frames in the first ten minutes as 0.1.0 did. The 300, 2400, 4800 and 9600 baud, HAPN, FX.25 and IL2P receivers have been tried only on signals generated by the same author as the receivers, so they agree with each other and with the specifications' worked examples, not with another TNC. Winlink Express and AGW programs have not been run against it. 9600 baud also needs the host's NFM audio to be wide enough, which is not known here. Written clean room from the KISS and AX.25 documents; no Dire Wolf or other GPL code. Not affiliated with ARSFI or Winlink.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.2.2: The plugin's table now has a Keys row that says where RESTART SERVER and DROP TX QUEUE are (on its key plate under Fitted modules); nothing else changed. 0.2.1: FX.25 reception now tries the four combinations of Reed-Solomon root and shortening and also reads frames sent without an opening flag or bit stuffing, so the worked example of the libmodem project decodes. Which form real transmitters use is not known; transmitting is unchanged and nothing was tried on the air.

A licensed amateur is required to transmit on amateur frequencies, and the operator must arm the transmitter on FoxSDR's TRANSMIT page for every session; nothing is radiated until you do. You alone are responsible for what your station emits: your licence, the frequency and band plan, your callsign and station identification, the deviation and bandwidth of the signal, the rules for third-party traffic and for the Winlink or packet network you connect to, and not interfering with other stations. The plugin's channel check is a courtesy, not a guarantee that a channel is free. Transmit only where, and as, your licence permits.

plugins.name: Solar System View
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: The Sun, planets and Moon drawn from orbital elements, with NASA's latest Sun pictures, the SOHO coronagraph, NASA's CME list, solar-wind readouts and the aurora forecast beside them.
plugins.description:
A picture of the solar system that turns by itself, and the space-weather pictures and numbers that go with it. The plugin contacts NASA and NOAA servers by itself, and only for what is on screen: sdo.gsfc.nasa.gov, services.swpc.noaa.gov and ccmc.gsfc.nasa.gov (https, GET only; what each is asked for, how often, and what it learns are listed below and in the plugin's README).

FOUR PAGES, ONE PICTURE. SYSTEM draws the Sun, the eight planets on their orbits and the Moon beside the Earth, dated now, from Keplerian elements (JPL's approximate positions, 1800-2050) with no network at all; it spins slowly and answers the plugin's keys - ROTATE LEFT and RIGHT, TILT, ZOOM IN and OUT - with an option for logarithmic orbit radii so Mercury is not lost in the Sun. SUN shows one of eight pictures from NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory (six AIA wavelengths, the HMI intensitygram and the magnetogram; NEXT CHANNEL) with how old it is and the solar-wind speed, density, Bz and Kp. CORONA shows the SOHO/LASCO C3 coronagraph and NASA DONKI's list of coronal mass ejections: time, speed, type, and whether DONKI's model has one reaching the Earth. AURORA draws NOAA's OVATION forecast over both poles and marks your locator if you type one into the settings. A table beside the picture carries the same numbers, with each planet's distance from the Earth and its elongation from the Sun.

It is a picture the plugin draws: plugins receive no mouse clicks, so nothing can be dragged - the keys on the plugin's plate do the turning. When a source stops answering, the last good data is shown with its age. NASA's own 'latest' Sun pictures were three weeks old on the day this was written (their web server had a storage failure); the plugin says when the same picture has been served for three refresh intervals, and the picture's own date label shows when the Sun was imaged.

SKY EVENTS (0.2.0). Two more blocks in the table, worked out on your computer from the same orbital elements with no network request: rise, upper transit and set of the Sun, Moon and the planets from Mercury to Saturn for the next 24 hours from your locator (it says so if no locator is set), and the next sky events - the next three eclipses in 400 days, the next transit of Mercury or Venus, the next New and Full Moon, the next three planet conjunctions closer than 5 degrees and the next opposition of Mars, Jupiter or Saturn. Checked against Horizons, the US Naval Observatory and NASA's eclipse and transit tables: all 16 eclipses of 2022 to 2025 and all 7 transits of 2000 to 2035 found, none missing or extra. Limits: the Moon is good to about two arcminutes and Jupiter and Saturn to minutes, so an eclipse at the very edge of the geometry can be classed on the wrong side and slow planets' conjunction times can be hours out; the eclipse and transit entries are worldwide, not 'visible from here'. Stars, comets and asteroids are not shown.

Data: NASA/SDO (courtesy of NASA/SDO and the AIA, EVE, and HMI science teams), NOAA/SWPC, SOHO/LASCO (ESA and NASA), NASA DONKI (experimental research information; NOAA/SWPC is the official source), JPL's approximate planetary positions (Standish and Williams), Paul Schlyter's lunar series, and Natural Earth's coastline. Drawn by FoxSDR; not an official product of NASA or NOAA and not endorsed by either.

Experimental: tested against responses recorded on 2026-10-12 and through a stand-in host, never inside FoxSDR's own window. Needs FoxSDR 0.99.43 or later. The picture is an image-decoder window, which the host may create only while the receiver is running; the table works either way.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.2.1: When online fetching is switched off the message now says so in plain words. 0.2.0: The table now lists rise, transit and set times of the Sun, Moon and planets from your locator, and the next eclipses, Mercury and Venus transits, New and Full Moons, close conjunctions and oppositions. Worked out on your computer with no network; the rise and set block needs the locator setting.
plugins.legalNotice: This plugin contacts three servers on its own, over https, whenever a window of it is open and showing something that needs them: sdo.gsfc.nasa.gov (the SDO Sun pictures, at most one picture per channel every 15 minutes, only the channel on screen and the one before it), services.swpc.noaa.gov (solar wind every 5 minutes, Kp every 30, the LASCO picture every 15, the aurora grid every 10) and ccmc.gsfc.nasa.gov (NASA's DONKI CME list, once an hour). Each server sees your internet address and the plugin's name and version; the DONKI requests also carry two calendar dates. Nothing about you or your receiver is sent: the locator you may type into the settings stays on this computer. The SYSTEM page makes no request at all. Do not install it if you do not want those requests to leave your machine.

plugins.name: Radio Email (Winlink-compatible)
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Read and send Winlink e-mail over the internet gateway: a mailbox, a compose form and the Winlink protocol; it makes no radio transmission. Not affiliated with ARSFI or the Winlink team.
plugins.description:
A Winlink-compatible e-mail client: it reads and sends e-mail through the Winlink INTERNET gateway (the "Telnet" session every Winlink client offers), using the same B2F protocol the radio sessions use.
