It makes NO radio transmission - it has no radio link - and it does not create a Winlink account: use an existing Winlink client once to create yours and get the password. Not affiliated with or endorsed by ARSFI or the Winlink team; "Winlink Global Radio Email" is a registered trade mark of the Amateur Radio Safety Foundation, Inc.

NETWORK. It opens one plain, UNENCRYPTED TCP connection to server.winlink.org, port 8772 (both changeable in the settings), only when you press CONNECT, on the schedule you set with Auto-check (off by default; 5 minutes at the shortest), or at the UTC times of day you list in Check at (UTC) (empty by default), and never while its window is closed. The server learns your IP address, your callsign, your locator if you enter one, the software name and version, and everything in the messages you send and receive - messages are not private on Winlink. Your password is never sent: Winlink's secure login sends only a number worked out from the gateway's challenge and your password. The gateway session contacts no other server and nothing is reported anywhere; the only other connections are the peer-to-peer ones described next.

PEER-TO-PEER (0.2.0). CONNECT PEER calls another station directly over plain TCP at the host and port you type (default port 8774, this plugin's own choice, not a Winlink number) and runs the same B2F exchange with it. A peer session has no callsign or password exchange and no secure login, and it never reads or sends your stored password. The plugin can also answer such a call: the Peer listen port setting is 0 (off) by default, and when you set it the plugin listens on 127.0.0.1, this PC only, unless you type another address. There is no login on a peer session, so anyone who can reach an open port can leave mail in your inbox and take what is in your outbox; do not expose it to a network you do not trust.

PASSWORD. The password field is write-only: what you type is stored protected on disk (Windows: DPAPI, for your Windows user. Linux: a file only your user can read, mode 0600 - file permissions, not encryption) and the field is emptied within a tenth of a second. FoxSDR keeps plugin settings in clear text and does not mask what you type, so for that moment it is visible and in the settings store.

WHAT YOU GET. A panel with a mailbox (inbox, outbox, sent, archive), the message you select and its text, thirteen command keys (CONNECT, QUEUE MESSAGE, DELETE DRAFT, next/previous message and page, MARK READ, ARCHIVE MESSAGE, REPLY, REPLY ALL, FORWARD, CONNECT PEER), a compose form in the settings (To, Cc, Subject, Message text, Attachment; the reply and forward keys only fill it in from the selected message, and you still press QUEUE MESSAGE) and, in the Decoder output, the whole session log and every received message in full. Messages and attachments are kept as files under %LOCALAPPDATA%\foxsdr\radio-email\<CALLSIGN> (Linux: $XDG_DATA_HOME/foxsdr/radio-email/<CALLSIGN>). Needs FoxSDR 0.99.43 or later; the attachment path field needs 0.99.74 or later (older versions hide it, so no attachments).

EXPERIMENTAL - IT HAS NEVER TALKED TO THE REAL WINLINK SERVERS. It passes its own tests against a fake gateway and against wl2k-go, another author's Winlink implementation, run as a gateway and as a client on this machine, and agrees with the published protocol documents; whether the real servers accept this client is unverified (src/winlink/README.md lists the steps for a first live check). Peer-to-peer mode was tried only against stand-in peers on this machine (in-memory pipes and 127.0.0.1 sockets); it has not been tried against Winlink Express or any other Winlink program. Not built: position reports, Winlink forms, automatic shrinking of image attachments, and VARA. Written from the public B2F and FBB protocol pages, RFC 1321 and the LZHUF algorithm; no GPL or AGPL Winlink client's code was read.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.2.1: The panel heading and its first line no longer carry a development word ('stage 1'): the heading is now just Radio Email. 0.2.0: Adds archive, reply, reply-all and forward keys, automatic sessions at UTC times of day, and a direct peer-to-peer session with another station over TCP (off by default). Still no radio link, and still not tried against the real Winlink servers or another Winlink program.
plugins.legalNotice:
This plugin connects to the Winlink radio e-mail network, which is run by the Amateur Radio Safety Foundation, Inc. (ARSFI). FoxSDR and this plugin are not affiliated with or endorsed by ARSFI or the Winlink team; "Winlink Global Radio Email" is ARSFI's registered trade mark.

Winlink is for licensed radio operators and authorised agencies: its terms say a new account's licence is validated and a user who cannot prove one is locked out. You need an amateur radio licence (or the authorisation of the agency you work for) and your own Winlink account and password, and you are responsible for using it within the rules of your licence. Winlink's terms and conditions apply to everything you send and receive through it - read them at https://winlink.org/terms_conditions . In short: messages are NOT private (gateway operators, administrators and, in some cases, authorities can read them); they are kept for 21 days; an account unused for 400 days is deleted; business use over amateur radio, obscene content and executable attachments are not allowed.

When you press CONNECT, or on the automatic schedule you set, this plugin sends your callsign and the messages you wrote to server.winlink.org over an unencrypted connection. You are responsible for what you send.

This plugin is distributed separately from the application, and is not included in it, so that installing it is your informed decision.

plugins.name: Station Labels (EiBi)
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Names the shortwave broadcaster that is on the air now on the frequencies in view, from the EiBi schedule.
plugins.description:
Puts a small label on the waterfall for each shortwave broadcaster that the EiBi schedule says is on the air now, on the frequencies the receiver is showing: station name and language, for example "Radio Example E". It uses the schedule's own times (UTC), days of the week, midnight-crossing broadcasts and season dates, so a station is labelled only while it is scheduled to be there.

The schedule is not part of this plugin. Press UPDATE SCHEDULE in its window to download the current season's file from eibispace.de (one request, only when you press the key), or download the CSV database (sked-b26.csv or similar) yourself and name it in MY SCHEDULE FILE, in which case the plugin never touches the network. The window says where the schedule came from and when it was downloaded. If a download fails, the schedule you already have stays in use and the window says why.

Your own table (0.2.0): name a delimited file in the settings and it is read instead of the EiBi schedule when its header line names recognisable columns (frequency in kHz, MHz or Hz, start and stop or one time, days, station, language, target, site, power, country). The plugin never downloads or ships such a file, the window credits it as your file, and its owners terms are yours to check.

On the map (0.4.0): the schedule names each transmitter by a site code and gives no coordinates, and no table of them is shipped. Name a text file of your own in Transmitter sites file (one line per site: code,latitude,longitude) and each station on the air now whose site is in it appears on the map as a station point labelled with its name and frequencies; the others are counted in the window and left off. With no file nothing is added to the map.

Find by time (0.5.0): type a frequency (9760 kHz or 9.76 MHz; empty means the tuned one) and a time in UTC (18:00, Tue 18:00, 2026-11-20 18:00, now, or any) in the Find settings and the window lists what the loaded schedule has on that frequency at that time, with its hours and days, nearest frequency first. It reads only the schedule already loaded; nothing is fetched.

Limits of this version: FoxSDR lets a plugin draw 64 markers, so when more stations are on the air in view than that, the 64 nearest the tuned frequency are drawn; labels can overlap on a busy band; and the plugin cannot see how far the waterfall is zoomed, so it labels the whole receiver span. A listing is a schedule, not a log: the only sure identification is the one you hear on the radio.

Schedule data by Eike Bierwirth (EiBi), eibispace.de, used under the terms on that site. Needs FoxSDR 0.99.77 or later for the pressable keys (the settings form needs 0.99.43).
plugins.whatsNew: 0.5.0: Find by time: what the loaded schedule lists on a frequency at a time you choose (UTC, or any time), from the schedule already loaded; three settings added (7 in all). 0.4.0: stations on the map, from a transmitter-site table of your own (code,latitude,longitude): none is shipped, and with no file nothing changes. Generated schedules and site tables only. 0.3.0: on FoxSDR 0.99.109 and later a station marker from the EiBi schedule carries EiBi's credit line; an older FoxSDR shows the markers as before. 0.2.0: besides the EiBi schedule it can read a delimited table you name (a file with a header line of column names); nothing is downloaded or bundled for it.

plugins.name: DX Spots (HamQTH, PSK Reporter, your DX cluster node)
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Recent DX spots as markers on the waterfall, from the HamQTH cluster feed, the Reverse Beacon Network via HamQTH, PSK Reporter, Parks on the Air, a cluster node you name and a logger's UDP feed. Off until you switch it on.
plugins.description:
Puts a marker on the waterfall for each recent DX spot inside the frequencies the receiver is showing: the spotted station's callsign and frequency, for example "DL1ABC 14025.0". Orange markers come from the HamQTH DX cluster feed, blue ones from PSK Reporter. Spots disappear after the lifetime you choose (30 minutes by default).

It is OFF until you switch on SHOW DX SPOTS in its settings: until then it makes no network request of any kind. You do not need a callsign, an account or a key, and none is sent. HamQTH is asked once a minute, never faster than every 15 seconds (its own page asks for no more than once every 15 seconds); PSK Reporter, which is off by default, is asked once every six minutes, never faster than every five, about the frequencies in view (its own page asks for no more than once every five minutes). A request made sooner is refused by the plugin itself. PSK Reporter's page asks callers to give a contact address; that setting is empty and is sent only if you type something into it.

NEW IN 0.2.0, a DX cluster node of your choice (green markers). Switch on USE A DX CLUSTER NODE and type the node's host, its port and your login callsign; nothing is filled in for you and nothing connects until all four are set. The plugin then opens one plain telnet connection to that node, sends your login callsign and a line end once, and reads the spot lines the node prints; it sends nothing else (apart from the refusals the telnet protocol requires if the node negotiates options). It reconnects after a drop, waiting 30 seconds, then longer, up to 15 minutes. Some nodes want a registration or a password; the plugin cannot give one.

NEW IN 0.3.0, Reverse Beacon Network spots (yellow markers), read from HamQTH. They show only when SHOW DX SPOTS and the new RBN SPOTS switch are both on, and the switch is off by default. No login, callsign or key is sent. HamQTH states no limit for this feed, so the plugin asks no more often than once a minute (you can set 60 to 3600 seconds, default 120), and says so in its window. Never tried against the real service.

Limits of this version: FoxSDR lets a plugin draw 64 markers, so when more spots are in view than that, the 64 nearest the tuned frequency are drawn; labels can overlap on a busy band; and the plugin cannot see how far the waterfall is zoomed, so it marks the whole receiver span. A spot is someone else's report, not a measurement of yours.

NEW IN 0.4.0, POTA SPOTS (teal markers) and SPOTS FROM YOUR LOGGER (violet markers). Both are off by default and both need SHOW DX SPOTS on as well.

POTA SPOTS (Parks on the Air) asks api.pota.app for the current activator spots, every two minutes and never more than once a minute, and labels each marker with the callsign and park reference. Nothing is sent but the request. POTA publishes no terms for programs that read this feed, so the plugin neither has permission nor is forbidden, and it uses no POTA logo, only the plain text POTA. The units and time format of the answer are assumed and could not be checked, and it has not been tried against the real service: a wrong guess shows up as no spots or skipped records in the window, not as wrong markers.

SPOTS FROM N1MM+ / DXLOG ON THIS PC listens on one UDP port of 127.0.0.1 only (default 12060, the one N1MM+ recommends; DXLog's spot feed is normally 13063, which you type in) for the spot datagrams those logging programs broadcast, and draws them. A spot deleted in the logger disappears from the waterfall. The spotter's callsign, the comment and the timestamp are dropped; a spot is dated by its arrival. It only reads: nothing is sent to the logger, and FoxSDR cannot put spots into their band maps. Not run against the real programs.

SOTA spots are not included (SOTA's API requires membership of a group and non-commercial use) and neither are IOTA spots (the programme publishes no feed).

Data provided by HamQTH.com, and by PSK Reporter (pskreporter.info), which is credited in the plugin's window when it is in use. Spots from Parks on the Air (pota.app) is credited in the window when POTA is on. Needs FoxSDR 0.99.77 or later for the pressable key (the settings form needs 0.99.43).
plugins.whatsNew: 0.4.2: On FoxSDR 0.99.109 and later each marker carries its source's own credit line (for example Data provided by HamQTH.com); an older FoxSDR shows the markers as before. 0.4.1: Reads the comment of a Reverse Beacon Network spot (for example "CW 15dB") and puts it in the marker. The line format comes from four captured spot lines, and none of the sources has been tried against the real service or program.

plugins.name: Weather Report (SYNOP) Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Reads weather-service radioteletype and turns SYNOP and SHIP weather reports into one line each: station, time, wind, visibility, temperature, pressure, weather.
plugins.description:
National weather services broadcast their observations as radioteletype: groups of five digits in the WMO FM 12 SYNOP code for land stations and FM 13 SHIP code for ships. This decoder runs the same teleprinter receiver as the RTTY plugin (the settings default to 50 baud and 450 Hz shift, the German weather service's maritime RTTY) and reads the text for those reports. Every well-formed report becomes one line: the station index or ship call sign, day and hour, wind direction and speed in the unit the report declares, visibility, cloud cover, air and dew-point temperature, station and sea-level pressure, the three-hour pressure tendency, precipitation, present and past weather in words, and for ships the position.

It is strict. A group that is not five digits or solidi, a value outside its WMO code table, groups out of order, a missing wind-speed group - any of these rejects that whole report, and a line says which report and why, rather than showing numbers that may be wrong. A report that is damaged but still looks valid cannot be caught, so a noisy copy can still show a wrong value. The station name is not shown, only its index number; sections 2, 4 and 5 of a report are skipped, and section 3 gives only the highest and lowest temperatures. It has been tested on generated signals and on the code tables of WMO-No. 306 only; no real broadcast has been decoded. Tune single sideband so the RTTY tone pair lies between 500 and 3500 Hz of the audio: since 0.1.1 the plugin finds the pair by itself within a few seconds, wherever it sits.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.1.1: Finds the tone pair itself anywhere between 500 and 3500 Hz of the audio (before, it decoded only within about 40 Hz of 2210 Hz), follows drift, and searches again if the signal moves. 0.1.0: New. SYNOP and SHIP weather reports from radioteletype, with strict checking. Generated signals only.

plugins.name: Wi-Fi Occupancy
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Shows how busy each Wi-Fi channel (1-13) and each 1 MHz of the 2.4 GHz band is, from raw samples taken while the receiver steps across the band. Energy only: it decodes nothing.
plugins.description:
Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Zigbee and microwave ovens all share 2400 to 2483.5 MHz. This measures how much of the time each 1 MHz of that band carries energy, and how strong it is, and summarises it for Wi-Fi channels 1 to 13. It looks at power only: no packet, name, address or network is read, decoded or kept.

It needs raw I/Q (8 MS/s is a good choice) and a receiver that steps its centre frequency across the band: 2403, 2409, 2415 ... 2481 MHz, staying at least a tenth of a second on each. When every 1 MHz from 2400 to 2483 MHz has been seen it prints one report: the noise floor it found, the level above which a band counts as busy (the floor plus 10 dB, adjustable), and for each channel the duty cycle (the share of short frames - 16 microseconds at 8 MS/s - that were busy), the peak and the mean level in dB below full scale per MHz. Left on one frequency it prints a partial report every five seconds. Tick 'Show every 1 MHz band' in its settings for the per-MHz lines.

Levels are relative to full scale (the receiver's gain is not known to the plugin), so compare channels with each other and with the floor rather than reading them as dBm. The plugin cannot step the receiver by itself: it follows whatever centre frequency the host reports, so the stepping has to come from the host or the operator. It is proven only on test signals made here (a tone calibrates to within 0.2 dB; the duty cycle of generated Wi-Fi-like bursts is read within 4 points); nothing has been received off air.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.1.0: New. Energy-only occupancy of the 2.4 GHz band per 1 MHz and per Wi-Fi channel from stepped I/Q.

plugins.name: LTE Cell Search
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Finds LTE cells on a carrier and reads their identity, frame timing, frequency offset and the broadcast bandwidth and frame number, from the centre 1.08 MHz of the signal.
plugins.description:
An LTE base station transmits two synchronisation signals and a broadcast channel in the middle 1.08 MHz of its carrier, whatever its bandwidth. This reads only those. For each cell it finds it prints the physical cell identity (0 to 503, with its group and sector), whether the cyclic prefix is normal or extended, the carrier's frequency offset from where the receiver is tuned, and - for a normal-prefix cell - the master information block: the downlink bandwidth, the PHICH setting, the system frame number and whether the cell uses one, two or four antenna ports.

Nothing else is read. There is no control or data channel, no system information block and nothing that identifies a user or a phone; nothing is transmitted and nothing is stored.

It needs I/Q at exactly 1.92 MS/s, tuned to within about 12 kHz of a carrier centre (carriers sit on a 100 kHz raster, so scan in 100 kHz steps and stay about a second on each). It finds the synchronisation signals down to about -3 dB signal to noise in the 1.08 MHz and reads the broadcast channel from about 0 dB in the test. Those figures are for test signals generated here from the 3GPP specifications; nothing has been received off air. A cell wider than 1.4 MHz is seen through a receiver that must not let the rest of the carrier alias into the 1.92 MS/s window.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.1.0: New. LTE cell identity, timing, offset and master information block from 1.92 MS/s I/Q.

plugins.name: GSM Broadcast
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Reads the broadcast channels of a GSM cell: the base station identity code, frame number, cell identity, location area, network and country codes and the neighbour list.
plugins.description:
Every GSM cell announces itself on a fixed channel in time slot 0 of its main carrier. This finds the frequency correction burst, reads the synchronisation burst (base station identity code and frame number) and then the broadcast control channel: system information 3 (cell identity, mobile country code, mobile network code, location area code), 4 (location area), 1 (the cell's channel list) and 2 (the neighbour list), when they use the common bit-map format.

It does not read the other common-control channels or any traffic, parses no subscriber identity of any kind, contains no decryption or key code, never transmits and stores nothing. Broadcast message types it does not decode are reported by number only.

It needs I/Q at exactly 1 083 333 samples a second (four per symbol), tuned to within about 20 kHz of a GSM carrier that carries the broadcast channels, and several seconds on it (each message type comes round about once every two seconds). In the test it locks down to about 3 dB signal to noise in 200 kHz and decodes the broadcast messages from about 5 dB, with carrier offsets to 20 kHz and sample-clock errors to 200 ppm. Those figures are for test signals generated here from the 3GPP specifications; nothing has been received off air, and the bit order of the 25 synchronisation bits and of the frequency lists rests on a reading of the specification that no real transmission has confirmed.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.1.0: New. GSM frequency correction, synchronisation and broadcast control channel (system information 1-4) from 1.0833 MS/s I/Q.

plugins.name: Bluetooth LE Advertising
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Lists the Bluetooth Low Energy devices announcing themselves on the three advertising channels: packet type, shortened address, signal level, name, services and manufacturer number.
plugins.description:
Bluetooth LE devices announce themselves on three channels, 37, 38 and 39 (2402, 2426 and 2480 MHz). This listens to those channels only and prints, for each device heard, the packet type, the advertiser's address, the signal level and the standard advertising fields: flags, name, service identifiers, transmit power and the manufacturer's number.

Those are other people's devices. Addresses are shown shortened (the last two octets) unless you turn off 'Hide addresses', which is on by default; names can be hidden too. Everything is kept in memory for the session only and is never written to disk, reported or uploaded. It follows no connection and no data channel (a connection request is reported as such and its parameters are not read), sends no scan request and transmits nothing. A device that keeps repeating itself is shown once, again when what it says changes, and about every ten seconds.

DRONE REMOTE ID (0.2.0). Remote ID broadcast in Bluetooth 4 legacy advertisements (and, from 0.4.0, in long-range extended ones) is decoded into an aircraft table (up to 64 aircraft, dropped after 120 s of silence, memory only) and printed as one line per aircraft: type, state, position, altitude, speed and track. 'Show drone Remote ID' is on by default and the aircraft's own position is shown, because it is broadcast data. 'Hide drone serial numbers' and 'Hide operator and pilot details' are also on by default: the serial, registration and session id, the operator position and id and the free text are replaced by 'id hidden', 'operator hidden' and 'self-id hidden', and the sender address stays shortened. It is passive, and the lines go to FoxSDR's decoder output, which the host's web mirror and Copy diagnostics can carry.

LONG RANGE (0.4.0). The Bluetooth 5 LE Coded PHY (S=8 and S=2) is decoded on each advertising channel: after the preamble the access address is found, the packet is error-corrected (rate 1/2 convolutional code, soft decisions), de-whitened and checked, and only a packet whose check passes is shown, with its extended advertising header (set and data ids, the channel where data follows) where it has one. Remote ID inside a long-range advertisement joins the aircraft table. 'Long-range (Coded PHY) receive' and 'Decode long-range packets' are on by default; 'Scan secondary channels' (the other 37 channels inside the band) is off because it costs about three times the CPU. A preamble whose packet cannot be read is still counted, with the reason. Written from the Bluetooth Core Specification v6.0, which is free to read. Nothing here has met a real drone or a real Coded PHY device.

It needs I/Q at 2 MS/s or more, a whole number of MHz (4 is the usual choice), with the centre about a megahertz away from the channel (the radio's own spur sits at the centre): 2403, 2427 or 2481 MHz. With a wider capture it reads every advertising channel inside the band. In the test it needs about 13 dB signal to noise in 1 MHz to read half the packets and 15 dB to read nearly all, which is less sensitive than a real Bluetooth receiver; those figures are for test signals generated here from the Core Specification, and nothing has been received off air.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.4.1: At a sample rate it cannot use (it needs a whole number of MS/s from 2 to 64) it now says what it needs and what it got instead of failing to start without a reason. Decoding is unchanged; generated signals only.

plugins.name: ALE Link Establishment Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Reads the calls and soundings of second-generation HF Automatic Link Establishment (ALE) and scores their link quality. Receive only.
plugins.description:
ALE - Automatic Link Establishment - is a way for HF stations to call each other and to announce themselves with 'sounding' transmissions, sent as 8-tone FSK at 125 baud. This decodes the second-generation words of MIL-STD-188-141B and prints one line per call or sounding, for example 'SOUND from #1A2B, TIS (calls welcome)', with the number of words and a link-quality score. It also keeps a sounding log, opened as a table: station, how often heard, last, best and mean quality, and seconds since last heard.

Every word is protected by a Golay code and sent three times. The decoder votes bit by bit over the three copies, corrects what the code can correct, and from the number of non-unanimous votes gives each frame a link quality from 0 to 100 (higher is better), with a rough signal-to-noise estimate from the tone band. When a station sends the link-quality report word, that is decoded and shown too. Extended addresses, all-call and group calls are read.

PRIVACY. Station addresses are shown as a short tag that changes each session unless you turn off 'Hide station addresses' (on by default). Everything is kept in memory only, nothing is written to disk, and the text of the free-message words is never shown. A second setting, 'Minimum unanimous votes (of 48)', sets how clean a word must be to open a frame (34 by default; our choice, the standard leaves it open).

WHAT IT WILL NOT DO / LIMITS: receive only, and it decodes ALE words only: no transmitting, no linking, and no AQC-ALE, data blocks (DBM, DTM) or other protocols. It has been tried on generated signals only (noise, frequency offset and clock error added), plus real recordings of other modes as controls on which it found nothing, as it should. No recording of real ALE was available, so its thresholds are untested on real fading HF channels, and two details taken from the standard's text - the bit order of a tone's three bits and the link-quality code table - have not been checked against an off-air signal. The signal-to-noise figure is an estimate, not a calibrated measurement. It takes audio at 8000 samples a second, with the tones at 750 to 2500 Hz in the audio, found anywhere in the passband (about 1500 to 2550 Hz of dial offset from the centre of the ALE channel's 3 kHz); it has no presets, and the choice of sideband was not checked on a real signal. The sounding table shows only the newest decoder if several run at once. Written from the public MIL-STD-188-141B text.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.2.1: Finds the ALE tones anywhere in the passband (before, the dial had to be within 100 Hz of the right place). 0.1.0: first release. Reads ALE calls and soundings with a link-quality score and a sounding log; tested on generated signals only.

plugins.name: SITOR-A, ARQ and FEC Telex Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Reads SITOR-A (ARQ) maritime telex and the text of several other HF radio-telex systems: ARQ-M2, ARQ-M4, ARQ-E3, G-TOR, four-frequency Twinplex and ARQ-E (ITA2-P). Receive only.
plugins.description:
This one decoder handles six HF telex systems that are not RTTY or NAVTEX, one at a time, chosen with the Mode number in its settings: 1 = ARQ-M2, 2 = ARQ-M4, 3 = ARQ-E3 (ITU-R F.342 and F.519: characters sent as 3-of-7 codes in repeating cycles), 4 = G-TOR (the Kantronics protocol), 5 = Twinplex (four-frequency diplex, two start-stop ITA2 channels), 6 = ARQ-E (ITA2-P: the character table, odd-count rule and repeat requests, not the five-character cycle; since 0.2.0), 7 = SITOR-A (ARQ) (since 0.3.0). Text is printed as it arrives; in the ARQ modes it says when it has locked on a signal and when the signal ends, and a damaged character is shown as '*'.

It needs no line polarity or cycle phase set by hand: it tries several tuning offsets and finds the character framing itself. It locks only after a run of consistent characters and refuses to lock while two alignments look equally clean, so noise gives no text. The tone pair centre (1700 Hz), tone shift (170 Hz; 200 Hz for G-TOR, and in Twinplex the spacing of adjacent tones) and baud rate (0 = the mode's default) can be set.

SITOR-A (mode 7, new in 0.3.0; it was the separate SITOR-A (ARQ) Decoder). SITOR-A, also called AMTOR-ARQ, is the error-correcting maritime radiotelex mode: 100 baud FSK with a 170 Hz shift, characters in a 7-unit constant-ratio code, sent three at a time in 210 ms blocks on a 450 ms cycle while the far station answers with 70 ms control signals. In mode 7 it listens to one side of a link. It finds the 450 ms cycle on its own, follows small drift in the tones and the clock, prints the traffic with letter and figure shift, drops blocks it can see are mutilated, and reports the selective call (four or seven signals) that sets a link up. A listener who hears only the sending station cannot see the block numbers, so a block identical to the one before is taken to be an ARQ repeat and dropped; the setting Keep repeated blocks (SITOR-A) keeps such blocks. The first few blocks of a transmission are spent finding the cycle. Only the information blocks are decoded, not the answering control signals. It is built from ITU-R Recommendations M.476 and M.625 and has been tested on generated signals only; no real SITOR-A has been decoded. Tune single sideband so that the two tones sit near 1615 and 1785 Hz in the audio.

PRIVACY AND TEXT. The message text of ARQ-M, ARQ-E3, G-TOR and Twinplex is printed, as the text of SITOR-A (mode 7) and NAVTEX is in this suite. G-TOR connect and disconnect calls are shown as short session tags unless you turn off 'Hide station calls (G-TOR)' (on by default). Nothing is stored or sent, and there is no network.

WHAT IT WILL NOT DO / LIMITS: receive only. It has been tried on generated signals only (offsets, clock error, noise, fading), with the standards' and the G-TOR paper's worked examples as the independent checks; no recording of ARQ-M, ARQ-E3 or G-TOR was available. Real SITOR-B and RTTY recordings were run through it as controls: the ARQ and G-TOR modes found nothing, as they should, and the Twinplex receiver read a real RTTY recording correctly when tuned to its tones, but it also produced a junk line from real SITOR-B audio on one tuning, a limit that is not hidden. The tone pair and shift defaults are not taken from the standards, G-TOR's default shift is a hypothesis, and ARQ-M4's channel numbers are the order in the signal, not the ITU letters. ARQ-E was tried on generated signals only, and it does not follow its five-character cycle or repeat procedure. It does not read CIS-36-50, CROWD36, Coquelet, FEC-A, the 7-unit Twinplex ARQ framing or PACTOR-II and III, because no usable free description exists or the licence is not settled; G-TOR does not combine a damaged frame with its repeat. It takes audio at 8000 samples a second.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.5.1: New Mode 0, automatic, is the default: it tries ARQ-M2, ARQ-M4, ARQ-E3, ARQ-E and SITOR-A at the same time, says which one it found and how to choose another; G-TOR and Twinplex are still chosen by hand. 0.4.0: On FoxSDR 0.99.109 and later the Mode is a drop-down list with the seven names instead of a number box; the setting and its numbers are unchanged, and an older FoxSDR still shows the number box, with a hint. 0.3.0: SITOR-A (ARQ) is now mode 7 of this decoder (it was the separate SITOR-A (ARQ) Decoder, which is gone): set Mode to 7; the Keep repeated blocks (SITOR-A) setting is the old one. 0.2.0: Adds mode 6, ARQ-E (ITA2-P): the character table, the odd-count rule and the repeat requests (counted) are read, but not the five-character cycle. Tested on generated signals only.

plugins.name: PSK31, Olivia, MFSK16 and DominoEX Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Reads PSK31 (with PSK63 and PSK125), Olivia, MFSK16 and DominoEX, the amateur HF keyboard-to-keyboard modes, from single-sideband audio, with one Mode setting; every PSK carrier in the passband at once. Receive only.
plugins.description:
PSK31 is the narrow, quiet keyboard mode that fills the digital end of the amateur HF bands: 31.25 baud, a signal about 60 Hz wide, carrying typed text in plain Varicode. This listens to the whole audio passband at once, finds every carrier that looks like PSK31 - you can have six on screen - and decodes each one, following it as it drifts. Every line begins with the audio frequency of the signal it came from, so a busy band reads like a conversation: "1500 Hz: CQ CQ DE G4ABC".

BPSK31 is the default. Tick 'PSK: QPSK instead of BPSK' in its settings for the error-correcting variant, which needs the right sideband: if QPSK text comes out as nonsense, tick 'PSK QPSK: lower-sideband sense' too. BPSK does not care which sideband you use. A squelch keeps noise from printing: nothing is shown until a carrier is both clean enough and modulated the way PSK31 is, so a plain carrier or a birdie is ignored, and it stops when the signal does. In tests on generated signals the text came through without error to 6 dB below the noise in a 2.5 kHz channel, and with a few percent of errors at 9 dB below.

When another station is sending its idle signal, a line says how clean its transmitter is: the IMD, the third-order distortion against the two tones of the idle, in dB - the figure operators quote when they tell each other 'your signal is splattering'. The presets tune the USB dial frequencies of the PSK31 calling segments from 80 m to 10 m, with the carrier near 1150 Hz of audio; the figures come from one amateur frequency chart that is not dated, so check them against your own band plan. Receive only. Settings are read when the decoder starts.

PSK63 and PSK125 are the same signal at two and four times the speed (62.5 and 125 baud, about 125 and 250 Hz wide). Set 'PSK rate 31 63 125 (0 = all)' to 63 or 125, or to 0 to listen for all three rates at once (each prints under its own name, and a signal is only ever read at its own rate). The faster rates need about 3 dB and 6 dB more signal in the same noise. They have been tested on generated signals only, and no PSK63 or PSK125 was heard off the air; the presets are PSK31 frequencies.

MODE SETTING. The setting "Mode 1PSK 2Olivia 3MFSK16 4DEX" chooses what the decoder reads, one at a time: 1 = PSK31 / PSK63 / PSK125 (the default), 2 = Olivia, 3 = MFSK16, 4 = DominoEX. It is read when the decoder starts, and FoxSDR remembers it. The old settings of the four former plugins keep their meaning (the PSK ones now start with "PSK", the Olivia one with "Olivia", DominoEX keeps "DominoEX 4 5 8 11 16 22"). All four read single-sideband audio at 8000 samples a second. Every one of them was tested on generated signals only.

OLIVIA AND MFSK16 (modes 2 and 3). Reads two amateur keyboard modes from demodulated single-sideband audio: Olivia with 32 tones at 125, 250, 500, 1000 or 2000 Hz bandwidth, and MFSK16 (16 tones at 15.625 baud, with error correction). You choose the mode and, for Olivia, the bandwidth in the settings (Mode 2 = Olivia, 3 = MFSK16; Olivia bandwidth defaults to 1000 Hz, and any other value falls back to it). The decoder finds the signal inside the audio by itself and prints the text, a line when it has locked, and "signal lost" when the signal goes. A lock takes a while: about 15 seconds of signal for Olivia at 1000 Hz and about 18 seconds for MFSK16, longer for the narrower Olivia bandwidths.

The public descriptions of both modes leave some details open, such as bit order, Gray-code direction, tone order and one interleaver. The receiver does not guess one answer: it tries every reading (up to 64 for Olivia, 16 for MFSK16) and accepts one only when several blocks in a row give clean, text-like output. Pure noise, a steady carrier and tones with no code behind them gave no text in the tests.

WHAT IT WILL NOT DO / LIMITS. Tested on generated signals from the author's own transmitter only: no real Olivia or MFSK16 recording was available, so whether any of the tried readings matches what real stations send is unverified. On generated white noise it copied at least half the text down to about -14 dB signal-to-noise in 2.5 kHz (Olivia 32/1000 and MFSK16); that says nothing about real on-air performance, and below that level it simply does not lock. Contestia, Olivia with other tone counts, MFSK8/32/64 and MFSK's secondary channel are not decoded. Receive only; it writes no files, opens no network connection and changes no setting.

DOMINOEX (mode 4). DominoEX is an amateur keyboard mode by Murray Greenman ZL1BPU. It sends 18 tones, but the data is not in which tone is sent: it is in how far the tone moved from the one before (incremental frequency keying, with a fixed offset so a tone never repeats). That makes it very tolerant of tuning error and drift, so the decoder finds the tone group itself anywhere in the audio passband. Text uses a nibble varicode in which common letters take one or two tones; when the sender is idle it sends a second, 'secondary' text (often a callsign), which this decoder prints on separate lines marked [idle text].

Choose the sub-mode in the settings (DominoEX 11 is the usual one; 4, 5 and 8 are slower and more robust, 16 and 22 faster). The decoder shows when it has locked on, the text, and when the signal is gone. In the tests, which use generated signals, it reads DominoEX 11 without errors down to a signal 6 dB below the noise in 3 kHz, and DominoEX 4 down to 10 dB below; pure noise and a steady carrier give no text. DominoEX with error correction, THOR and the two fastest modes are not decoded, and it has not been checked against a real DominoEX transmission. Tune single sideband and keep all 18 tones, about 200 Hz at DominoEX 11, inside the audio passband.
plugins.whatsNew: 1.3.0: On FoxSDR 0.99.109 and later the Mode, the PSK rate and the DominoEX sub-mode are drop-down lists with names instead of number boxes; the settings and their numbers are unchanged, and an older FoxSDR still shows the number boxes, with a hint. 1.2.0: New plugin: PSK31 Decoder (1.1.0), Olivia and MFSK16 Decoder and DominoEX Decoder are now modes of one decoder. Set Mode to 1 PSK31 / PSK63 / PSK125, 2 Olivia, 3 MFSK16 or 4 DominoEX; the old settings keep their names. DominoEX now runs at 8 kHz audio like the others. Generated signals only; no PSK63, PSK125, Olivia, MFSK16 or DominoEX has been heard off the air.

plugins.name: METAR Airport Weather
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: A table of decoded airport weather reports (METAR) for the airports you name, from NOAA's Aviation Weather Center. Off until you switch it on.
plugins.description:
METAR is the coded weather report an airport issues, usually every hour, such as "EGLL 121120Z 24012KT 9999 FEW030 12/06 Q1018". Beside an airband monitor this shows what the wind, visibility, cloud and pressure are at the airports you are listening to. Type up to eight airport codes (ICAO, for example EGLL or KJFK), switch it on, and the plugin's window shows a row for each: time, wind, visibility, runway visual range, weather, sky, temperature, pressure and the raw report. Both the US form (statute miles, altimeter in inches) and the international form (metres, metres per second, CAVOK, pressure in hectopascals) are decoded; trend and remarks are kept as text. Each new report also prints one line of text in the Decoder output, and a Refresh now key asks again at once.

NETWORK: it is OFF until you switch on SHOW METAR; until then it makes no request of any kind. The service needs no key or login and none is sent. What is sent is the airport codes you typed, to aviationweather.gov, the Data API of NOAA's National Weather Service Aviation Weather Center. It asks every 10 minutes by default (you can choose 60 to 3600 seconds), never more than once a minute, and backs off to at most 30 minutes after failures; reports already held are kept through a failure and dropped after 4 hours. ALSO NEAREST TO THE RECEIVER is a separate switch, off by default. It needs the receiver's position set in FoxSDR and the plugin's permission to read it, and adds the three nearest airports. To do so it sends a box about 3 degrees square whose edges are whole degrees, built from that position; the position itself is never sent, logged or stored in a setting.

The window carries the credit "Weather data: NOAA / National Weather Service, Aviation Weather Center", and says that this is a decoded view and not for flight planning. The settings boxes appear in FoxSDR 0.99.43 and later.

WHAT IT WILL NOT DO / LIMITS: it does not decode radio; it only reads what the service publishes, and most airports report hourly, so the table is not live. It has not been tried against the real service. It was tested on a stand-in server on this computer, on the worked examples in the US Federal Meteorological Handbook No. 1 and the WMO METAR code (No. 306), and on four invented whole reports; the service's JSON field names come from its published description. It was driven through a stand-in host, not seen in a FoxSDR window.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.1.0: first release. Decoded METAR table for airports you name; off until switched on, and never tried against the real service.

plugins.name: FSK Status Telegrams: FMS and End-of-Train
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Reads German FMS status telegrams and, experimentally, North American End-of-Train telemetry bursts from FM audio; unit addresses hidden by default, receive only.
plugins.description:
The Funkmeldesystem (FMS) is the short status burst that German emergency-service radios send inside the audio of an ordinary FM voice channel: 1200 and 1800 Hz subcarrier tones at 1200 bit/s with a 7-bit check. This plugin reads those telegrams from demodulated FM audio (it asks the host for 12 kHz audio; the FM demodulator does the radio part) and prints the status, direction, stage and short information for each telegram that passes the check.

END-OF-TRAIN (EOT), EXPERIMENTAL (new in 0.2.0). The North American End-of-Train telemetry burst from the last car to the locomotive is also two-tone FSK at 1200 bit/s on FM audio, so the plugin now listens for it too, at the same time as for FMS, from the same 12 kHz audio. The burst layout (two identical 144-bit blocks, an 11-bit Barker frame sync, a 17-bit unit address, chaining, battery, message type, rear brake-pipe pressure, valve, motion and marker-light fields) is taken from expired US patents. What no free source gives is not guessed: the BCH generator polynomial of the check code is typed by you in the setting "EOT BCH generator" (19 binary digits, from the AAR standard you hold); without it a burst is shown only when two copies 0.12 s apart are identical, and says "BCH not checked". The tone pair (1200/1800 or 1200/2200 Hz, the better fit is shown), the bit order, the message-type and battery codes and the pressure scale are unconfirmed, so raw numbers are shown without a unit. The unit address is hidden by default like the FMS address (unit #n, memory only). Head-to-rear (HOT) bursts are not decoded. Tested on generated signals only; nothing off air.

PRIVACY. A telegram carries vehicle identifiers of emergency services. By default each line shows only a session tag such as veh #1, and the real address is kept in memory only. The setting Hide vehicle addresses (which also hides the End-of-Train unit address) is on by default; turning it off shows the address in the text, and with the web mirror on those lines can then leave the machine. Nothing is written to disk. Receive only and no network. The plugin prints a first line that you are responsible for receiving only what the law where you live allows; in some countries receiving these transmissions is restricted.

WHAT IT WILL NOT DO / LIMITS. Tested on generated signals only: no real FMS recording was available. Two details are not written out in the published text (the exact Barker-7 sync pattern and the order of the check bits), so the plugin uses the usual reading, and a real transmitter could differ, in which case real telegrams would fail the check. Built from the 1999 Technische Richtlinie; no channel presets are included.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.2.1: Decodes with the carrier off the dial by a kilohertz or more (before, about 250 Hz low or 600 Hz high was enough to lose every telegram). 0.2.0: End-of-Train mode (experimental: layout from expired patents, BCH generator typed by the user, generated signals only).

plugins.name: Caller ID (CLIP) Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Reads the 1200 baud V.23 caller-ID burst of a European analogue phone line from audio; numbers and names hidden by default, receive only.
plugins.description:
On a European analogue telephone line the calling line identity is sent as a short burst of 1200 baud FSK (1300 Hz for one, 2100 Hz for zero). This plugin reads that burst from demodulated audio (12 kHz) and prints the kind of message, a session tag for the caller, the date and time the exchange sent, and whether the number was withheld or unavailable. It checks the message type, length, parameter structure and checksum before showing anything.

PRIVACY. By default caller numbers, called numbers and names are not shown: each line carries a tag such as caller #2, and the real values are kept in memory only. The setting Hide caller numbers and names is on by default; turning it off shows them in the text, and with the web mirror on those lines can then leave the machine. Nothing is written to disk. Receive only and no network. The plugin prints a first line that you are responsible for receiving only what the law where you live allows.

WHAT IT WILL NOT DO / LIMITS. Tested on generated signals only: no real recording was available. In the generated tests 89 of 90 messages decoded; the one miss was a weak signal with a 0.15 percent clock error. Only the European ETSI format is built. The North American Bell 202 variant (1200/2200 Hz) is not decoded, because no free description of it was found; a test frame of that kind is not misread as a European one.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.1.1: Decodes with the carrier off the dial by a kilohertz or more (before, about 250 Hz low or 500 Hz high was enough to lose every message). 0.1.0: first release. European CLIP caller-ID bursts from audio, numbers hidden by default; generated signals only.

plugins.name: GSC Golay Pager Decoder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Finds Golay Sequential Code (GSC) paging preambles and two-word blocks in NFM audio and shows their error-corrected code words; it does not read pager numbers or messages.
plugins.description:
GSC is the Golay Sequential Code, an older Motorola paging format. This plugin listens to demodulated narrowband FM audio, finds the preamble and the two-word blocks that follow it, repairs bit errors with the (23,12) Golay code - up to three wrong bits in each word - and prints the corrected 23-bit words in hexadecimal with how many bits were repaired in each. A line looks like: GSC block w1=2D1B0F w2=4E6A55 corrected=0+1 code=A.

Two settings, both off by default: Strict, which repairs at most two bits per word so that a word with three errors is refused instead of repaired, and Show raw received words, which adds the words as received. There are no presets, because GSC channels are allocated locally.

THIS IS A STAND-IN, NOT A MESSAGE DECODER. No free source says which words are the sync, activation and address words, so those blocks are not told apart by their content and no pager number is derived. Since 0.2.0 the block one block time after a preamble is learned as the sync block and later blocks are numbered within a batch of 17, and a Known words setting takes sync and activation words you fill in from a recording. The data slots that carry numeric and alphanumeric text are not read at all; the tables for them are in a Motorola guide that could not be opened. Which of the two Golay generator polynomials a system uses is not known, so both are accepted and it locks to the one it sees (shown as code=A or code=B). The sign of an FM discriminator cannot be read from the signal, so words are shown with positive audio as 1, and an inverted channel shows the complement words.

The Golay code is perfect: a word with four or more errors is never seen as bad, it is corrected to a different valid word. Rejecting damaged blocks relies on the framing checks; in the tests, at the noise level where 55 of 60 bursts decoded, one block came out with a wrong word.

TESTED ON GENERATED SIGNALS ONLY: no GSC recording was available, and the framing comes from two expired Motorola patents and a manufacturer help page, so a real transmission may differ in details they do not give. Receive only. Nothing is written to disk or printed to a console. Intercepting messages you are not authorised to receive is an offence in many places (for example section 48 of the UK Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006); use it only where the law permits.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.2.0: Learns which block is the sync block after a preamble, numbers the slots of each batch (17 blocks to a batch), and can take a list of known words you type in. It still does not read pager numbers or messages, and it has been tried on generated signals only.

plugins.name: Voice Inversion Detector
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Says when the speech in the audio looks frequency-inverted, as a simple voice scrambler leaves it, and estimates the carrier; it only detects and never restores the speech.
plugins.description:
A simple voice scrambler mixes speech with a fixed carrier and keeps the difference, so the speech comes out upside down in frequency. This plugin listens to demodulated audio and says when speech in it looks inverted about a fixed carrier, with an estimate of that carrier. It works from the pitch structure of voiced speech, not from any content: natural speech and inverted speech put their harmonics in different places, and it tells a mirror from a simple upward shift. A line is printed when the verdict changes, about a second after it settles - for example 'speech is frequency-inverted about 3099 Hz' - and a panel shows the verdict, the carrier, how consistent it is and how many voiced frames stand behind it.

IT IS A DETECTOR ONLY. It never produces or plays audio and never undoes the inversion; the plugin declares no audio output, and its own test checks that. Nothing is written to disk and no speech is kept, only a few numbers in memory. There are no presets: it listens to whatever audio is open.

WHAT IT WILL NOT DO / LIMITS: it needs about a second of voiced speech with a moving pitch; whispered or unvoiced speech gives no verdict. A carrier outside 1200 to 4500 Hz, a changing carrier, a split-band scrambler or encrypted voice is not detected. When the pitch hardly moves, the carrier may be known only to a multiple of the pitch, and the line says so.

TESTED ON GENERATED SPEECH-LIKE AUDIO AND ONE REAL RECORDING: a real dispatch recording (about 11 seconds of speech, one speaker) was read as natural, and the same recording inverted by software at five carriers was detected within 1 Hz, also with added noise at one carrier. A real recording of KiwiSDR audio with no speech gave no alarm. No recording of a real hardware voice inverter was available, so how it behaves with a real scrambler's band-limiting and carrier leakage, and with other speakers and channels, is untested.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.1.0: first release. Detects fixed-carrier inverted speech and estimates the carrier; detection only, tried on generated and software-inverted speech but not on a real hardware voice inverter.

plugins.name: FPV Video Link Detector
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Tells you whether an analogue 5.8 GHz FPV video link is on air in the tuned window, how strong it is, whether it is 625-line or 525-line and for how long. It never makes a picture.
plugins.description:
Analogue FPV video transmitters use a small set of named 5.8 GHz channels (the A, B, E, F and R tables). This plugin watches the window you have tuned and reports when an analogue video link appears: present or gone, the level in the window and over its floor, the line rate it measures (about 15.6 kHz for 625-line, PAL-like; about 15.7 kHz for 525-line, NTSC-like), how long it lasted, and the channel names from the tables within 3 MHz of the tuned centre. It has 39 presets, one for each distinct frequency in the tables, and it decides about a fifth of a second after the signal starts.

It is a detector only. There is no frame store, no line store, no video level and no sync separator; the only things made of the signal are two power spectra a few kilohertz wide, looked at for the line rate. No picture is ever produced. It has no settings, and nothing is stored, written to disk or sent anywhere. It is receive only, and it does not scan: you tune it, and nothing steps the receiver for you. It needs I/Q at 2 MS/s or more; it used about 8 percent of one processor core at 8 MS/s and 16 percent at 20 MS/s.

WHAT IT WILL NOT DO / LIMITS. Tested on generated signals only: no 5.8 GHz recording and no real FPV link was available, so how it behaves on a real link, with its real deviation, video bandwidth and pre-emphasis, is unproven. The channel table rests on manufacturer documents, but band B and two channels of band E rest on a single hobby page. It does not show the picture or the carrier offset, and it looks for analogue video only. The legal status of receiving 5.8 GHz video where you live was not checked.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.1.1: exact digital silence is no longer reported as a link (it printed present at -99 dBFS after a short burst). 0.1.0: first release. Detects analogue 5.8 GHz FPV video links and reports level, 625-line or 525-line, duration and channel name; no picture. Tested on generated signals only.

plugins.name: Signal Identifier (MIL-STD-188-110, STANAG 4285, PACTOR and reference table)
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Measures the signals in your receiver's I/Q against a built-in reference table, and runs three named detectors on USB audio: the HF Modem Identifier (MIL-STD-188-110), the STANAG 4285 Identifier and the PACTOR Monitor (PACTOR-II and PACTOR-III). They identify only and decode nothing.
plugins.description:
Give it the receiver's live I/Q, or the path of an I/Q recording, and it finds each occupied signal and measures it: centre, occupied bandwidth, spectral lines, keying and burst structure, symbol rate, and a modulation class (AM, narrow and wide FM, SSB, CW, FSK, PSK, QAM, OFDM, noise-like and others; for PSK and QAM it names the class, not the order). It then compares those measurements with a reference table of 97 signals (amateur, aircraft, marine, paging, broadcast, time, navigation, satellite, sensors, utility and numbers-station TYPES) and shows the best three with a confidence, or 'unknown' when nothing fits. It shows up as many signals at once as the Most signals to report setting allows (1 to 24, 8 by default; the panel showed four before 0.4.0). The confidence is a share between the candidates and a fixed allowance for 'not in the table'; it is not a probability.

It also looks, in captures of 2 seconds or more, for an RSID identification burst (15 tones) and reports its tone numbers and the frequency of its first tone. It names the mode only from a code table that you supply; none is shipped, because the construction that turns a mode number into the tones was not available from any source the project could use.

Three detectors listen to demodulated USB audio, each with its own tick box in the settings (all on by default; all three together use under 2 % of one core): the HF Modem Identifier finds the MIL-STD-188-110 serial-tone preamble and says the data rate and interleaver it announces, and the tone header of the 188-110A-MOD hybrid waveform; the STANAG 4285 Identifier says when the repeating frame structure of STANAG 4285 is present and when it is gone; the PACTOR Monitor finds PACTOR-II and PACTOR-III bursts and says the tone set, the speed level, the packet kind and the cycle. Each reports in its own words in the decoder output. They identify only: no message is read, nothing is stored or sent, and no network is used. All three were tried on generated signals only (no recording of these waveforms was available), so their thresholds are untested on real fading HF channels. The reference-table match is a tick box too (on). Their limits: the HF Modem Identifier does not follow mid-stream mode changes; STANAG 4285's preamble, probe symbols and pulse shape are unchecked on a real signal; PACTOR-II order is shown as "3 or 4" where it cannot be told apart, and PACTOR-I and IV are not recognised.

WHAT DEPENDS ON DATA. The reference table is built into the plugin (97 rows, each with its source address and a status). Of those, 47 were checked against a primary page (ITU-R, ETSI, US regulations and similar), 39 only against Wikipedia, and 11 could not be confirmed and are shown as unverified; even checked rows have fields that could not be confirmed, and the bandwidths are ranges a measurement could show, not exact widths. You can add your own rows with an extra table file, and a code table for RSID names. The plugin uses no database or service on the internet and has no network access.

LICENCE AND PRIVACY LIMITS. Only facts (numbers and names) were taken from the sources; no text, sound or picture is copied. Wikipedia material is CC BY-SA 4.0 and its credit is recorded in the project. No sample sounds or pictures are shipped, because the Signal Identification Wiki states no licence. No broadcast schedules are shipped, because the one complete schedule source is licensed for non-commercial use only; numbers stations appear as signal types (a buzzer, voice, Morse, digital), and a station cannot be told apart by measuring the radio signal. The plugin keeps only properties of the signal (where, how wide, how it keys and modulates) in memory for the latest analysis, writes nothing to disk, prints nothing to the console (the detectors below report in the decoder output) and receives only.

HOW WELL IT WORKS (the reference-table match; the three detectors are described above). It is modest. It was run on real recordings from a local sample folder, many of which are audio put on a carrier or processed audio rather than radio captures, and part of them were used to set its thresholds. The right table entry was among the three shown for 52 to 56 percent of the recordings and was the first for 25 to 39 percent. It did well on RTTY, CW, SSTV, FLEX, EAS, VHF DSC, DAB, VDL2, TETRA, VHF ACARS and VOR, and badly on bursts of very unequal strength (AIS), wide signals that fill the capture (ADS-B, ERT), pagers recorded as processed audio, simultaneous tones and look-alike FSK families (NXDN, M17, P25, DMR). On generated signals the class was right in 24 of 24 trials at 30 dB, 22 of 24 at 15 dB and 12 of 24 at 8 dB, and white noise gave no signal in 40 captures. It has only been run against a stand-in host, never inside FoxSDR on a live radio, so the live path is untested. Treat every verdict as a lead, not an answer.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.4.2: A service is no longer offered for a signal far outside its band (a 2.44 GHz burst had been named ADS-B / Mode S at 1090 MHz, and signals at 162 MHz or 405 MHz had been named Loran-C or DRM), and an FM signal with a clean data-rate clock line is no longer called Narrow FM voice (a real RS41 radiosonde carrier was). 0.4.1: Names a strong FM broadcast station as FM broadcast (stereo): its 38 kHz stereo subcarrier had been read as a data signal, so every strong real station came out unknown or as a satellite downlink. Checked on real recordings. 0.4.0: A setting for the most signals to report (1 to 24, 8 by default); the panel showed only four however many the analysis found. Generated signals only. 0.3.0: Adds three detectors, each with its own tick box and all on by default: the HF Modem Identifier (MIL-STD-188-110), the STANAG 4285 Identifier and the PACTOR Monitor (PACTOR-II and III). They identify only and say what they see in their own words. The reference-table match is now a tick box too (on). The detectors were tried on generated signals only. 0.1.0: first release (the reference-table match).

plugins.name: Fox Hunt Homing Aid
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Turns the received signal level into a rising pitch or faster beeps, with a peak-hold bar, to help you find a hidden transmitter.
plugins.description:
A homing aid for transmitter hunts. It reads the signal level of the channel you have tuned and turns it into a tone you can hear while you move or turn the aerial: the stronger the signal, the higher the pitch, the faster the beeping, or both. A window shows the level as a bar with a held-peak marker, the reading, the scale and the tone in use.

The tone is mixed into the audio you are already hearing, after the receiver's own squelch and AGC and before volume and mute, so your volume and mute controls act on it. A setting makes it play the tone only and mute the programme. You choose the scale (bottom and top level), the curve, the lowest and highest pitch, the slowest and fastest beep rate, the tone volume, how quickly the reading rises and falls, and how long the peak is held before it falls back (or latch it until you press Reset peak).

Attenuator offset: type the number of dB of attenuation you have added in front of the receiver and it is added to every reading. Atten + and Atten - keys instead lower or raise the receiver's own gain stage in steps you set, and the reading is corrected for the gain taken off; this needs the 'radio settings' permission on the plugin's row, and without it the window says the request was refused. Stages that are set in steps rather than in dB are never touched.

WHAT IT WILL NOT DO / LIMITS. It does not find a direction - it only tells you how strong the signal is. Levels are dB relative to the receiver's full scale, not calibrated dBm. It writes no file, sends nothing over the network and prints nothing. It has been tested on generated level sequences and against a stand-in host only: it has not been used on a real hunt, and it has not been checked that the receiver's level really falls dB for dB when the gain is lowered, or that the tone keeps sounding while the squelch is closed. The window can only show text and a character bar. The Atten and Reset keys are read only while the window is open.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.1.0: first release. Tested on generated level sequences and a stand-in host only, not on a real hunt.

plugins.name: Meteor Scatter Ping Counter
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Counts meteor echoes on a steady VHF carrier, such as 143.050 MHz, per hour, and can save the counts to files.
plugins.description:
Meteor-scatter observing: a distant transmitter's steady carrier is normally too far away to hear, and each meteor trail briefly reflects it towards you as a short burst. This plugin watches a narrow window around the carrier (143.050 MHz by default; you set the frequency), notes every echo as a ping, and counts them per hour.

For each ping it records the start time, the duration, the Doppler offset, the peak signal-to-noise ratio and level, and a class: head (a large Doppler offset, 300 Hz or more), long (2 seconds or more) or trail (the rest). Those classes and their limits are this plugin's own working rule, not a published standard, and you can change the limits. The window shows the state, this hour, last hour and today's counts, the last ping, a 24-hour table in UTC and the most recent pings, and a marker is put on the spectrum at the carrier. It learns the background noise for about 8 seconds on start, and says so if the carrier is outside the band you are receiving. It works on raw I/Q at any sample rate; 250 kS/s is the preferred rate, and a very wide rate costs a lot of processor time.

Saving files is OFF until you tick Save files. Then it appends, in a folder you choose (by default Documents/SDR-recordings), a daily CSV of pings, a monthly CSV of hours with the head, trail and long split and the seconds actually watched, and an RMOB-style monthly .dat file (appended) with one row per finished hour watched for at least 50 minutes, and an RMOB .txt table that is rewritten whole and merged with earlier runs. Reset counts and Export now keys are on its plate. The files hold only times, counts and levels, nothing about you. It never deletes anything and nothing is uploaded.

WHAT IT WILL NOT DO / LIMITS. It has been tested on generated signals only; no recording of a real carrier or real meteor echoes was available, so the count on a real aerial is untried. In tests with white noise it gave no false pings in 12 hours, and it found nearly all pings 17 dB or more above the noise but about 8 in 10 at 12 dB and fewer below that; real interference is not white noise, so expect more false counts. The RMOB-style file follows the one third-party description of the format that could be found and has not been checked against RMOB itself, which publishes no format; RMOB upload is not built, so you send the file yourself. The default threshold (12 dB over the noise) and minimum ping length (64 ms) favour few false counts over sensitivity.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.1.1: Also writes the RMOB-style monthly text table (MMYYYYrmob.txt), merged across runs. It needs one real RMOB file to confirm the layout; tested on generated signals only, not on real meteor echoes.

plugins.name: Touchstone Viewer
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Opens an antenna analyser or VNA sweep file (.s1p or .s2p) and plots SWR, return loss, impedance and a Smith chart.
plugins.description:
Reads a Touchstone file - the .s1p and .s2p files that a network analyser or an antenna analyser exports - and draws it as a picture: SWR, return loss, magnitude, phase, impedance (resistance and reactance) and a Smith chart. You type the file's path or browse for it, and the plot re-reads the file when it changes on disk.

Up to six markers can be typed as frequencies (for example 145.5M, 433M, 1.2G); each is listed in the window with its SWR, return loss and impedance, and for a two-port file the S21 gain and phase. Keys step through the plots and through the four traces (S11, S21, S12, S22) and reload the file. A reference impedance setting re-references the display. The window also shows the lowest and highest SWR and the best return loss across the sweep.

It understands Touchstone versions 1.0, 1.1, 2.0 and 2.1: frequency units Hz to GHz, S, Y, Z, H and G parameters, and the RI, MA and DB number formats. It uses no radio and no network, and writes no file.

WHAT IT WILL NOT DO / LIMITS. It does not talk to a NanoVNA or any other instrument - export the file (since 0.2.0 a NanoVNA shell capture saved to a file can be read too) and open that. Files with three or more ports or mixed-mode data, more than 200,000 points or over 32 MiB are refused with a sentence saying why, as are H and G files with a reference other than 1 ohm. Noise data in a file is ignored. It has been checked against the specification's own worked examples and calculated networks, and against many damaged files, but no real instrument file was available. It has not been checked that FoxSDR shows the picture when no radio is running; the panel and keys do not depend on that.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.2.0: Reads a NanoVNA shell capture saved to a file and draws it like any other sweep. There is no serial connection to an instrument, and no real NanoVNA was tried.

plugins.name: Clip Uploader
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Watches a folder of finished recordings and sends each new clip, with its frequency and time, to a server on your own machine or LAN. Off until you switch it on.
plugins.description:
Watches a folder of finished audio recordings (wav, mp3, m4a, flac and ogg by default) and sends each new clip to a web address you choose, with the details a scanner-style server wants: the frequency, mode, start time, duration and a system name you type. The clip itself goes as an ordinary form upload. Frequency and mode come from a small <clip name>.json file beside the clip if there is one, otherwise from the receiver's state when the clip was found finished, which can differ from when it was recorded; the duration is read from the WAV header.

IT IS OFF BY DEFAULT. Until you tick Upload clips and name a folder, it watches nothing and opens no network connection. Clips already in the folder when you switch it on are not sent, a clip is sent only after it has stopped growing, and clips over a size limit (25 MB by default) are skipped and counted. A failed send is tried three times, a refusal by the server (such as 404) is final, and a full queue drops the oldest clip and counts it. The window shows the queue, what was sent, failed, dropped and skipped, and the last result.

WHAT IT WILL NOT DO / LIMITS. It uses plain http only: there is no encryption. The default target is this machine (http://127.0.0.1:8080/upload). It never looks up a name - the address must be a number or localhost - and a public address is always refused. A private network address is accepted only if you tick the separate box for it, and then the clip, its frequency, mode, time and your system name cross your network unencrypted. There is no password, key or token field, nothing is stored, and no login is sent, so it cannot reach services such as Broadcastify, OpenMHz or a hosted rdio-scanner. The upload field names are this plugin's own, so a server that expects different names will not accept the clip. It has been tested only against a stand-in server on this machine, never a real service, and FoxSDR has no squelch-clip recorder, so it works on any folder of finished recordings.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.1.0: first release. Off by default and limited to this machine or an explicitly allowed private LAN over plain http; tested only against a stand-in server.

plugins.name: Effect Chain
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Runs the audio you hear through up to eight effects in an order you set, with wet/dry mix and bypass. It can load third-party VST3 effects that you supply yourself.
plugins.description:
Passes the final audio of the receiver through a chain of up to eight effect stages, in the order you give, before it reaches your speakers. A stage is a VST3 effect (a .vst3 file or package) that you put in a folder yourself, or one of the small test effect modules (.dll) used to check the plugin. Each stage has a wet percentage and can be bypassed on its own, and the whole chain has a bypass that returns the audio unchanged. Each stage's own delay is added up, kept in time with the dry path so bypassing never makes a jump, and shown in the window with the effect's name, its state, its parameters and its processor use.

YOU SUPPLY THE EFFECTS. The plugin ships none and never downloads or installs any. Nothing is loaded until you name an effects folder; the window then lists the .vst3 files in it (listing runs none of them) and loads only the ones you name in the stage list. Network folders and path tricks are refused. An effect that will not load, is not an effect, will not start, or does not fit mono or stereo audio is reported in plain words in the window and the log, never as a dialog box, and the audio goes on untouched. An effect's parameters are set in one text row (stage:parameter=value, for example 2:0=0.5) and take effect without reloading it. The state an effect keeps of its own (beyond those parameters) is saved a moment after you change them, up to 3000 bytes per stage, and given back to the same effect the next time it loads; a damaged or oversized saved state is refused with a plain sentence and the effect starts from its own settings.

WHAT IT CAN AND CANNOT CONTAIN. An effect runs inside FoxSDR's own process, with FoxSDR's rights: it is someone else's program and there is no sandbox. If an effect crashes, hangs while loading or while playing, is too slow or returns invalid numbers, that stage is bypassed (a crashed one is not called again until you reload) and you are told once. By default each stage runs on its own thread and the audio waits for it at most a set time per block (8 ms); three bad blocks in a row bypass the stage. Run stages inline removes the wait but then cannot survive a hang. What this cannot stop: an effect that corrupts memory or overflows a stack can still take the whole program down, and an effect that does something harmful on purpose is not stopped at all. Load only effects you trust.

LIMITS. Audio effects only: no instruments, no effect windows, no list of an effect's own presets, no MIDI, no side-chain, mono or stereo only. FoxSDR cannot be told about the chain's delay, so the delay is shown only in this plugin's window. Tested with small effects written for the test and with a stand-in host, not in the full application and with no third-party effect; a real third-party effect may behave differently. Windows only. The plugin has no network code and prints nothing.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.3.0: an effect's own saved state is kept with the chain and given back at the next load (up to 3000 bytes a stage; a damaged one is refused in plain words). 0.2.0: loads VST3 effects that you supply: scans a folder you name, sets effect parameters, bypasses and unloads them, and says in plain words when one cannot be used. Tested with small effects written for the test, never with a third-party effect. A crashing or hanging effect is bypassed; one that corrupts memory can still stop FoxSDR.
plugins.legalNotice: VST is a registered trademark of Steinberg Media Technologies GmbH. This plugin is built with the Steinberg VST 3 SDK, which is under the MIT licence (copyright 2026 Steinberg Media Technologies GmbH); the licence text is in the plugin's notice file. The effects you load are other people's programs, run inside FoxSDR without a sandbox, and are not supplied, checked or supported by this project.

plugins.name: Window Recorder
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Records FoxSDR's own main window to a video or picture files, only when you tick the box, name a folder and press Start.
plugins.description:
Records the FoxSDR main window - only that window - to a file, so you can keep a short video of a decode or a pass. It finds the window because it runs inside the same program, and takes its pictures from that window alone: another window lying on top is not in the picture, and a window belonging to another program is refused. It does not read the rest of the screen, the desktop, the keyboard or the clipboard, and it has no network code.

IT IS OFF BY DEFAULT. A recording starts only when you have ticked Recording allowed, named a folder, and pressed Start; each missing step is refused and the reason logged. While it runs, the window shows RECORDING with the time, and the host log says so. A Stop key ends it; it also stops by itself at a time limit (60 seconds by default, up to 3600), a size limit (500 MB by default, up to 1900 MB), when the window closes or when the disk fills, and the finished file is complete. Files are named with the date and time, go only into the folder you named, and an existing file is never overwritten.

Formats: avi (uncompressed, large), png (a folder of pictures) and mp4 (H.264 through the encoder built into Windows, where it is present). Pictures per second default to 10. A minimised window gives skipped pictures, counted; a window resized mid-recording is cropped or padded in black to the first size.

WHAT IT WILL NOT DO / LIMITS. It records no sound. It has been tried on stand-in windows only: it has not been run against the real FoxSDR window, which may come out black or partly drawn with this capture method. Writing to a full disk was tested with an injected failure, not a real full disk, and mp4 on a Windows without the media components is untested. Windows only.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.1.0: first release. Off until you allow it, tick the box and start it; tested on stand-in windows, not on the real FoxSDR window.

plugins.name: AM Stereo (C-QUAM)
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Plays an AM stereo (C-QUAM compatible) station in stereo. Tried on generated signals only.
plugins.description:
Takes raw I/Q, finds the carrier of an AM stereo station itself, locks to it and plays left and right through the host's audio output: the sum from the signal's envelope, the difference from its phase. It asks for the speakers after one second of lock and gives them back after two seconds without. A mono AM station locks too and plays as two identical channels.
