Wire it to a Channel centred on the station, or to a Radio with the station within 8 kHz of the centre; any input rate from 16 kS/s up works. It is written from two expired Motorola patents (read through a summarising page tool, not as full text); no other program's code was used. C-QUAM is a Motorola trademark, used only to name the system.

WHAT IT WILL NOT DO / LIMITS. There is no pilot-tone check: the patents it was written from do not contain the 25 Hz pilot, so a stereo-or-mono indicator and the polarity check are not built. It has been tried on generated signals only (channel separation 42 to 59 dB there); behaviour on real stations, over-modulation, selective fading and 9 kHz channels is untested. Freedom from any other patent is not established.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.1.1: a station found exactly on a whole frequency bin (3000.0 Hz from the centre at 48 kS/s, for one) now separates left and right; its start phase was wrong. 0.1.0: first release. Stereo from AM stereo (C-QUAM compatible) stations; tested on generated signals only.

plugins.name: Rig Link (DXLab Commander, N1MM+, FLRig)
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Follows the frequency and mode of DXLab Commander, N1MM+ or FLRig on this PC. Read-only: it never sends FoxSDR's frequency, or anything else, to those programs. Off until you switch a back-end on.
plugins.description:
Follows the frequency of the rig-control program or contest logger running on this PC. For DXLab Commander it polls the rig's receive frequency (and mode, if you ask) over TCP, by default to 127.0.0.1 port 52002; for N1MM+ it listens for RadioInfo broadcasts on 127.0.0.1 (port 12060 by default, added in N1MM+'s Broadcast Data list), follows radio 1 or 2, marks the logger's frequency on the waterfall and counts contacts logged. It only follows: it never keys a rig and never changes anything on a rig or sends anything to the rig program.

FLRig (a program you run, controlling your radio) is followed through its XML-RPC server: type the port that FLRig's own server settings show, and the plugin asks it three read-only questions (the radio's name, frequency and mode) every 1 to 60 seconds. It can not change anything on the radio. Not tested against a real FLRig: the request path, its default port and the exact text of its answers are unconfirmed.

EVERYTHING IS OFF BY DEFAULT. Until you switch a source on in the settings the plugin opens no socket and sends nothing. Following needs the TUNE permission on this plugin's row (following the mode needs SETTINGS); the panel says so when it is missing. A callsign looked up in N1MM+ labels one marker for 30 seconds and is never printed, logged or stored.

LIMITS. It was written from DXLab's command document, the N1MM+ maker's page and FLRig's description of its server and tested only against stand-ins on loopback, not against the real programs. The N1MM+ port 12060 is also the default of the DX Spots plugin's logger feed; if you run both, give one of them another port.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.3.0: read-only. The settings that sent FoxSDR's frequency to Commander and N1MM+ (and the Commander decimal sign) are gone; the plugin only follows the rig. 0.2.0: first release. DXLab Commander, N1MM+ and FLRig back-ends, all off by default. Tested against stand-ins only.

plugins.name: P25 Trunk Follower
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Reads the control channel of a P25 Phase 1 trunked system and lists the talkgroup grants, and can follow a talkgroup you list. Following is off by default; encrypted calls are never followed. No voice.
plugins.description:
Tune the control channel of a P25 trunked system (48 kHz FM discriminator audio). The plugin finds the frame sync, corrects the network identifier, reads the trunking blocks and prints lines such as "P25: TG 1001 -> 852.2500 MHz", with EMERGENCY and ENCRYPTED (not followed) marked, plus the site and network lines. It decodes no voice.

FOLLOWING IS OFF BY DEFAULT. It needs the setting switched on, a list of talkgroups you give, and the TUNE permission on this plugin's row. plugins.name: Falcon 9 Legacy Telemetry
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Reads recordings of the Falcon 9 second stage S-band downlink made before April 2021, when it was reportedly not encrypted; tried on generated signals only. Receive only.
plugins.description:
Reads raw I/Q recordings (5.5 MS/s or more) of the Falcon 9 second stage telemetry downlink. It demodulates the signal, finds the frame marker, undoes the scrambling, corrects errors with Reed-Solomon, reassembles the packets and counts them by identifier. It prints the stage's text debug log lines, the time stamps of the GPS packets, and, only if you type a file path, writes the video packets as an MPEG transport stream without overwriting an existing file.

GPS RECEIVER LOG (new in 0.2.0). The stage's text debug log includes the log of its GPS receiver, and the free sources describe only that log, not the binary GPS packets. The plugin now reads those lines as data: the position fix (latitude, longitude and height, worked out from the logged solution as WGS-84), PDOP, the number of satellites used, the GPS week and time of the fix, the satellites tracked per group, the carrier-to-noise range and mean, and the receiver's events (tracking, hot start, PLL stress, channels dropped). Log text is joined across packets per downlink frequency, a line that may have lost its end is never read, and a fix that is not on or near the earth is counted as "ignored" and never shown as a position. The text output gets "[GPS log]" lines and the panel a "GPS RECEIVER LOG" block; they follow the "Show debug-log text" setting. The line formats come from a published decode of a recording made in March 2021; the plugin itself was tried on generated signals only, and that the logged x, y and z are WGS-84 earth-centred coordinates is assumed, not stated by the log.

The downlink has been reported encrypted since April 2021 (from secondary reports; the operator made no statement that was found). The plugin holds no key and tries nothing against encryption. When it sees marker hits that do not decode, it says "encrypted or not Falcon 9" and outputs nothing for those frames.

LIMITS. It has been tried on generated signals only; no recording of this downlink was available. Which CRC-16 the packets use is not known: eleven are tried and until one is confirmed on three frames the packets are labelled unverified. The binary layouts of the GPS time, raw measurement and position packets are not documented in any source used, so those packets are counted and time-stamped, not interpreted.

plugins.name: Radar Sweep
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Finds the secondary radars around you from the Mode A/C replies aircraft give them, using ADS-B aircraft as references, then gives rough bearings and, where two radars' bearings cross, a position for an aircraft without ADS-B.
plugins.description:
Secondary surveillance radars turn and interrogate every transponder their beam crosses, and the aircraft answer in Mode A/C. Aircraft that broadcast ADS-B answer too, and they also say where they are - so each one shows where a radar's beam was pointing at that moment. From many of them this plugin works out each radar's site, how often it turns and which way. After that, an aircraft that answers Mode A/C but broadcasts no position gets a bearing line from each radar that lights it, and where two radars' lines cross it gets a position, shown with its squawk and flight level. It is the same idea as PlanePlotter's Beamfinder, except that Beamfinder is given the radar stations' positions and this plugin works them out itself; it is not made or endorsed by COAA, PlanePlotter's authors.

IT NEEDS HOURS, NOT MINUTES, AND RESULTS DEPEND ON WHERE YOU ARE. A radar's site is only found from ADS-B aircraft spread around it in different directions, so plan on leaving it running for hours in busy airspace; a quiet spot, or traffic all on one airway, is not enough. Tested on a 12.8-hour recording: 82,283 of 94,122 beam dwells (87%) matched to 470 ADS-B aircraft, and two radars' rotations were confirmed - 7.478 s and 7.479 s, 2.1 km and 4.7 km from the published reference points of the two aerodromes they are believed to serve (a radar head's own position is not published, so this is a proximity check, never a fixture). A third, 4.094 s, has a candidate site - found but not confirmed in that recording. Until a site is confirmed the radar is listed in the plugin's panel as calibrating and nothing is drawn for it; after a restart a site confirmed before is drawn marked as stored until fresh aircraft agree with it again.

SITES AND FIXES CARRY THEIR OWN UNCERTAINTY (+/- km) ON THE MAP AND IN THE PANEL; A BEARING LINE DOES NOT, since one line alone has nothing to cross it and bound it. A two-radar fix needs two lines crossing at 15 degrees or more. Single-radar (same-pulse) ranging uses one radar's own bearing plus a second aircraft answering the same interrogations to range the target directly from that one radar; it would only ever be drawn once a SECOND, independent same-pulse fix of the same aircraft (a genuinely different antenna rotation, a genuinely different reference aircraft) agrees with the first, because either alone inherits a bearing bias real hardware measurably has. This version computes and measures single-radar ranging but does not draw it: leave-one-out validation on the same 12.8-hour recording (hiding one aircraft's identity at a time, corroboration checked with drawing forced on to measure what it would find) - of 30 aircraft with enough reference dwells, 23 got a bearing (median error 0.30 deg, 90th percentile 1.12 deg), and single-radar ranging produced no candidate position for any of them. No aircraft, real or held out, ever got a two-radar crossing fix in this recording either. A same-pulse fix needs a second aircraft sharing the radar's pulses, and 87% of dwells came from ADS-B aircraft, which leaves few opportunities in busy, well-equipped airspace like this recording's; single-radar ranging is computed but not drawn, because a longer or busier recording would be needed to give the corroboration check a genuine match. The receiver's own position is never given to the plugin; it is worked out from pairs of ADS-B aircraft sharing one radar's pulses, and is never shown, stored, or sent anywhere. It has not been tested here on military aircraft.

The map shows the confirmed radars with their uncertainty ellipses, their most recent bearing lines, the fixes, and the ADS-B aircraft being used as references. It needs 1090 MHz at 2 MS/s or more (its preset sets 2.4 MS/s) and says so when the radio is slower. It runs its own ADS-B decoding beside the Mode A/C detector: measured 2026-09-28 at about 151 ms of decoding time per second of signal, next to about 118 ms for the ADS-B plugin on the same recording. Only one copy decodes at a time: a second Radar Sweep on the patch page waits, and takes over if the first one stops. On FoxSDR 0.99.31 or later the radars it has found are remembered across restarts; a stored radar that fresh aircraft contradict is re-checked and replaced automatically. Older versions work but start again each time. Written clean-room from the published Mode A/C and Mode S specifications.

WHERE IT WORKS: nothing in the plugin is specific to one country - it needs 1090 MHz, ADS-B aircraft and secondary radars within range, and uses no regional data table. It was tested on one recording made in the United Kingdom; it has not been tested elsewhere. Whether you may use it where you are is for you to check (see the legal notice).

Whether you may receive and use these signals is a matter of the law where you are, and the law differs from country to country: in the United Kingdom, for example, it is an offence under section 48 of the Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006 to intercept a message you are not authorised to receive or to disclose its contents. It is your responsibility to check that receiving and using these signals is lawful where you are before you run this plugin. It is available to everyone, and is distributed separately from the application, so that installing it is your informed decision.

plugins.name: Frequency Counter
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Measures the frequency of a steady carrier near the tuned channel from the receiver's I/Q, and says separately how precise the measurement is and how far the radio's own clock may be wrong. Off until you switch it on.
plugins.description:
A counter that gives a number and says how sure it is. It finds the strongest steady carrier within a window around the tuned channel (5 kHz either side by default), measures the carrier's phase over a gate time you choose (0.1 to 10 s, 1 s by default) and fits it, so the reading is the frequency averaged over the gate, with the precision of the fit (a few millihertz) and a drift figure. A panel shows the frequency, the fit precision, the scatter really seen between readings, the radio-clock term, the carrier-to-noise ratio, the level, the drift and the spread of the readings; one line of text is printed for each reading.

ITS ACCURACY IS THE ACCURACY OF YOUR RADIO'S CLOCK, AND THE COUNTER CANNOT KNOW THAT. The fit precision it prints is how well one gate's samples fix the carrier against the radio's own sample clock; it is not the error of the frequency. A radio's clock is out by parts per million (1 ppm is 145 Hz at 145 MHz) and wanders from one reading to the next by about a hertz or more (measured on real carriers), so the panel shows the scatter between readings, and says the clock error is not known unless you state a tolerance in Radio clock tolerance (+-ppm), when it prints a total uncertainty that includes it. The counter measures against the radio's own reference: a reading is the radio's idea of the frequency. Tune a carrier whose frequency you know (a time-signal station, a GPS-locked source) and enter the radio's error in Radio clock correction (ppm); every later reading is corrected by it. A reading is refused, and says why, when no carrier is above the minimum carrier-to-noise ratio (15 dB by default) or when the carrier does not hold still (modulated, or drifting fast). It is a counter for carriers and keyed carriers, not for modulated signals. One reading takes the gate time plus about a third of a second.

Tested on generated I/Q only, at several sample rates, with noise, a radio clock error, a drifting carrier, two carriers and noise alone; it has never been compared with a real frequency counter. It listens to nothing but the receiver's samples, sends nothing and writes nothing.
plugins.whatsNew: 0.1.1: The uncertainty is no longer printed as if it were the accuracy. The fit precision, the scatter between readings and the radio-clock term are shown apart (a real carrier read about 1.5 Hz apart reading to reading against a printed 0.007 Hz); a new setting states the radio clock's tolerance in ppm and a total uncertainty then includes it. 0.1.0: New. Frequency of a steady carrier with its uncertainty, gate time, drift and a clock correction in ppm. Generated I/Q only.

plugins.name: SID Monitor
plugins.author: FoxSDR project
plugins.licence: Free to use, source not published
plugins.summary: Logs the level of a few very-low-frequency carriers you name, to show sudden ionospheric disturbances as steps. Off until you switch it on.
plugins.description:
A sudden ionospheric disturbance (a solar flare, for example) changes how well a very-low-frequency transmitter is received over a long path: its carrier steps up or down for minutes or hours. This plugin watches up to eight carriers that YOU name (frequency in kHz and a name of your own, for example "24.0 Alpha, 19.8 Bravo"), measures each one's level and the noise beside it every log interval (10 s by default), shows the level, the signal-to-noise ratio and the change in a window, and flags a carrier that has moved by the threshold (3 dB by default) against the median of the previous minutes (10 by default) for two intervals running. It can write one CSV file a day (time in UTC, name, frequency, level, noise, signal-to-noise, state) under Documents/SDR-recordings/SID, and can post a change to FoxSDR's own event feed, where the Event Outputs plugin can pick it up. The CSV file and the event feed are both off until you switch them on; nothing is ever sent to an outside service by this plugin.

No table of transmitters is shipped: you type the carriers. The receiver has to be able to hear them (a very-low-frequency receiver, an up-converter or direct sampling) and the carrier must lie inside the delivered band; one that does not is shown as out of band. Levels are UNCALIBRATED dBFS of your receiver chain: a step means something, the absolute number does not. The measurement bandwidth (100 Hz by default) must be wider than your receiver's frequency error, or the carrier falls out of the bin; an up-converter with a known oscillator error can be corrected in Receiver frequency error. The noise figure is exact only when the carrier is not much stronger than about 50 dB above the noise in the bandwidth.

Experimental: proved on generated signals only (a carrier with noise, a frequency offset and a sample-rate error; steps; a strong neighbour); it has never been run on a real very-low-frequency signal. With eight carriers it uses about 0.5% of one processor core at 192 kS/s and about 6.5% at 2.4 MS/s on the development machine, in proportion to the sample rate.

The decoder itself is a separate program that you add; this small plugin starts it, feeds it the signal of the radio you give it, and shows what it decodes and how it is doing (running, restarted, stalled, stopped and why). Several companions can run at the same time, each on its own radio. This program cannot hide identifiers: whatever it decodes (callsigns, addresses, serial numbers, message text) is shown exactly as the program prints it. The program's source is published at https://github.com/wonderingStars/foxsdr-companions.

Modes and what to search for: AX.25 1200 baud (APRS and packet radio); AX.25 300 baud (HF packet); AX.25 9600 baud.

Search words: afsk aprs ax25 fx25 g3ruh hf il2p packet tnc.
